units.title: Introduction to software architecture
units.description: Explain architectural decisions, compare intended and implemented structures, and choose views and patterns for a system.

chapters.title: Why software needs architecture
paragraphs: Software supports everyday activities, and a large system can exceed what any one developer can understand at once. The historical codebase examples in the slides illustrate growth and complexity. Their exact line counts are snapshots, not a measure of design quality or a rule for when architecture becomes necessary.

Complexity creates practical questions: where should a change go, what might it break, how can we inspect security and quality, and how will the system run and evolve? Architecture provides a manageable account of important parts, their relationships, and the decisions that constrain them. It connects a problem and its requirements to a solution that developers can implement and test.

The engineering analogy in the slides emphasizes planning, coordination, and checking the result. It does not require every decision to be completed before coding. Architectural reasoning can continue as implementation and feedback reveal new constraints. Maintenance and evolution make preserving the reasons behind important decisions valuable.
chapters.prediction: Two systems have the same number of source lines. Must they need the same architectural effort?
chapters.explanation: No. Relationships, stakeholder concerns, quality requirements, and the cost of changing important decisions matter. Line count alone does not reveal these factors.

chapters.title: Systems, stakeholders, and decisions
paragraphs: A system exists in an environment and serves a mission. Its stakeholders are people or organizations with an interest in its behavior or development. For a museum catalog, the mission might be to help visitors discover exhibits; curators, visitors, and maintainers have different concerns. State the system boundary so that external people and systems are not mistaken for internal components.

The definitions in the slides emphasize components, relationships, interfaces, behavior, composition, and guiding principles. Architectural decisions are the design decisions significant to the system as a whole: they shape how major responsibilities fit together and how important qualities can be achieved. Architecture is design, but a local design choice is not automatically architecturally significant.

Significance depends on context. An algorithm or data structure can become an architectural concern if it determines system-wide performance, compatibility, or feasible behavior. Conversely, a small local implementation choice may be easy to replace. Architecture supports communication among stakeholders, analysis of a proposed system, and reuse of successful structures; a diagram is useful only when people agree on its meaning.
chapters.prediction: Is choosing an algorithm always outside software architecture?
chapters.explanation: No. A locally replaceable algorithm may be detailed design, but one that constrains the whole system or determines a critical quality can be architecturally significant.

chapters.title: Intended and implemented architecture
paragraphs: Prescriptive, or intended, architecture describes how the system is supposed to be organized. Descriptive, or implemented, architecture describes what actually exists. The two can differ because software evolves, documentation becomes stale, or implementation decisions bypass agreed boundaries. Treat an intended diagram as a statement of design intent, not proof of the current code structure.

Architecture drift means new implementation decisions are absent from the intended description without violating it. Architecture erosion means the implementation violates the intended architecture. Suppose the intended design permits a presentation module to call only an application interface. An allowed new implementation behind that interface may be undocumented drift; a direct presentation-to-storage dependency violates the stated boundary and is erosion.

Architecture recovery reconstructs an account of the implemented system from evidence such as source code, executable structure, configuration, and developer knowledge. Record uncertainty rather than filling gaps with guesses. Compare the recovered account with the intended one, investigate differences, and decide whether to repair the implementation or deliberately revise the intended design and its rationale.
chapters.prediction: An undocumented component is added within all permitted dependency rules. Is that necessarily erosion?
chapters.explanation: No. Under the distinction in the slides, a compatible undocumented decision is drift. Erosion requires evidence of a violated intended rule.

chapters.title: Views and meaningful diagrams
paragraphs: A single box-and-arrow picture rarely answers every architectural question. A static decomposition can show code responsibilities and dependencies. A runtime view can show processes and interactions. A deployment view can show where software executes across devices. State what each box and arrow represents, and distinguish a code dependency from a runtime message or a deployment relationship.

The 4+1 model organizes complementary views. The logical view describes key abstractions and responsibilities; the process view addresses runtime concurrency and interactions; the development view describes code organization; the physical view maps software onto hardware or execution nodes. The additional scenarios connect and help examine the views through representative system behavior.

For a museum catalog, a logical view might distinguish exhibits and collections, a development view might show modules, and a physical view might place the application on a server. A visitor searching for an exhibit is a scenario that can be traced through the relevant views. These descriptions must agree, but they need not contain identical boxes or identical levels of detail.
chapters.prediction: A maintainer asks which device runs a process. Would a class diagram alone answer the question?
chapters.explanation: Usually not. A physical or deployment view identifies execution placement. A class diagram describes a different concern and needs an explicit mapping to runtime and deployment elements.

chapters.title: Abstraction, reuse, and C4
paragraphs: Architectural descriptions can reuse ideas at different scopes. A style describes a family of structures through constraints on elements and relationships. A reference architecture gives a reusable architectural organization for a domain. A product-line architecture captures shared structure and planned variation across related products. These concepts help teams reuse reasoning, rather than copy a diagram without checking its assumptions.

C4 provides four nested levels of structural description: system context, containers, components, and code. Context shows the system in relation to people and external systems. Containers show major running applications or data stores within the system; components describe responsibilities within a container; code shows implementation detail when useful. A C4 container is a modeling concept, not necessarily a Docker container.

C4 levels and 4+1 views answer different organizing questions. C4 changes the level of detail; 4+1 separates concerns such as code organization and runtime processes. Neither requires every diagram for every audience. Architectural significance also does not follow a fixed line-count threshold or a rule that architecture happens only early: revisit consequential decisions as the system evolves.
chapters.prediction: A context diagram contains every class in the application. Does the extra detail necessarily help its audience?
chapters.explanation: No. A context audience needs the system boundary, people, and external relationships. Class detail can obscure that purpose; move it to a more detailed description when it answers a relevant question.

chapters.title: Patterns and architectural styles
paragraphs: An architectural pattern describes a recurring design problem and an arrangement of responsibilities that addresses it in a context. A style constrains the kinds of elements and relationships allowed in a family of architectures. The terms can overlap in use; explaining the responsibilities, constraints, and consequences is more useful than relying only on a name.

The three-tier example separates presentation, application processing, and data management. This helps identify responsibilities and the interfaces between them. A logical separation of these concerns does not by itself prove that they run on three separate machines. MVC separates model, view, and controller responsibilities around an interface; it should not be assumed to be a one-to-one synonym for three deployment tiers.

The sense–compute–control example organizes observation, computation, and action on an environment. It highlights a different set of responsibilities from a typical presentation-and-data application. When selecting any pattern, state the problem it addresses and the constraints it imposes. A named style may support desired qualities, but its name alone cannot guarantee maintainability, performance, or other outcomes.
chapters.prediction: A team labels three boxes MVC. Has it demonstrated a three-machine deployment?
chapters.explanation: No. MVC describes responsibilities. Deployment requires separate evidence about where those responsibilities execute; a diagram label does not establish placement.

quiz.question: How does an architectural decision differ from an ordinary local design choice?
quiz.answer: Its significance comes from its system-wide consequences, relationships, quality concerns, or cost of change. The boundary is contextual, not a fixed size or phase rule.

quiz.question: What evidence distinguishes architecture drift from erosion?
quiz.answer: Compare the implemented decision with an explicit intended constraint. An undocumented compatible addition is drift; a violated constraint is erosion. Without a known constraint, do not assert a violation.

quiz.question: How do C4 levels differ from the 4+1 views?
quiz.answer: C4 organizes structural descriptions by abstraction level. The 4+1 model separates architectural concerns and relates them through scenarios. They are not a one-to-one mapping.

exercise.prompt: Design an introductory architecture description for a museum exhibit catalog. State its mission and two stakeholders. Draw a system-context diagram and one complementary view, with a legend. Describe one significant decision, then explain how you would check whether the implementation follows it.
exercise.answer: A possible mission is helping visitors find exhibits. Visitors need understandable search results; curators need a maintainable catalog. The context diagram shows people, the catalog boundary, and any explicitly assumed external system. A development view can show presentation, application, and data-access modules with arrows meaning permitted dependencies. Record a decision that presentation uses the application interface, then inspect code dependencies for direct storage access. Other decompositions are valid when their rationale and notation are clear.

units.title: Jeromy: architecture, resilience and customer value
units.description: Connect architectural decisions to quality attributes, trace an outage through recovery dependencies, and design graceful degradation around customer value.

chapters.title: Architecture is a set of consequential decisions
paragraphs: Architecture centers on decisions that are difficult to change and strongly affect a system’s quality attributes. A component diagram helps describe a system, but architectural reasoning also explains why its boundaries, dependencies, storage and recovery mechanisms were chosen.

Whether a choice is architectural depends on context. A language choice may deeply affect latency, maintainability or hiring for a long-lived system; for a disposable prototype its consequences may be smaller. Avoid declaring a technology universally architectural without identifying the quality impact and cost of reversal.

For a new campus alerting service, ask which decisions determine whether acknowledged alerts survive a crash, whether operators can diagnose a failure, and whether a new delivery channel can be added. These questions connect the opening lecture to later requirements, database, microservices and QODA units.
chapters.prediction: Is a language choice always an architectural decision?
chapters.explanation: Its importance depends on how strongly it affects relevant qualities and how costly it is to reverse in the particular system.

chapters.title: Start with the customer’s quality priorities
paragraphs: The example’s simplified observability pipeline ingests telemetry, persists it, processes and indexes it, and supports alerts and queries. Those functions depend on one another: an alert cannot be trustworthy if the relevant data was never ingested.

In the historical Datadog example, durability is central to customer trust. Availability priorities include preserving ingestion and monitoring before less urgent query behavior. Another important measure is ingestion-to-use latency, including the time until data can support an alert. This ordering belongs to that business context, not every application.

A quality requirement should state which user outcome it protects. For a campus safety system, preserving an accepted urgent alert and delivering it on time might outrank historical report generation. State what may be delayed, what may be dropped, and what must not be lost. Apply authorization and data-retention constraints as part of the design.
chapters.prediction: If a dashboard is unavailable but accepted data is durably retained, are availability and durability identical outcomes?
chapters.explanation: No. The service can retain data while failing to provide timely access or alerts. Measure both properties and explain the user consequences.

chapters.title: Trace a correlated failure across the system
paragraphs: The case describes the March 2023 Datadog outage as a historical case study. An unattended operating-system update restarted networking software and disrupted routing on many nodes. A change outside the ordinary staged rollout path crossed otherwise separate deployment boundaries.

The lesson is about correlated causes. Multiple machines, regions or cloud providers do not guarantee independence when a shared update mechanism can affect them together. Include operating-system packages, configuration, identity, networking and management services in the dependency and change-control review.

Recovery behavior also differed across cloud environments in the case described. Replacing a machine and rebooting a machine can have different consequences for local state. Treat these as historical observations from the recording, not guarantees about current cloud-provider behavior. A recovery plan must specify what survives each action and how service state is reconstructed.
chapters.prediction: Can a geographically replicated system still have one broad failure mechanism?
chapters.explanation: Yes. A shared configuration, update, credential or control-plane dependency can fail across regions. Geographic diversity protects only against the failure classes it actually separates.

chapters.title: Durability, bootstrap dependencies and tested restoration
paragraphs: Multiple persistence stages helped preserve data in the case: client-side buffering, local journals and durable messaging provided different opportunities for recovery. Buffers still need capacity and a policy for sustained downstream failure. A persistent queue is not an infinite sink.

One protective circumstance was that many messaging nodes did not share the affected operating-system version. The case explicitly cautions against treating delayed upgrades as the lesson. The useful questions concern failure-domain diversity, safe update procedures and tested recovery, not avoiding security maintenance.

Startup dependencies can form cycles even when normal operation seems healthy. If service A needs B to start and B needs A, restoring both from zero may require an independent bootstrap path. Identify such cycles in advance, document the minimal recovery set, and rehearse it.

A stored backup is not proof of recoverability. Test restoration into the environment that will exist after the failure, measure recovery time, and verify the resulting data. The case also contrasts independently recoverable shards with systems that need enough cooperating members before serving; actual behavior depends on the design and failure assumptions.
chapters.prediction: A team has daily backups but has never restored them. What is missing?
chapters.explanation: Evidence that the restore process works with available keys, dependencies, capacity and state. Rehearse restoration and validate the result and recovery time.

chapters.title: Recover customer value, not just machine count
paragraphs: A fleet can regain machines before customers regain useful service. Dependencies, backlog and competing work can make recovery uneven. The case emphasizes graceful degradation: as capacity falls, preserve the most valuable outcomes and relax lower-priority service where the requirements permit it.

Self-monitoring can also fail with the monitored system. Keep independent signals and operational access for diagnosing an outage. Manual procedures are useful only when practiced; a recovery runbook should identify its dependencies and how it is tested.

New teaching calculation: incoming work is 100 items/second, recovered capacity is 120, and a durable backlog contains 6,000 items. Only 20 items/second remain for old work, so ideal drainage takes 300 seconds. At capacity 100 the backlog does not drain. This fluid model omits retries, variation and downstream bottlenecks; real recovery needs measurement.

Define priority classes, throttle backfill, and avoid overwhelming control services during mass provisioning. Exercise capacity loss in a controlled game day and measure end-to-end customer outcomes. Do not assume a universal percentage of remaining capacity guarantees useful service.
chapters.prediction: After machines return, why might service recovery still be slow?
chapters.explanation: Live arrivals, retries and stored backlog compete for limited resources; some dependent services may still be unavailable. Measure useful completed operations and backlog drainage, not only node count.

chapters.title: Apply quality thinking to AI-assisted development
paragraphs: A related question concerns a discussion of AI-assisted software development. Its architectural connection is long-term maintainability: rapidly producing code does not by itself show that a team can understand, operate, secure or change the result.

Treat the lecture’s tool usage and industry predictions as a 2025 discussion rather than current adoption statistics. The durable question is whether the resulting software meets explicit quality scenarios. A disposable personal prototype and a long-lived production service have different consequences if no one understands the implementation.

New exercise: an AI-generated incident dashboard works for a demonstration. Before deploying it as a lasting service, specify authorization, safe handling of untrusted input, failure behavior, diagnostic visibility and changeability. Review the implementation, test the relevant scenarios, and assign ownership for maintenance. Generated output still requires engineering evidence.
chapters.prediction: A generated application works in a demo. What architectural questions remain?
chapters.explanation: Whether it remains correct, secure, diagnosable, operable and maintainable under the intended workloads, failures and future changes. A demo demonstrates only the behavior exercised.

chapters.title: Read and write class diagrams
paragraphs: A class diagram summarizes selected structural facts. Class boxes can show names, attributes and operations; visibility symbols communicate access, while inheritance and interface realization express different contracts. Associations describe relationships between instances, with multiplicity constraining how many may participate. The BankAccount and Student–Course examples connect these symbols to code so that notation supports an explanation rather than becoming a memorization exercise.

Read multiplicity from the relevant association end and distinguish capacity from actual participation. An array with thirty slots is not evidence that thirty courses are always assigned. Composition expresses strong ownership in the model, whereas an ordinary association need not imply a shared lifetime. Nested classes, dependencies and notes add detail when needed. Correct partial snippets before treating them as runnable implementations, and state conventions where the diagram omits information.

chapters.title: Patterns as reusable design knowledge
paragraphs: UML can be used selectively to resolve a design question rather than to document every implementation detail. The cited industry study illustrates different usage patterns, not a universal adoption rate for every team. A diagram earns its place by helping collaborators reason. Design patterns likewise provide reusable language for a problem, a solution structure and the consequences that accompany it.

A pattern is not a mechanical recipe. Its forces and tradeoffs must fit the system, language and expected changes. The architectural-doorway example makes this concrete: the layout responds to patterns of movement rather than to an abstract preference for doors in corners. Composition delegates behavior through collaborating objects, while inheritance commits to a subtype relationship and its contracts. Prefer the mechanism that expresses the relationship and controls the intended variation.
chapters.prediction: Should every recurring code fragment be replaced by a named design pattern?
chapters.explanation: No. Use a pattern when its problem and tradeoffs match; adding structure without a need can reduce clarity.

chapters.title: Single responsibility and cohesion
paragraphs: The single responsibility principle asks whether a class has one coherent reason to change. Responsibilities arise from the concerns and policies it serves, not simply the number of methods. A cohesion graph connecting methods that share fields can expose clusters, but shared state is only a clue. Methods can share a field while serving unrelated purposes, and a coherent responsibility can use several data structures.

The split-class exercise asks which changes should remain independent. Separating storage, formatting or domain calculations can reduce the number of clients affected by a change. The historical Date API example illustrates the long-lived cost of mixing concerns in a public library. Compatibility limits cleanup after release, so careful boundaries matter. Avoid splitting every method into its own object; the goal is a coherent model with understandable responsibilities and interfaces.

chapters.explanation: No. Shared fields suggest structural cohesion but do not establish a single policy or reason to change.

chapters.title: Design for extension
paragraphs: The painter example initially knows how to draw each concrete shape. Adding a triangle requires another branch or loop in the painter, spreading the variation into a client. Introducing a Shape operation moves drawing behavior behind a shared contract. The painter can then iterate over shapes without naming every concrete type, making the supported extension point explicit.

Open–closed design protects stable behavior from selected kinds of change; it does not forbid editing code or demand inheritance for every extension. Composition, strategies and registration can serve the same purpose. Adding a shape may still require creation or configuration changes elsewhere. The key question is whether the abstraction matches the expected variation, and whether its contract is sufficient for new implementations to work without special cases in the client.

chapters.title: Substitutability and contracts
paragraphs: Substitutability concerns behavior visible to clients. If a client works under a supertype contract, replacing an object with a subtype should not invalidate those expectations. A subtype must not demand stronger preconditions or provide weaker guarantees. Phrase this through implications: every input accepted by the supertype must remain acceptable, and the subtype’s successful outcome must satisfy the supertype’s promised result.

The mutable Rectangle example promises independently adjustable width and height. Square breaks that promise by changing both dimensions in a setter, so a client expecting area fifty receives one hundred. This is a contract problem rather than a statement about geometry. The unmodifiable List example needs different care: Java documents optional mutators, so an exception can be permitted by the declared contract. A client requiring mutation needs a stronger capability guarantee.
chapters.prediction: Does the mathematical fact that every square is a rectangle prove mutable Square is a behavioral subtype?
chapters.explanation: No. The programming interface’s mutation promises, not just geometric membership, determine substitutability.

chapters.title: Client-focused interfaces and dependency inversion
paragraphs: Interface segregation focuses on what each client needs to depend on. A broad interface can mix reading, writing and event handling even when many clients need only one role. Smaller role interfaces make capabilities clearer. An adapter with default no-op callbacks may reduce implementation effort, but it does not erase the conceptual breadth of the original interface.

Dependency inversion places policy behind stable abstractions instead of binding it directly to implementation details. JDBC illustrates application code using a database-facing API implemented by drivers. The boundary can localize many implementation changes, while behavioral differences and contract changes may still affect clients. Together, these principles encourage focused contracts owned by the needs of the caller, with concrete implementations replaceable only to the extent that they preserve those contracts.

chapters.explanation: No. Changes in observable behavior, contract or supported capabilities can still affect callers even when method signatures remain stable.

units.title: Requirements & quality attributes
units.description: Translate stakeholder concerns into clear requirements and measurable quality scenarios that guide design.

chapters.title: Discover the problem and its stakeholders
paragraphs: Requirements begin with stakeholders who have needs, constraints and competing priorities. Elicitation gathers these concerns; analysis examines consistency, feasibility and completeness; specification records an agreed account; validation checks that the account addresses the actual problem. A request to use a particular technology may reflect a real operational constraint, or it may be a proposed solution that hides the underlying need.

Ask why a statement matters and who is affected if it is unmet. Distinguish a business goal from an observable system behavior and from a contractual or organizational constraint. A system boundary helps expose missing actors and dependencies. Conflicts should become explicit tradeoffs rather than being concealed in vague wording. Architecture then starts from a clearer problem, avoiding detailed optimization of a solution that stakeholders never needed.
chapters.prediction: A stakeholder says “use Java.” Is that automatically a functional requirement?
chapters.explanation: No. It is a technology constraint or proposed solution; discover its rationale and whether it is actually mandatory.

chapters.title: Write specifications people can test
paragraphs: A specification bridges stakeholder needs and implementation. It may describe functions, data, interfaces, quality constraints, operating environments and delivery obligations. Good requirements are understandable, consistent, verifiable and traceable to goals. Completeness does not mean unlimited detail; it means including what is necessary for the intended agreement and identifying unresolved questions instead of hiding them.

Ambiguity becomes visible when different readers can produce different valid interpretations. Soup or salad and bread has more than one grouping; a name that “can be 127 characters” leaves optionality and length boundaries unclear. Rewrite statements so a tester can distinguish compliance from noncompliance. Preserve links to rationale and design choices, because changing a requirement after deployment may affect architecture, tests, training and operational procedures as well as code.
chapters.prediction: Can two reviewers agree that a sentence sounds reasonable yet disagree about an implementation passing it?
chapters.explanation: Yes. Missing boundaries, definitions and acceptance criteria allow incompatible interpretations; testable examples help expose them.

chapters.title: Classify requirements and quality attributes
paragraphs: Functional requirements describe what the system does, while quality requirements constrain how well relevant behavior occurs under stated conditions. Delivery or technology constraints form additional categories. These categories do not determine priority: a quality requirement can be essential, and a proposed function can be optional. “Secure login” needs decomposition into authentication behavior and explicit security properties rather than a stronger adjective.

Quality attributes often span multiple responsibilities. Reliability can depend on persistence, retries, status reporting and recovery; performance can depend on database work, communication and workload. They therefore influence architecture, even though the system can continue evolving after an initial design. Express these concerns in scenarios and acceptance checks. Asking how an attribute is observed makes it easier to compare designs and prevents quality from becoming a list of aspirations.
chapters.prediction: Is a two-second response requirement less mandatory because it is nonfunctional?
chapters.explanation: No. Mandatory status depends on the agreement and system context, not whether the requirement describes a function or a quality attribute.

chapters.title: Make quality measurable
paragraphs: A measurable requirement names the observation and the conditions under which it must hold. The search example gives a proportion and a latency threshold, but still needs a workload, dataset and measurement window. Counting registered users does not specify concurrency or request intensity. Define how failures, timeouts and warm-up periods enter a measurement so that different tests answer the same question.

Other qualities require equal care. Accuracy needs a defined error measure; maintainability needs a relevant change task or evidence rather than a vague hope. XML, Java or a SQL database may be design constraints, but they do not by themselves establish interoperability. Distinguish the objective from a proposed mechanism and choose a test that addresses the objective. Any additional numerical targets in a teaching exercise should be marked as assumptions.
chapters.prediction: Do twenty million registered users imply twenty million simultaneous requests?
chapters.explanation: No. Registration, activity, concurrency and request rate measure different things and require separate workload assumptions.

chapters.title: Optimize the system rather than isolated parts
paragraphs: The C1, C2 and T1 example models producers feeding a consumer on one CPU. Under the stated teaching assumptions, each stage operation has equal cost and completed throughput is limited by the smaller of combined production and consumption. A CPU budget of twelve stage operations per second must cover both producing and consuming work, so maximizing each component independently is not a valid objective.

With producer rates three and three and a consumer rate six, completed throughput is six while the total CPU budget is twelve. Giving all three components four operations per second consumes the same budget but only completes four because consumption is slower than production. This is a deliberately simplified capacity model. Real systems add scheduling, unequal costs and queueing; one hundred percent utilization leaves no headroom and should not be described as unlimited capacity.
chapters.prediction: Why can rates 3,3,6 beat rates 4,4,4 with the same CPU cost?
chapters.explanation: Both consume twelve stage operations per second, but throughput is min(C1+C2,T1): six in the first case and four in the second.

quiz.answer: For example: under a specified workload and dataset, at least 95% of search requests complete within 2 seconds over a stated measurement window; define how errors count. Numbers are a proposed teaching example, not a source requirement.

quiz.answer: It does not say whether these are registered, daily active or concurrent users, what requests they issue, or what latency/error objectives must hold.

quiz.question: In the slide’s producer/consumer model, C1=3, C2=3, T1=6 operations/s. What are throughput and CPU use?
quiz.answer: Throughput=min(3+3,6)=6 completed requests/s; CPU consumption=3+3+6=12 stage operations/s, or 100% of the stated budget. This depends on equal per-operation cost and the stated flow.

units.title: Scalability, services & HTTP
units.description: Move from a program to a concurrent service, identify resource limits, and trace an HTTP request through a web application.

chapters.title: From programs to services
paragraphs: Imagine a sorting program that reads one file, produces its answer, and exits. Its running time can be studied as the input grows. Now expose that calculation as a network service. The process remains available, accepts requests from unrelated clients, and may still be working on one request when another arrives. The input size of an individual job is no longer the only source of growth: the arrival rate and the overlap between jobs matter too. In the diagram, several clients feed one worker pool. Increasing the number of clients without increasing useful processing capacity creates waiting, even if every individual calculation uses an efficient algorithm.

Consider a service that completes 80 small lookups per second under a particular workload. If arrivals rise to 100 per second for ten seconds, a simplified model accumulates 200 unfinished requests. When arrivals return to 60 per second, the service has 20 completions per second available to remove that backlog, so recovery takes another ten seconds. The queue is a temporary reservoir, not an extra processor. This example explains why a capacity claim must include more than registered users or a peak request count. Follow arrivals, completions, waiting time, and errors together; otherwise an apparently successful service may merely be postponing the work until clients abandon it.

A useful workload description specifies operation types, input sizes, arrival patterns, and acceptable outcomes. Searching a short record is different from exporting a large collection, even when both count as one request. Monthly active users measure an audience over time, whereas simultaneous requests describe overlap at a particular moment. Neither can be converted into processing demand without additional assumptions. Architecture adds further concerns: requests cross networks, share mutable data, and encounter component failures. Start with a measurable service objective, then ask whether additional resources can support more demand while maintaining that objective. Efficient code remains necessary, but the system must also coordinate its resources and remain available throughout repeated use.

chapters.explanation: No. Throughput alone hides queueing and user experience; the result must meet a stated latency and error target.

chapters.title: Scaling up and scaling out
paragraphs: Suppose a service spends most of its time waiting for a file or a remote database. While one request is blocked, another request can use the processor. Several threads can therefore improve utilization even on a machine with only one core. That does not mean the core executes several computations at the same instant: the operating system schedules runnable work while blocked work waits. In the illustration, request A uses the CPU, waits for storage, and resumes; request B occupies part of A's waiting interval. If the work instead consists almost entirely of computation, overlapping threads cannot manufacture additional execution capacity on that same core.

Vertical scaling replaces or upgrades a machine with more useful resources: cores, memory, storage bandwidth, or faster processors. Horizontal scaling adds machines and distributes requests between them. Picture two application replicas that both query the same database. Adding the second replica helps only while that database and the connecting network can support the extra work. If the database already limits completions, two application queues simply converge on the same narrow point. The figure contrasts extra execution capacity with an unchanged shared dependency. Diagnose the limiting resource first, change one capacity assumption, and repeat the same workload measurement to establish whether the bottleneck has actually moved.

A larger single machine often keeps deployment and data sharing simpler because coordination can remain within one operating system. Its limits include the largest available configuration, the cost of high-end capacity, and the effect of losing that machine. Multiple machines offer additional aggregate resources and opportunities for replacement, but introduce network communication, request placement, and shared-state problems. Neither choice guarantees linear speedup. For example, a global lock can serialize work across many cores, while additional replicas may overload a downstream database. Choose the smallest architectural change that meets the measured objective, and include capacity during failures and maintenance rather than reasoning only about the all-healthy case.
chapters.prediction: Will doubling CPU cores necessarily halve request latency?
chapters.explanation: No. IO waits, serial work, locks and external dependencies can dominate.

chapters.title: Request processing and HTTP
paragraphs: A server framework separates network handling from application work. The network-facing component accepts a request and makes it available to a worker. A worker removes one request, runs the application handler, and places its response where the networking component can send it. When the request queue is empty, waiting workers can block instead of continuously polling. When the response side is congested, completed work may also wait before reaching a client. The diagram deliberately includes both queues: observing a fast application function alone does not establish a fast end-to-end response. Time can be spent before the function starts and after its computation has finished.

Now fill the arrival queue while every worker is busy. An unlimited queue keeps accepting requests but consumes memory and lets waiting time increase without bound under sustained overload. A bounded queue creates an explicit decision point: accept work while space remains, then reject it or apply backpressure when capacity is exhausted. The illustration shows a full queue diverting a new arrival to an overload response instead of hiding it behind an ever-growing backlog. Rejection is not automatically desirable, but an early, meaningful failure can be more useful than a response that arrives after the client has already timed out and submitted another request.

HTTP describes the external exchange rather than prescribing this worker design. A request contains a method, target, fields, and sometimes content; a response supplies a status, fields, and possibly content. Frameworks parse and construct these messages so application code can focus on routing, validation, and domain behavior. Some frameworks use worker threads, others processes or asynchronous event handling. These approaches differ in how they schedule computation and waiting, but clients should observe the same documented contract. During a design review, draw the protocol messages separately from the implementation queues, then mark where deadlines, cancellation, queue limits, and error responses apply. This connects interoperability to the practical behavior of overload.
chapters.prediction: What happens if requests enter faster than workers can finish them for a sustained period?
chapters.explanation: The queue grows unless bounded; latency rises, and a bounded system eventually rejects or slows arrivals.

chapters.title: A Wikipedia request, end to end
paragraphs: Follow a reader opening an encyclopedia article in the historical architecture example. The browser sends an HTTP request identifying the article. The application extracts that identity, retrieves the article's saved wiki text from a database, transforms it into HTML, and adds navigation and other page structure. The database retains the editable content; the application computes a representation of it. These are different responsibilities even if a small deployment initially puts them on the same machine. The illustration highlights the storage read and rendering step separately, so we can later ask whether repeated reads or repeated transformations dominate the cost of serving the page.

Next compare two readers requesting the same article. Most of the article body may be identical, but the page header can differ because a signed-in reader sees account controls or notifications. The browser supplies a cookie with its request, allowing the application to obtain the relevant identity or session information. In the diagram, shared article content and user-specific information enter different branches before the final page is assembled. Reusing the entire assembled response without distinguishing users could disclose one reader's information to another. A cache design should therefore begin by identifying which fragments are shared, which vary, and which request properties select the correct representation.

This walkthrough also explains why merely multiplying web servers does not complete the scaling story. Each application replica may still read from the same authoritative database, while large media objects may use a separate file or object store. An optional cache can avoid some repeated work, but it must preserve the intended freshness and privacy behavior. Treat the historical product names and instance counts as context for the example, not as current deployment recommendations. The transferable skill is to trace one request, label each component's responsibility, and then repeat the trace for an edit, a second reader, and a component failure. Those variations expose the architectural decisions that a static collection of boxes conceals.
chapters.prediction: Can the entire personalized HTML response always be reused for another visitor?
chapters.explanation: No. Shared article content and user-specific response content require different reuse policies.

exercise.prompt: A portal receives 15 requests per second. Each worker can process 5, but all requests use a database capped at 12. Describe the effect of moving from two to four workers, and propose a measurement plan.
exercise.answer: Two workers cap ideal throughput at 10; four workers move the cap to the database at 12. At a steady arrival rate of 15, the queue continues to grow. Measure throughput, tail latency, errors, CPU, database wait time, and query costs under a reproducible workload. Consider reducing database work and controlling admission before adding further workers.

units.title: Stateless services, proxies & caches
units.description: Make worker state explicit, understand intermediary roles, and reason about cache hits, eviction, and stale data.

chapters.title: Where does state live?
paragraphs: A useful way to discover state is to interrupt a conversation halfway through it and move the next message to a fresh worker. Consider an email submission dialogue: earlier commands establish the sender and recipients, while a later command supplies the message body. A worker that sees only the final body cannot reconstruct the complete operation. It needs information retained from the earlier messages. The diagram shows these pieces accumulating in one conversation context. State is therefore not simply data in a database; it includes any remembered information that later processing depends on, including process variables, an open connection's context, or a partially completed user interaction.

HTTP requests are designed to carry the information needed to interpret each individual exchange, but an HTTP application can still introduce a dependency on a particular worker. Imagine worker A storing an unfinished game only in its own memory. The next request contains the game identifier but reaches worker B, whose dictionary has no corresponding entry. Identical code does not make these workers interchangeable because they have different histories. The illustration follows the identifier to the wrong memory store and exposes the missing information. Before adding replicas, ask whether another worker can complete the request using the request itself and explicitly shared services, without consulting the original worker's private history.

A stateless application tier does not imply a stateless system or a mathematical pure function. Workers can read changing records, write durable changes, consult the clock, or produce nondeterministic results. The important deployment property is that a particular client's previous requests need not have visited that same process. State may be carried by a client token or maintained in shared storage, each with its own security and coordination requirements. Avoid moving arbitrary authoritative data to the client merely to remove server memory: clients can alter untrusted input. Draw the owner and lifetime of every important state item, then simulate a worker restart between consecutive requests to reveal hidden dependencies.
chapters.prediction: If two stateless workers read a database at different times, must they produce identical responses to the same URL?
chapters.explanation: No. Shared data, time or randomness can change; statelessness concerns worker-local conversational state.

chapters.title: Stateless workers with stateful data
paragraphs: Start with a chess application that keeps a dictionary of active games inside one process. Cloning that process creates several independent dictionaries, so each game becomes tied to the worker holding it. Instead, put the authoritative game record in shared storage and include its identifier in each request. A worker loads the board, validates the requested move, saves the result, and returns the updated representation. A replacement worker can now continue after the original process disappears. The diagram shows two interchangeable application workers converging on one game record. We have removed a placement constraint from the application tier, but we have deliberately created a shared dependency that needs its own capacity and availability design.

Externalizing state does not automatically make concurrent updates correct. Suppose two requests both read game version twelve. The first valid move updates the record to version thirteen. If the second request blindly writes its earlier view, it can erase the accepted change or apply a move to an obsolete board. A conditional update that succeeds only while the version is still twelve lets exactly one of these competing updates win. The second request must reload and reconsider its action. The diagram marks the two reads and the rejected stale write; it makes clear that a common storage location and a correct update protocol solve different problems.

Login state illustrates the complementary role of the client. After authentication, a browser can receive an opaque session identifier and return it in later requests. Any worker uses that identifier to look up the session in shared storage. A signed token can instead carry verifiable claims, but its contents are not confidential merely because it is signed, and expiration or revocation still requires a policy. Neither approach authorizes every requested game move: the application must still verify the user's rights and the current game state. These separations make the system easier to reason about: tokens identify a session, shared records retain domain state, and atomic update rules preserve invariants when requests overlap.

chapters.explanation: No. The update must enforce the game rules with appropriate transactions, conditions or version checks.

chapters.title: Proxies and cache hits
paragraphs: A proxy is an intermediary: it accepts the client's request, knows which upstream service can answer it, and relays the response. Add storage to that intermediary and it can remember reusable answers. On the first request for article A, the cache has no matching entry, so it forwards the request to the application. The application reads data and constructs the response; the proxy saves an eligible copy while returning it. A second equivalent request can be answered directly from that copy. The diagram shows the miss visiting origin and the hit stopping early. The performance gain comes from avoiding repeated work, not from making the original computation intrinsically faster.

Because a cache has a finite budget, admitting a new object may require evicting another. Consider room for three equally sized items and accesses A, B, C, A, D. After the second access to A, B is the least recently used entry. An LRU policy evicts B when D arrives, preserving A and C. The illustration emphasizes that a hit updates the recency order even though it does not fetch another object. This policy exploits temporal locality: recently useful data may be needed again soon. It is a prediction about the workload, not a guarantee; a scan of unrelated objects can displace a genuinely useful working set.

Two placements give different responsibilities. With an application-managed cache, the application explicitly checks a fast store and fetches from authoritative storage on a miss. With a transparent caching proxy, the client uses one ordinary service interface and the intermediary performs the lookup and forwarding. In both cases define the key, eligibility rules, eviction policy, and response to cache failure. A missing cache entry should not be confused with missing authoritative data. Also distinguish latency from load reduction: a miss may pay both a cache lookup and origin work, while a hit avoids origin entirely. Measure hit ratio alongside actual costs and correctness so a high hit count does not disguise cheap hits and expensive misses.

chapters.explanation: B, because A was accessed more recently.

chapters.title: Popularity, freshness and HTTP caching
paragraphs: Why can a small cache remove a large fraction of service traffic? Requests are often unevenly distributed. A few popular articles receive repeated reads while many less popular articles form a long tail. If a cache stores the frequently requested subset, its fraction of all stored documents can be small even while its fraction of answered requests is large. For an illustrative workload of one thousand requests per second with a ninety percent hit ratio, only about one hundred misses per second reach origin, ignoring validation and other traffic. The diagram separates the hot set from the long tail rather than treating all documents as equally likely to be requested.

The price of reuse appears when an authoritative value changes after a cached copy was saved. Suppose a public timetable response can remain fresh for sixty seconds. At time zero the proxy stores version one; at time twenty the origin publishes version two. An otherwise eligible request at time forty can still receive version one under that freshness policy. At expiry, the cache must refresh or validate before ordinary reuse. The diagram places the edit and expiry on separate paths to show why updating origin does not instantly update every copy. Select a freshness window from the application's tolerance for stale information, not only from the hit ratio you hope to achieve.

HTTP caching fields express different permissions. A public response may be eligible for shared-cache storage; private restricts storage to a private cache. A long freshness lifetime does not override private. No-cache permits storage but requires validation before reuse, whereas no-store prohibits storing the response. Validators can avoid retransmitting unchanged content, but validation still involves communication. Personalized responses need keys and policies that prevent one user's representation being served to another. Finally, a successful cache may become a dependency of the capacity plan: after eviction or restart, a burst of misses can overwhelm an origin sized only for the warm-cache load. Plan and measure warm, cold, and stale-cache behavior separately.
chapters.prediction: Can a cache with a 95% hit rate still be incorrect?
chapters.explanation: Yes. A high hit rate can serve stale or identity-inappropriate data; correctness and hit rate are separate.

review.issue: Stateless workers are equated with deterministic pure functions and no side effects.
review.correction: No durable per-client state is required in a particular worker between requests. Workers can read changing shared data, use randomness, and perform database writes; slide 6 conflicts with slide 7 on identical responses.

review.issue: Stateful requests always must go to the same handler; pushing state away removes coordination.
review.correction: Affinity is one solution; shared/replicated state is another. Coordination remains in storage, including atomic updates and concurrency control.

review.issue: Cookies are treated as uniformly sent to all later site requests.
review.correction: Cookie scope and attributes govern delivery. A cookie may hold an opaque session ID or signed claims. Signature verification is not encryption and revocation/expiry still need a design.

review.issue: Proxy transparency and load-balancer capacity appear unconditional.
review.correction: A reverse proxy needs deployment configuration and can become a bottleneck or failure point; replication and health checks are separate design decisions.

review.issue: Invalidation automatically creates coherence.
review.correction: Invalidation must reach relevant caches and be ordered correctly; races or delivery failures can leave stale copies.

review.issue: Statelessness alone makes responses reusable; only GET may be cached.
review.correction: Reusability depends on method semantics, cache directives, freshness, and request variants. GET/HEAD are common; POST caching has explicit conditions. Distinguish no-cache (revalidate) from no-store (do not store), and private from public.

exercise.prompt: A public course page and a private student-results page share an application. Design a caching policy and explain what happens when a course description changes.
exercise.answer: Cache public responses only when their freshness and variation rules allow it. Keep personalized results out of shared caches unless a carefully designed private partitioning scheme permits it. Define TTL, validation, or invalidation for updated course content. Versioned immutable assets simplify cache reuse. Include cache keys, user identity, and stale-content tolerance in the design.

units.title: Relational databases & scaling
units.description: Connect storage, schemas, indexes, read replication, and sharding to the queries a service needs to execute.

chapters.title: Why state moves into the database
paragraphs: Start with two application workers behind a load balancer. A visitor edits a page through worker A and then reads it through worker B. If the edit exists only in A's memory, B cannot produce the new page. Sticky routing can hide that problem until A fails, but it does not create a shared, durable record. Moving page state into a database lets either worker load the same authoritative information. The application becomes replaceable because its process lifetime no longer determines the lifetime of user data. This is why adding stateless workers is straightforward, while adding independent copies of a database is a different architectural problem.

The database now carries two responsibilities: persistence and coordination. Persistence keeps an accepted edit after the application stops. Coordination makes concurrent operations agree on shared facts, such as which page revision is current. Draw arrows from both workers into one database: the drawing explains both the benefit and the next bottleneck. Every worker can consult a common authority, but all their storage operations also converge there. A load balancer normally performs relatively little work per request; the database may locate rows, check constraints, update indexes and write durable records. Increasing the worker count therefore does not automatically increase the capacity of the whole system.

Storage hierarchy explains why this concentration matters. Registers and memory are fast but limited and normally volatile; persistent storage supplies capacity at higher access cost. The useful objective is not simply to buy enough disk space, but to keep frequently used data and indexes in memory and avoid unnecessary transfers. A database manages much of that movement while exposing queries instead of raw file offsets. Files can preserve bytes, but implementing multiple indexes and safe concurrent updates on top of files recreates database responsibilities. Before scaling, distinguish capacity, request throughput, durability and coordination: a system can have ample storage capacity while still being unable to complete its peak workload quickly.

chapters.explanation: No. All copies may still wait on the same overloaded database or storage path.

chapters.title: Relational models and query execution
paragraphs: Consider a staff directory containing people, departments and buildings. Each person refers to one department, and each department refers to its building. Keeping the building address in one row means an address correction has one authoritative destination. A person can also have an arbitrary number of positions without inventing position1, position2 and position3 columns: store positions as separate rows connected by identifiers. These references are the reason a normalized schema uses several tables. The final page may look like one object, but its facts have different owners and different repetition patterns. A join reconstructs the view that a particular screen needs from those separately maintained facts.

Follow the arrows in a directory query: select the person, locate the department using the referenced identifier, and then find the building. SQL describes the desired result rather than requiring the application to prescribe every lookup. The database chooses an execution plan. Suppose a different query asks for recent posts written by users over a hundred years old. Starting with the tiny set of qualifying users can avoid inspecting a large fraction of recent posts; starting with recent posts can produce much more intermediate work. Both plans can return the same answer. Their cost depends on selectivity, available indexes and the actual distribution of data, not merely on the number of tables named.

Inspect an execution plan when a query is slow. Ask which table is scanned first, how many rows are expected at each stage, and whether a lookup can use an index. Keep filtering and aggregation near storage when possible: transferring millions of rows to an application to compute a single count wastes bandwidth and application memory. Normalization is not a promise that every query is cheap, and denormalization is not proof that a schema is better. The architectural decision is where the work happens and which updates remain easy to keep correct. Preserve a clear source of truth, then introduce a derived view only for a measured access pattern that justifies its maintenance cost.
chapters.prediction: If a department changes name, how many authoritative rows should change?
chapters.explanation: With the shown normalized schema, one department row changes; staff references retain the same department identifier.

chapters.title: Indexes and their costs
paragraphs: A product catalog can be ordered by price, but that arrangement does not also order it by manufacturer or product name. Scanning the entire catalog for each alternative lookup wastes work. An index supplies a separate search structure containing values and references to the corresponding rows. The printed-catalog analogy is useful: the products need not move when a reader switches from a manufacturer index to a name index. A database goes further because its indexes must support insertions and deletions during operation. Balanced tree structures can preserve efficient lookup without rewriting half the data to make room for every new entry in a physically sorted list.

Now consider a directory query for a particular first name and last name. Two independent indexes can locate either set of matches, but the database may still need to filter or combine those sets. A composite index on first name followed by last name organizes the pair together. Its ordering also explains a limitation: it can support lookups beginning with the first-name component, while a last-name-only lookup generally cannot use that prefix in the same direct way. Index design follows actual query predicates and ordering requirements. The diagram should show the query entering a small search structure and then following a pointer to selected rows, rather than pretending that every row is read.

An index is stored data that must remain consistent with the table. Adding a row can require changes to the table and several separate search structures; changing an indexed value requires removing its old entry and creating the new one. More indexes consume memory and storage and can make writes slower. Therefore, indexing every column as a precaution can damage the workload that matters most. Start with representative slow queries, inspect their execution plans, and compare latency and write cost before and after a candidate index. A primary key identifies rows and enforces uniqueness; a foreign key expresses a reference; an index accelerates an access path. These concepts interact, but they are not interchangeable names for the same guarantee.
chapters.prediction: Will an index on every column always improve a busy system?
chapters.explanation: No. It can increase write maintenance and storage cost without helping the queries that dominate the workload.

chapters.title: Read scaling and failover
paragraphs: Assume a publishing application receives thousands of reads for each edit. Sending all operations to one database makes the read workload compete with the much smaller write workload. A primary with read replicas separates them: the primary accepts changes and streams them to additional copies, while ordinary reads can use those copies. The replicas are not independent authorities allowed to invent conflicting versions. They reproduce the primary's history. This gives the system more places to execute read queries without requiring every write to be decided jointly by all application workers. It also reveals the limit: each replica still needs to process the stream of changes, so replication does not divide the primary's write workload.

Walk through an edit followed immediately by a refresh. The primary has revision 12, while one replica still has revision 11. A read routed to that replica can return an apparently lost edit even though the write succeeded. The replica may be internally consistent with an earlier point in the primary's history, yet it is stale relative to this user's action. Possible policies include reading recent writes from the primary or waiting until a replica reaches a required replication position. Those policies have latency and availability costs. A label saying read replica is incomplete unless the design also explains which reads may tolerate lag and what the user sees when lag grows.

Replicas can contribute to recovery, but read scaling and safe failover are different responsibilities. Promoting a lagging replica can lose changes that were acknowledged only on the old primary. Allowing both old and new primaries to accept writes can create divergent histories. A credible failover design therefore specifies failure detection, fencing, promotion criteria and client reconnection. Monitor replication lag alongside request latency and resource use; otherwise successful but stale reads can look healthy. For a read-heavy service, query improvements, additional memory and replicas may be sufficient for substantial growth. Move to partitioning when the write or storage workload requires division, rather than treating it as an automatic next step after adding a replica.
chapters.prediction: After saving a profile, is any replica safe for the immediate confirmation page?
chapters.explanation: Only if its consistency policy ensures it has the required write; otherwise use an appropriate primary or session-aware read.

chapters.title: Sharding and fan-out
paragraphs: Replication puts copies of the same data on several machines. Sharding instead assigns different rows to different homes, allowing independent writes to proceed on different machines. For a service organized around accounts, an account identifier can determine the shard holding that account's records. A request with that identifier can be routed directly to its destination. The important property is bounded participation: adding more shards should not force an ordinary account request to involve more machines. Co-locating related rows can also keep transactions and joins within one shard. This is why choosing a shard key is a decision about the application's operations, not merely a way to divide a large table into equal pieces.

Now change the question from one account's orders to all orders containing a particular product. If rows are partitioned by account, the product identifier does not identify a single destination. The application may ask every shard, combine results and sort or aggregate them. That scatter-and-gather query grows more expensive as shards are added and can wait for the slowest participating shard. Dividing data can therefore improve one access path while making another harder. The diagram needs both paths: a direct arrow from account key to one shard and a branching arrow from a global query to all shards. A secondary read model may improve the global query, but it creates additional data to maintain.

Balanced row counts also do not guarantee balanced load. One large tenant or popular account can dominate a shard while others remain idle. Measure bytes, operation rate, expensive queries and key popularity, then consider finer partitioning or special handling for hot tenants. Resharding needs a migration protocol that routes reads and writes correctly while ownership changes; changing a modulo divisor is not itself that protocol. Evaluate failure boundaries and transaction scope as well as capacity. A useful design exercise is to list the five most common operations, annotate the shard key available to each, and count participating shards. If the dominant operation touches every shard, more machines may add coordination overhead rather than useful scalable capacity.
chapters.prediction: Does adding more shards necessarily accelerate a global top-ten feed?
chapters.explanation: No. Each feed may still contact every shard, and the coordinator must merge results; skew and network cost can also grow.

quiz.question: A table has indexes on SSN and (firstName,lastName). Which is the natural index for an SSN equality lookup, and why is lastName-only lookup less predictable?
quiz.answer: SSN index targets that equality directly. A B-tree composite index generally favors its leading firstName column; lastName-only efficiency depends on optimizer and data.

quiz.question: Why can read replicas make a recently saved profile appear to revert?
quiz.answer: The write is on the primary while an asynchronous read replica may still hold the older version. Use a suitable primary/session-consistent read policy.

quiz.question: With 8 nodes at 200 requests/s each and 2 node operations per request, what is ideal throughput? What if every request reaches every node?
quiz.answer: Balanced equal-cost model: 8×200/2 = 800 requests/s. Fan-out to all 8 gives 200 requests/s; network, skew and coordination can lower both.

review.issue: Hardware capacities/latencies and PCIe bandwidth are presented as universal.
review.correction: Label all figures illustrative historical values; do not reproduce them as current specifications.

review.issue: Binary trees described as typical disk indexes; primary key described as merely unique.
review.correction: Teach B-tree-family page-oriented indexes; a primary key is unique AND non-null, while unique-constraint NULL behavior depends on database.

review.issue: Composite-index limitations and indexing rules too absolute.
review.correction: Leading-column predicates are generally most efficient for B-trees, but optimizer/index type matter; PostgreSQL can use skip scans. Measure selectivity and EXPLAIN rather than indexing every predicate.

review.issue: N=R presented as optimal replica count.
review.correction: The algebra uses a simplified load model and does not divide total read rate across N replicas consistently. Omit universal optimum; model primary replication cost, per-replica apply cost and distributed reads explicitly.

review.issue: Primary-primary label for active/standby; sharding said to guarantee consistency or forbid SQL.
review.correction: Call it primary/standby failover. Sharding does not itself guarantee transaction consistency. SQL and sharding coexist; cross-shard behavior depends on the product.

review.issue: All SQL sharding must be hacked in application code.
review.correction: Present application-managed sharding as the illustrated architecture, not a definition of all relational databases.

exercise.prompt: A social feed shards data by user ID. Compare fetching one user’s posts with fetching the latest ten posts from all their friends. Explain the role of indexes and read replicas.
exercise.answer: A user’s own posts can be located in one shard and filtered with a suitable index. Friends may span many shards, requiring parallel queries and a merge of candidate results. The shard key trades locality against balance. Read replicas share read load but may lag and do not inherently distribute writes or increase per-replica data capacity.

units.description: Follow keys through a distributed store and reason about replication, partitions, consistency, and quorum availability.

chapters.title: Data locality and denormalization
paragraphs: Imagine drawing a normalized database as a graph. Each row is a node, and each foreign-key reference is an edge. Placing rows on storage machines becomes a partitioning problem: keep related rows together while keeping the machines reasonably balanced. An edge crossing a partition boundary suggests a network lookup during a join. Some graphs divide naturally, such as independent accounts with their own orders. Social relationships and shared reference data are harder because many users connect across any boundary we choose. Even an excellent placement cannot remove every crossing. Counting rows alone misses the workload: a frequently followed edge can matter more than thousands of rarely used references.

Denormalization changes that problem by copying information into the aggregate that needs it. A profile document can contain the region name, employment entries and education entries instead of requiring a separate lookup for each item. Fetching the profile then requires one bounded access path, which is easier to distribute by user identifier. The cost appears when shared information changes. A region rename that once modified one row may now require updates to many profiles, and intermediate states can disagree. Follow the arrows from one shared region to two copied profiles: duplication removes read-time communication but creates write-time maintenance. It moves work and responsibility rather than making them disappear.

A key-value interface does not physically prevent storing references. You can place a region identifier inside a user value and issue another get for that region. However, repeatedly doing this reconstructs application-managed joins, often as serial network round trips. Referential integrity may also become the application's responsibility. The simplified distributed key-value model is useful for understanding this tradeoff, but it is not a complete description of every database sold as NoSQL. Many products provide additional query and transaction features. Judge the chosen model by a specific request: which values must be fetched, whether they can be fetched together, what is duplicated, and how a partially completed update is repaired. Locality is valuable only when its maintenance costs fit the workload.
chapters.prediction: Will copying an industry name into every profile make renaming the industry easier?
chapters.explanation: No. It can make profile reads local, but the rename now affects many copies or requires accepting temporary disagreement.

chapters.title: Hash partitioning
paragraphs: A local hash table turns a key into a storage location. A distributed hash table extends that idea by assigning ranges of hash values to different machines. Suppose a teaching example uses hashes from zero through ninety-nine: node A owns zero through thirty-two, B owns thirty-three through sixty-five, and C owns the remainder. A client hashes an account key, finds the containing range in its routing map and contacts the responsible node. The same key must produce the same hash for all clients using that configuration. No central dispatcher needs to execute every data request, which helps different clients make progress independently as the cluster grows.

Hashing deliberately scatters nearby input keys. That is useful for distributing many distinct keys, but it removes the original key order. Asking for one known account is easy; asking for every account between two identifiers cannot generally be answered by scanning one contiguous hash interval. Nor does a uniform distribution of keys imply uniform traffic: one extremely popular key still maps to one replica group. In the diagram, distinguish the key-to-hash calculation from the routing map. The first is deterministic computation; the second is shared configuration that can change. A correct hash calculation with an obsolete ownership map can still send a request to the wrong machine.

Membership changes expose the coordination that the simple picture hides. When a node joins, leaves or fails, clients and servers must discover current ownership, move or reconstruct data and handle requests during the transition. Virtual partitions or consistent-hashing techniques can limit movement, but they do not replace the migration protocol. Replication also means that one key maps to a bounded group rather than necessarily one physical copy. The scalability argument is therefore conditional: ordinary operations should contact a small number of nodes, work should be balanced, and membership management should not become the dominant cost. Explain these assumptions whenever claiming that capacity grows with node count. A useful test changes both the number of keys and the skew of requests, because the two stress different parts of the design.
chapters.prediction: If one key receives half of all requests, will a better hash spread those requests?
chapters.explanation: No. All requests for that key still map to its owner or replica set unless the application introduces another distribution or caching strategy.

chapters.title: Replication and partitions
paragraphs: A cluster containing many machines should expect individual failures. If every key has only one copy, losing a node makes that node's range unavailable and may lose data permanently. Replication stores each key on several nodes so another copy can survive. Keep the distinction between cluster size and replication factor clear: a cluster might contain hundreds of machines while each key has three replicas. A write to all replicas of one key then involves three destinations, not every machine in the cluster. This bounded redundancy preserves the basic scaling idea while improving durability and recovery options, provided the replicas do not all share the same failure boundary.

Replication introduces a new timing problem. Initially A, B and C store x equal to one. A client writes x equal to two, and A receives the update before B and C. During this interval, different replicas can answer the same read differently even though no disk has failed. Network delays, queueing and scheduling make simultaneous arrival unrealistic. Now imagine that the network separates A from the other copies. If both sides must answer immediately, they cannot always know whether an unseen write has occurred elsewhere. If they must preserve a single real-time-consistent history, some requests must wait or fail. The partition makes this choice unavoidable; it is not solved by drawing more replica arrows.

This is the useful reading of CAP: during a network partition, the system cannot guarantee both linearizable behavior and availability for every request to a nonfailed node. It is not a menu that permits eliminating network failures by selecting two letters, and availability here has a precise meaning beyond an uptime percentage. Designs can make different choices for different operations. A social counter might tolerate a delayed view, while a scarce-item reservation may refuse a decision without the required coordination. Document what counts as a completed write, which failures are tolerated and how replicas converge after communication returns. Redundancy alone says little about the values clients are permitted to observe.
chapters.prediction: Can both sides of a 2+1 split independently accept arbitrary writes while guaranteeing one real-time order?
chapters.explanation: Not while also remaining available for every request; they cannot coordinate the conflicting decisions across the partition.
