chapters.title: Session guarantees
paragraphs: Consistency becomes easier to discuss when we describe an actual user's sequence of operations. Monotonic reads means that after a session observes a version, a later read does not go backward to an older version. Read-your-writes means that after the session completes an update, its later reads include that update or a later one. These promises are different. A user who has never written anything can still suffer a nonmonotonic read when requests alternate between a current replica and a lagging one. A user who saves a profile can fail to read their own write even if every subsequent read consistently returns the same old version.

Draw two read arrows from one client: the first reaches A at version eight, and the second reaches B at version seven. That is a monotonic-read violation. Then replace the first arrow with a completed write of version eight: the same stale second response violates read-your-writes. Routing the session to one sufficiently current node can help, but the promise must survive reconnection and failover. A session can carry a minimum version or replication position that a new node must satisfy. Waiting until that position is applied preserves the promise at the cost of delay; accepting an older response preserves immediate availability at the cost of the promise. The system needs to choose deliberately.

Monotonic writes preserves a session's write order. If a client completes an update and then issues another, delayed delivery must not make the earlier operation overwrite the later one. Sequence information and an ordering protocol can prevent that reversal. Wall-clock timestamps are not a universal solution because clocks differ and concurrent operations need a defined conflict rule. These session guarantees constrain a client's experience; together they still do not establish every property of global linearizability. Test them with histories containing replica switching, retries and failure, rather than only a successful single-node run. For each API operation, decide which ordering information travels with the request and what the service does when it cannot yet honor that information.
chapters.prediction: A client reads version 8 and then version 7 after failover. Which guarantee is broken?
chapters.explanation: Monotonic reads. Read-your-writes is also broken if version 8 represented that client’s own completed write.
chapters.narration: Consistency becomes easier to discuss when we describe an actual user's sequence of operations. Monotonic reads means that after a session observes a version, a later read does not go backward to an older version. Read-your-writes means that after the session completes an update, its later reads include that update or a later one. These promises are different. A user who has never written anything can still suffer a nonmonotonic read when requests alternate between a current replica and a lagging one. A user who saves a profile can fail to read their own write even if every subsequent read consistently returns the same old version. Draw two read arrows from one client: the first reaches A at version eight, and the second reaches B at version seven. That is a monotonic-read violation. Then replace the first arrow with a completed write of version eight: the same stale second response violates read-your-writes. Routing the session to one sufficiently current node can help, but the promise must survive reconnection and failover. A session can carry a minimum version or replication position that a new node must satisfy. Waiting until that position is applied preserves the promise at the cost of delay; accepting an older response preserves immediate availability at the cost of the promise. The system needs to choose deliberately.

chapters.title: Quorums and their limits
paragraphs: A quorum is a threshold of replica responses required before an operation is treated as complete. With three replicas, consider writes acknowledged by two and reads answered using two. If A and B acknowledged a completed write, any set of two read responders must contain A or B. The overlap is the essential arithmetic: R plus W greater than N guarantees intersection between the selected read set and the acknowledged write set, under a stable replica membership. It does not mean the two read values must be identical. A read can receive one older value and one newer value, so the system still needs meaningful version information and a reconciliation rule.

Change the thresholds to see the workload tradeoff. With W equal to three and R equal to one, a completed write has reached every replica, allowing a subsequent read to use a single response under the model's assumptions. But the write must wait for the slowest required participant, and one unavailable replica prevents completion. With W and R both equal to two, one unavailable replica can still leave enough responders for both kinds of operation. This is a latency and failure-policy choice, not just a consistency switch. The relevant replicas belong to this key; another key may have a different replica group and remain unaffected by the same failed machine.

Quorum intersection alone does not implement linearizability. Concurrent writes, partially completed operations, membership changes and version ordering all require a protocol. A timestamp can be useful metadata without being an infallible global clock. A timed-out write may have reached some replicas, so retry handling must account for an uncertain outcome. Distinguish a durable acknowledgment from a response that merely accepted work into volatile memory. When presenting a quorum design, state the failure model, which versions can be returned, how conflicts are resolved and what happens during repair. An excellent exercise enumerates every two-member subset of three replicas, proves the intersection property, and then constructs a concurrent-write history to show what that small proof does not establish.
chapters.prediction: For N=3, R=1 and W=3, what stops when one replica fails?
chapters.explanation: New writes cannot obtain all three acknowledgements. Reads may still obtain one response, subject to the system’s consistency and failure rules.

chapters.title: Stronger consistency and synthesis
paragraphs: Begin with an observable history rather than a product label. A user completes an update to a shared register and then another user starts a read. Linearizability requires that read to behave consistently with a single order in which each operation takes effect at one instant between its invocation and response. Real-time precedence matters: an operation completed before another began must appear earlier in that order. Operations that overlap may admit more than one order. This is stronger than merely preserving each client's own sequence. A diagram should therefore show request and response intervals, not just a list of values with no indication of when clients were told an operation had finished.

Compare that promise with a replicated social display. One session may always read its own updates and never move backward, while another session still sees a previous version. Those session guarantees can make the interface understandable without creating a globally linearizable object. Conversely, a linearizable single-key operation does not automatically make a transaction spanning several keys serializable. The design question is which unit of state needs which guarantee. For a shared reservation count, ordering updates may be essential; for a cached display of recent activity, bounded or eventual freshness may be acceptable. Naming the guarantee prevents students from treating every successful quorum read as proof of the strongest possible model.

Synthesize the data architecture in three separate decisions. Partitioning assigns keys to bounded groups and divides work. Replication supplies redundant copies and creates synchronization questions. Consistency protocols specify when operations complete and which histories clients may observe. These decisions interact but are not synonyms. The final design should identify the key, replica group, acknowledgment rule, conflict behavior and failure response for a concrete operation. Then walk through a normal request, a delayed message and a failed replica. If the explanation cannot say what the client sees in each case, the architecture is incomplete even if its component diagram includes all the expected database boxes. Stronger guarantees can be valuable, but their coordination and availability costs must support an actual application requirement.
chapters.prediction: A write finishes before another client starts a read. May a linearizable read return the prior value?
chapters.explanation: No, unless a later intervening operation legally restored that value; the completed write must precede the later read.

quiz.question: With N=3, R=2 and W=2, why must a read quorum overlap a completed write quorum?
quiz.answer: Two subsets of size two drawn from three replicas share at least one replica. This gives intersection, but correct version/protocol behavior is still needed.

quiz.question: A client reads version 8 then version 7 after switching replicas. Which session property fails?
quiz.answer: Monotonic reads. If version 8 was that client's own completed write, read-your-writes also fails.

quiz.question: Does preserving each client's own write order prove linearizability?
quiz.answer: No. Linearizability also requires a single legal operation order consistent with real-time precedence across clients.

review.issue: NoSQL defined as no references, no schema, one table and one indexed key.
review.correction: Scope this to a teaching key-value model. NoSQL is a family; document/wide-column stores can have schemas, references, secondary indexes and richer queries. Do not define NoSQL by absent joins.

review.issue: Hashing implies no bottlenecks and exact equal data/work distribution.
review.correction: Hash distribution is approximate; hot keys, value size, network, rebalancing and coordination constrain scaling. MD5 demonstration is not a security recommendation.

review.issue: Hexadecimal ranges have inconsistent digit widths and replication diagrams disagree.
review.correction: Use consistent 00000000–3fffffff,40000000–7fffffff,80000000–bfffffff,c0000000–ffffffff. Define replica ownership explicitly rather than transcribing conflicting ranges.

review.issue: CAP pick two and centralized SQL as solution to both timeliness and consistency.
review.correction: State the trade-off specifically during network partitions. Centralization does not guarantee bounded latency or availability. Staleness from ordinary lag is not itself a network partition.

review.issue: MongoDB does not replicate.
review.correction: False: MongoDB replica sets replicate data and support primary election.

review.issue: Quorum overlap with client timestamps treated as sufficient for consistency.
review.correction: State fixed replica-set, completed-write and version-order assumptions. Overlap alone is not a general linearizability proof; concurrent/incomplete writes and clock skew need protocols.

review.issue: Program-order preservation called linearizability; three session properties equated with it.
review.correction: Linearizability additionally respects real-time precedence across clients. Session guarantees are weaker; present them separately.

review.issue: HDFS, BigTable and S3 all described as DHT filesystems.
review.correction: Treat these as different distributed storage designs. Avoid asserting common hash routing or filesystem semantics without product-specific evidence.

exercise.prompt: A key has three replicas. Compare R=2,W=2 with R=1,W=3 when one replica becomes unreachable. State what you can and cannot conclude about consistency.
exercise.answer: Both choices satisfy R+W>N, so successful read and write quorums overlap in the simple fixed-replica model. With one unreachable replica, R=2,W=2 can still meet both quorums; R=1,W=3 can read but cannot complete its configured write quorum. Overlap alone is not a proof of linearizability. Discuss version ordering, concurrent writes, repair, and the failure assumptions.

units.title: Choosing a data store
units.description: Choose storage by workload and correctness requirements, from transactions to analytics, search, documents, and objects.

chapters.title: Start with workload and invariants
paragraphs: Choosing a database starts with the operations the application must perform. A store provides more than persistence: it can supply indexes, concurrency control, analysis close to data and a boundary separating application code from storage management. Consider a workshop service that reserves machines, searches project descriptions and serves tutorial photographs. A reservation changes a scarce resource under concurrency. A search retrieves documents by words rather than by a known identifier. A photograph is a large object usually fetched as a whole. These operations share a user interface, but they ask storage to do different work. Listing them explicitly is more informative than beginning with a contest between SQL and NoSQL labels.

For each operation, write down its lookup key, result size, update frequency and required invariant. A machine cannot have two overlapping confirmed bookings. Search results may tolerate a brief indexing delay, while confirmation cannot depend on an arbitrarily stale availability count. Images may be immutable after publication, allowing long-lived delivery caches. This exercise can justify a relational source of truth for reservations and object storage for media without automatically requiring a separate search service. The first question is whether the simpler existing store can meet the search requirement. Every extra component introduces another update path, recovery procedure and opportunity for two representations to disagree.

Compare candidates using representative queries and failures. A flexible document shape does not remove the need to validate data; a schema does not mean change is impossible. A key-value interface makes a known-key lookup convenient, but an unplanned query may require a scan or a secondary index. Operational constraints also matter: backup restoration, migration, monitoring and the team's ability to diagnose problems are part of the architecture. Finish with an ownership map: which dataset is authoritative, which copies are derived, and which service changes each one. A good selection explains why the required guarantees are achievable with manageable complexity. It does not merely list features that the chosen product happens to advertise.
chapters.prediction: Should video files and seat reservations necessarily use the same persistence interface?
chapters.explanation: No. Large-object delivery and concurrent invariant-preserving updates have different access patterns and can justify different stores.

chapters.title: Transactions and concurrency
paragraphs: A checkout using a gift card changes several related facts: the remaining balance, an order and its line items. Suppose the balance is deducted but the process crashes before inserting the order details. The customer has lost purchasing power without a complete order. A database transaction groups the changes so they commit together or are rolled back together. This is atomicity. Draw a boundary around the balance update, order insertion and line-item insertion; the boundary expresses the all-or-nothing outcome. It does not by itself explain what happens when another checkout reads and changes the same balance concurrently. That requires considering isolation and the update protocol as well.

Let two requests each read a balance of one hundred and each attempt to spend eighty. If both independently decide that funds are sufficient and overwrite the balance with twenty, the system can create two orders while deducting only eighty. A safer approach performs an atomic conditional decrement that succeeds only if sufficient balance remains, checks the affected-row result, and creates the order within the same transaction. The losing request reports insufficient funds. Appropriate row locking or serializable execution can provide other valid protocols. If the order insertion then fails, the successful decrement rolls back. Trace both the competing-request path and the mid-transaction failure; they are distinct tests of correctness.

Distributed transactions add coordination because participants must agree on the outcome despite delay and failure. Keeping a related aggregate within one transaction boundary can simplify the design. An illustrative lock loop is not a production solution unless it also addresses ownership, expiry, crashed holders, stale clients and recovery. Retries create another problem: a client can lose the response after a transaction committed and then submit the same purchase again. An idempotency identifier linked to the recorded outcome can prevent an accidental duplicate. Storage selection should therefore ask which operations must be atomic together and which concurrency conflicts are expected. Prefer a well-supported transaction mechanism over rebuilding these guarantees from a few low-level read and write calls.
chapters.prediction: Does adding BEGIN and COMMIT to the slide’s plain SELECT then overwrite necessarily stop double spending?
chapters.explanation: No. The operation needs appropriate isolation, locking or an atomic conditional update, plus balance validation and failure handling.

chapters.title: Storage models and analytics
paragraphs: Operational requests usually touch a small part of a dataset: retrieve an order, update a delivery status or reserve one seat. Analytical questions often inspect a large fraction: over several years, which districts had the longest delivery times? The first workload values quick individual decisions under concurrency. The second may perform a few expensive scans and aggregations. Both can use tables and SQL, so the query language alone does not identify the right physical layout. A system optimized for thousands of tiny updates is not automatically optimized for a broad historical scan. Begin by tracing how much data the operation must examine and how much it ultimately returns to the application.

Suppose an analytical query needs district, duration and date from millions of delivery records, but not addresses, notes or package descriptions. A column-oriented layout can read the relevant columns together and compress repeated values. The engine groups rows and computes averages close to storage, returning a small result instead of shipping every raw event over the network. The diagram should show many stored rows becoming a few grouped results. This explains the benefit more clearly than saying that analytics needs a faster database. Parallel execution can divide large scans, but layout, compression, pruning and query shape also influence performance; not every analytical query requires a cluster or avoids indexes entirely.

Separating analytics from operational storage introduces a freshness boundary. If an ingestion pipeline updates the analytical copy every fifteen minutes, a dashboard can omit a recently completed delivery even though the operational transaction succeeded. A manager deciding whether a particular delivery is complete should consult the appropriate current source, while a historical trend may tolerate the delay. Record the ingestion watermark and expose freshness where it affects interpretation. Benchmark the actual mix of scans, joins and updates rather than selecting a category from the size of the dataset alone. The architectural goal is to isolate expensive analysis when useful, reduce unnecessary data transfer and preserve a clear explanation of which representation answers each business question.
chapters.prediction: For a three-year average grouped by location, why might reading columns beat fetching complete rows?
chapters.explanation: The calculation needs only selected attributes, so reading and compressing those columns can reduce I/O substantially.

chapters.title: Documents, search and wide-column stores
paragraphs: A document store groups related nested information into an aggregate, such as a profile containing positions and education entries. That representation can match the object an application reads or updates, but a document is not automatically a good search index. Search asks a different question: which documents contain a term or satisfy several text conditions? An inverted index maps terms to document identifiers. If bronze appears in documents four, nine and twelve, while river appears in nine and fifteen, intersecting the lists finds document nine for an AND query. Ranking, tokenization and language handling add more rules, but the posting-list example exposes the core access path without scanning every document's text.

Time-series data suggests another arrangement. Store readings under a partition key composed of sensor identifier and day, then order records by observation time inside that partition. A request for one sensor's morning readings can find the partition and scan a bounded time interval. Hashing the partition key distributes partitions, while the within-partition ordering supports the range query. These are two different roles, so a hash-based design need not make every range query impossible. The diagram should show the device-and-day key selecting a partition before the time range is applied. A query across all devices may need another access path because it does not identify the same bounded destination.

Model the update path alongside the lookup. A changed document must eventually update its search representation, and deleted material must be removed from both. A very active sensor can create a hot or oversized partition even when the key design looks tidy; time bucketing bounds growth but needs sizing against actual rates. Secondary indexes and alternate tables provide useful access paths at a storage and maintenance cost. Product capabilities evolve, so use these abstractions to ask precise questions rather than memorizing historical feature lists. For each candidate, demonstrate the common query, the difficult query and the repair process after a partial update. The best model is the one whose cheap operations align with the workload and whose expensive operations remain manageable.
chapters.prediction: How would a basic inverted index answer a two-term AND query?
chapters.explanation: Find the document-ID list for each normalized term and return their intersection.

chapters.title: Caches and memory data structures
paragraphs: An application cache stores reusable values that help build responses. For example, every page may include the same leaderboard even though the rest of each page is personalized. Caching that leaderboard avoids repeating its calculation without requiring the entire HTTP response to be shared. A reverse-proxy cache operates at a different layer: it reuses complete eligible HTTP responses. Both can reduce load, but they have different keys, owners and invalidation rules. Draw the application between the browser and its value cache, then draw a response cache before the application. The placement makes clear which work is avoided by a hit at each layer and which work still happens.

In-memory stores can expose operations on structures such as sets, counters and sorted sets rather than treating every value as an opaque string. Updating one leaderboard score can then avoid reading, modifying and rewriting the whole ranking in application code. Fast access does not settle durability, however. Ask whether the ranking is authoritative or rebuildable from durable events, what happens after restart, and whether eviction is allowed. Memory is limited, so a cache may discard values according to an eviction policy. Expiry determines how long a cached copy remains eligible for reuse; it does not guarantee that the underlying fact has stayed unchanged during that interval.

A cached availability count illustrates the correctness boundary. The home page can display a slightly old count to reduce repeated reads, while the booking operation checks and changes the authoritative reservation record. Treating the cached count as permission to allocate the last place would turn a performance optimization into a correctness bug. Plan cache misses as well: after a restart, many simultaneous misses can overload the database that the cache normally protects. Request coalescing, controlled warming or other workload-specific policies can reduce that burst. A cache is therefore a complete data-flow decision involving source, key, update policy, expiry and recovery. Its software name or storage medium alone does not tell students whether losing its contents loses business data.
chapters.prediction: If a leaderboard cache disappears, should authoritative course records disappear too?
chapters.explanation: No. If it is designed as a rebuildable cache, the source records remain elsewhere and the leaderboard can be recomputed.

chapters.title: Files, objects and final selection
paragraphs: Files, objects and blocks expose different interfaces. A network filesystem provides familiar paths and file operations, which can be valuable when an existing program expects to open and modify files. An object store provides named objects through a service API and is often convenient for images, recordings and other large media. A block volume exposes lower-level storage on which a filesystem can be built; it is not itself a shared file service. These distinctions affect application behavior. Replacing a mounted directory with an object bucket is not simply a configuration change if the program relies on operations or coordination semantics that the object interface does not provide.

Consider a recording archive. Store the audio object under a stable identifier and keep searchable metadata in a database. A browser fetches media through a delivery URL while the application queries metadata by date, topic or owner. This avoids forcing large media bytes through the same query path as structured records. But the two stores create a workflow: an upload can succeed while the metadata transaction fails, leaving an abandoned object. Publishing metadata before the upload is complete can expose a broken link. The diagram should include the publish step after durable upload, plus a cleanup or retry path. Choosing specialized storage does not remove the need to coordinate its lifecycle with the rest of the application.

Large-scale processing adds a locality question. A distributed filesystem and processing framework can place computation near stored partitions to reduce data movement. Other architectures deliberately separate compute from object storage, trading different operational and performance properties. Neither arrangement is universally best. Finish the selection by identifying the required interface, dataset owner, identifiers, access control, recovery path and expected transfer volume. Test restoration as well as normal retrieval. If a simple database and object store satisfy the workload, adding more storage categories should need a concrete justification. The completed architecture should explain where each byte lives and how users recover from a failure between steps, rather than presenting an assortment of products without a coherent data flow.
chapters.prediction: Can an application replace any mounted filesystem with an object bucket without changing behavior?
chapters.explanation: Not necessarily. It must check required file operations and semantics against the object API and adapt its access pattern.

Publishing metadata before the upload is complete can expose a broken link. The diagram should include the publish step after durable upload, plus a cleanup or retry path. Choosing specialized storage does not remove the need to coordinate its lifecycle with the rest of the application.

quiz.question: Why does START TRANSACTION plus reading a balance into a variable not by itself prevent two checkouts from overspending?
quiz.answer: Atomicity does not guarantee the required isolation. Both may read the same value; use locking or an atomic conditional decrement with balance checks and rollback behavior.

quiz.question: How can a search index answer Watertown AND gift?
quiz.answer: Store a posting list of document IDs for each term, then intersect the two lists; index analysis and normalization determine token matching.

quiz.question: Choose stores for lecture videos, seat reservations and full-text notes search. Explain one reason for each.
quiz.answer: Object storage for large media objects; a transactional database for seat-count invariants; a search engine/inverted index for text retrieval. Integrate them with explicit ownership and update propagation.

review.issue: Repeats CAP/session guarantees errors.
review.correction: Apply the DB 2 corrections: CAP is conditional on partition, and session guarantees are not linearizability.

review.issue: EBS listed as a network filesystem.
review.correction: EBS is block storage; EFS is file storage. Keep object, file and block abstractions distinct.

review.issue: SQL requires all writes on one master.
review.correction: Describe the single-primary relational design in the slides rather than every SQL system. SQL is a query language and relational data model does not dictate one write topology.

review.issue: Gift-card transaction claims atomicity prevents double spend, but plain SELECT then overwrite races.
review.correction: Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with balance validation, or an atomic conditional UPDATE balance=balance-amount WHERE balance>=amount and check affected rows within the order transaction; handle rollback/retry.

review.issue: Distributed transactions must lock all replicas; naive CAS spin lock offered without failure behavior.
review.correction: Present distributed transaction protocols as product-dependent. The sketch lacks leases, fencing, backoff and crash recovery and must not be offered as production code.

review.issue: _id always sharding key; journaling preserves document history.
review.correction: The shard key is configured and need not be _id. Journaling supports crash recovery, not application version history.

review.issue: Ancient product/version and licensing tables presented as current.
review.correction: Label those tables historical and replace with durable design trade-offs. Do not repeat current licensing/protocol/feature claims without checking current vendor docs.

review.issue: NoSQL always disk/persistent, caches always expiring, network filesystems obsolete.
review.correction: These are workload defaults rather than definitions. TTL/persistence/eviction are configurable product policies; file APIs remain appropriate when filesystem semantics are needed.

exercise.prompt: Choose storage roles for an online course service with enrolments, uploaded videos, text search, and yearly analytics. Explain how derived stores stay synchronized without becoming independent sources of truth.
exercise.answer: Use a transactional source for enrolment invariants, object storage for large media, a search index for text retrieval, and an analytical store when broad scans justify one. These are workload-based candidates rather than mandatory products. Define authoritative ownership, change propagation, rebuildability, freshness, access control, and failure recovery for derived indexes and reports.

units.title: REST APIs & serialization
units.description: Design resource operations with clear retry semantics, and turn data structures into valid network representations.

chapters.title: HTTP as an API contract
paragraphs: A network API plays the role of an interface between programs that do not share a process. The caller needs to know what operation is available, how to supply its inputs, and how to interpret success or failure. It should not need to know the implementation language or internal database schema. Consider a weather service: a client requests a forecast for a named location, and the service returns structured data with a documented meaning. The diagram distinguishes the resource identifier, request parameters, and response representation. These pieces form a contract that lets a browser application, a mobile application, or another backend use the same service independently of its implementation.

HTTP provides an existing envelope for that contract. A request selects a target and method, supplies fields such as authorization or accepted media types, and may carry a body. The service responds with an appropriate status and a representation whose content type tells the client how to decode it. For a forecast endpoint, a successful JSON response and an unknown-location error are different documented outcomes. The diagram branches on the service's result rather than assuming every response contains usable forecast data. A client that ignores status and attempts to parse every body as a forecast can turn a clear service error into a confusing application failure.

Design the interface around stable resource concepts and meaningful operations. Query parameters can select a location or filter a collection, while request content can describe a new or replacement representation. Put credentials in an appropriate authorization mechanism rather than exposing secrets in a URL that may be logged. Specify units, timestamps, missing values, validation failures, and authorization behavior in addition to field names. HTTP does not supply these domain meanings automatically. Its value is a common transport-level vocabulary and a large ecosystem of clients, servers, proxies, and diagnostics. The architecture boundary is useful only when callers can rely on both the message structure and the meaning of the result.

chapters.explanation: No. Methods, resource identity, status/error behavior, authentication and data meaning also matter.

chapters.title: Retries and resource identity
paragraphs: A client sends a write and waits, but the connection fails before it receives a response. The server may have completed the write; the client simply cannot tell. Retrying can therefore repeat an operation that already happened. Compare two ways to create a document. A PUT to a client-chosen identifier replaces the representation at that identifier, so repeating the same intended operation has the same effect on that resource. A POST to a collection may ask the server to allocate a new identifier each time, creating two documents after a retry. The diagram follows the lost response, then contrasts the stable target with two newly allocated targets.

The important distinction is the intended effect, not whether repeated responses have identical bytes or status codes. Deleting an existing resource and deleting it again can leave the same final absence even if the second response reports that nothing was found. A safe read does not request a state change; an idempotent write can request a change whose repetition has the same intended effect. For an operation such as charging an account, the API can define an idempotency key and atomically associate that key with one accepted result. The illustration shows a repeated key returning the recorded result rather than initiating a second charge, provided the documented retention and parameter rules are satisfied.

Do not infer retry safety from a method name alone if the implementation violates its contract, and do not assume every method other than POST is automatically idempotent. PATCH, for example, depends on the patch operation. An idempotency mechanism must deal with concurrent duplicate requests, conflicting parameters, failures during execution, and expiration of remembered results. A client also needs a bounded retry policy and a deadline so retries do not amplify an outage. Write down the uncertainty window explicitly: the response is missing, but the effect may already exist. Then show how resource identity, conditional updates, or a deduplication record lets the client recover without creating an unintended second effect.
chapters.prediction: After a timeout, is retrying DELETE /posts/latest as safe as DELETE /posts/42?
chapters.explanation: No. Latest may now identify a different post, whereas 42 remains the same target.

chapters.title: Serialization and references
paragraphs: Objects in memory cannot simply be copied onto a network and expected to retain their meaning in another process. The receiver may use another language, object layout, or machine architecture. Serialization converts values into a defined representation, while deserialization reconstructs useful values from it. JSON works well for combinations of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null, but domain types still need conventions. The diagram shows two different client languages meeting at one wire representation. A timestamp needs a timezone convention, a large numeric identifier may need a string representation, and an absent field must have a meaning distinct from an explicitly supplied null when the API requires that distinction.

References make serialization more interesting than printing nested values. Suppose two people share one hometown object. Embedding the complete hometown under both people repeats data and can obscure that they refer to the same entity. A cycle is worse: if Alice references Ben and Ben references Alice, recursively expanding both objects never reaches a natural end. Assign stable identifiers and serialize a table of objects plus those identifiers as references. The diagram shows two people pointing to one shared city record. The receiver can create the records first, then resolve links, preserving sharing without duplicating the entire city or endlessly following a cyclic chain.

References exchange a simpler-looking nested document for additional coordination. Producers must collect referenced objects, choose identifiers, and ensure they are unique within the stated scope. Consumers must handle missing targets, forward references, and possibly more than one pass through the data. A resource identifier is not a raw memory address, and receiving one does not authorize unrestricted access to that resource. Decide whether the response contains a complete graph, a partial graph with external links, or a convenient snapshot with deliberate duplication. Also define schema evolution: new optional fields, removed fields, and incompatible type changes affect clients differently. Test realistic values and graph shapes rather than validating only a flat demonstration object.
chapters.prediction: What happens if Jess includes Tom, Tom includes Kate, and Kate includes a fully nested Jess?
chapters.explanation: Naive recursive serialization never terminates; IDs turn the cycle into finite references.

chapters.title: Choosing a protocol
paragraphs: Choosing HTTP-based APIs means adopting an ecosystem as well as a message format. Existing libraries handle connections, encryption, compression, and response parsing; established proxies and observability tools can inspect familiar exchanges. For a public catalogue API used by many independent clients, that shared vocabulary can matter more than shaving a few bytes from each response. The diagram connects different clients through one documented interface, with common operational tooling beside it. These benefits still require configuration and correct semantics. A cache does not become safe merely because the protocol supports caching, and encryption does not replace authentication or authorization. Reuse the infrastructure while explicitly defining the application's contract.

Now imagine a high-volume internal call with a stable schema and many generated clients. A schema-driven RPC approach can define operations and types once, generate language bindings, and use a compact representation on the wire. The illustration shows one schema producing two compatible client libraries and a server interface. This can reduce repetitive integration work and catch some mismatches earlier, but it introduces schema-evolution rules, generated artifacts, and tooling that every participant must manage. Serialization format and transport are separate decisions: Protocol Buffers does not itself prohibit HTTP, and an RPC system may use HTTP as its transport. Compare complete stacks instead of treating JSON, HTTP, and RPC as interchangeable categories.

The right choice follows the clients and workload. Consider whether third parties need an easily inspected interface, whether streaming or low-latency calls dominate, whether operations naturally map to resources, and whether the team can maintain compatible schemas over time. Measure payload size, encoding cost, connection behavior, and debugging effort under realistic traffic rather than assuming that binary always wins or that text is always adequate. A smaller message has little effect when database work dominates the response. Conversely, a heavily repeated internal exchange may justify tighter encoding and generated bindings. Document why the chosen protocol fits the boundary and what evidence would justify revisiting that choice later.
chapters.prediction: Does choosing Protocol Buffers imply that the service cannot use HTTP?
chapters.explanation: No. gRPC commonly uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2.

review.issue: Every HTTP method except POST is idempotent; identical result is required.
review.correction: Idempotence concerns the intended server effect of repeated identical requests, not identical responses. Safe methods plus PUT and DELETE are idempotent; do not assume PATCH is. A retry of DELETE can return a different status.

review.issue: Custom headers are frowned upon; verbs in paths define whether RESTful; PUT is always better.
review.correction: Teach noun-oriented resource naming as useful guidance, not the formal definition of REST. Standard headers are preferred when applicable; extension fields are legitimate. POST creation and PUT replacement fit different resource-ID ownership models.

review.issue: API keys in query URLs are shown as ordinary authentication.
review.correction: Use HTTPS and an appropriate authorization header in teaching examples; query credentials can leak through logs and copied URLs.

review.issue: XML hometown tag is unclosed; HTML is asserted to be XML.
review.correction: Use <hometown city="Seattle"/> or an explicit matching end tag. HTML and XML have distinct syntax rules.

review.issue: HTML is an XML document.
review.correction: Ordinary HTML uses HTML syntax; an XML serialization is separately supported.

review.issue: Each UTF-8 character is one byte.
review.correction: The ASCII characters shown use one byte each; UTF-8 encodes Unicode code points using one to four bytes.

review.issue: JSON example includes a trailing comma after hometown_id.
review.correction: Remove the trailing comma; valid JSON does not allow it.

review.issue: Protocol Buffers is a network API transport that does not use HTTP.
review.correction: Protocol Buffers is a serialization format/schema system. gRPC commonly combines it with HTTP/2, so binary encoding does not imply avoiding HTTP.

review.issue: Live third-party demo endpoints may be stale.
review.correction: Use self-contained fictional examples instead of requiring Twitter or obsolete homework endpoints; do not claim these old links were verified.

exercise.prompt: Design creation and deletion operations for submissions so a client can safely retry after a timeout. Include resource identifiers, statuses, authentication, and valid JSON.
exercise.answer: Use stable identifiers or an idempotency key with a defined deduplication lifetime. PUT to a client-chosen stable resource can support retry-safe creation if the semantics fit; POST can also support application-level idempotency. DELETE a stable submission ID, not a moving “latest” target. Define authorization and conflicts. Validate JSON without trailing commas and distinguish protocol semantics from payload format.

units.title: Microservices & client architectures
units.description: Compare a modular monolith with independently deployed services, accounting for contracts, failures, and team coordination.

chapters.title: One deployable application
paragraphs: A monolithic application is one principal deployable application, not necessarily one physical machine. In the historical encyclopedia design, many interchangeable workers run the same application code, each capable of handling the application's request types. A caching proxy in front and a database behind do not automatically turn that application into microservices. The diagram shows one application artifact copied to several workers. Replication increases the capacity for independent requests while keeping the code and release unit together. This distinction prevents a common category error: counting deployment machines tells us about runtime topology, while identifying independently developed and deployed responsibilities tells us about the structure of the application itself.

For a small team, keeping related functionality in one application can make development practical. A developer runs one application locally, steps through one request in a debugger, and can coordinate a database transaction without crossing service boundaries. In the diagram, catalogue lookup, reservation validation, and reservation storage are modules inside the same deployable boundary. They should still have clear interfaces; a monolith need not be an undifferentiated pile of code. The simplicity comes from sharing a runtime and deployment process, not from abandoning modularity. Before splitting the system, identify a concrete limitation that separate services would address and compare that benefit with the new coordination work the split introduces.

As the codebase and team grow, shared releases and dependencies may slow change. A modification in one area can break another, a small feature may require redeploying the whole application, and developers need agreements about shared libraries and data. These are reasons to improve boundaries, testing, and ownership; they are not proof that every module needs a network endpoint. A modular monolith can preserve local calls while clarifying responsibility. Horizontal replication can remain useful under either structure. Evaluate architecture against actual development and operational pressures: independent scaling, release cadence, failure isolation, and ownership. The useful question is which boundary should become independently deployable, not whether a large application deserves a fashionable label.

chapters.title: Choosing service boundaries
paragraphs: A service boundary turns a local collaboration into an explicit network contract. Imagine separating a shop's catalogue from its order workflow because they have distinct owners, change patterns, and scaling needs. The order service asks the catalogue for product information through an API rather than reading its private tables or calling internal functions. The diagram marks both the request boundary and the data owned behind it. Each side can change its implementation while preserving the contract, but only if callers respect that boundary. If every release still requires coordinated changes to both services, the network split has not delivered much independence and may simply have made an existing coupling more expensive.

Splitting a checkout across services also changes failures. A payment service might accept a charge before an inventory reservation fails, leaving a partially completed business operation. There is no automatic single-process rollback across those independent boundaries. The diagram stops the inventory branch after payment succeeds and then adds a compensating action such as releasing or refunding the payment under a defined policy. This is a design decision, not a generic promise that compensation perfectly erases history. Timeouts, duplicate delivery, and uncertain outcomes need explicit handling. Follow the full operation rather than evaluating each small service only in isolation, because customers experience the combined result.

Independent services can use different languages and runtime environments, and can be deployed or scaled separately. Those freedoms introduce costs in tracing, compatibility, operations, and team knowledge. A request may cross several logs and machines before failing, so correlate work across boundaries and assign ownership for failures between teams. Separate data ownership helps prevent accidental coupling, but it makes cross-service invariants and reporting more difficult. Start from cohesive business responsibilities and the information each responsibility controls. Avoid one service per class, table, or technical layer by default. A good boundary reduces the amount of knowledge that must be shared while making the unavoidable communication and failure behavior clear.
chapters.prediction: If every service release requires all other services to release simultaneously, what promised benefit is weakened?
chapters.explanation: Independent deployment; the system retains release coupling despite network separation.

chapters.title: Teams, mocks and multiple clients
paragraphs: When several teams build a system at the same time, agreeing on API behavior allows them to make progress before every implementation is finished. A messaging client can initially call a mock inbox service that returns a fixed list of messages in the agreed response format. The diagram shows the same client first connected to a mock and later to the real service through the same contract. This helps developers build parsing, presentation, and basic error handling early. It does not prove end-to-end correctness: a mock that always returns the same inbox will not reflect newly sent messages, enforce permissions, or reproduce real persistence and concurrency behavior.

The same backend contract can serve several kinds of client. A mobile application, a desktop application, and a browser interface may all fetch messages, send messages, and authenticate through the same service API while presenting different user interfaces. In a traditional web design, a server builds HTML; in a single-page design, browser code obtains data and updates the interface. The diagram shows different presentation layers converging on the same domain operation. These choices form a continuum, and a system can combine server-rendered pages with browser interactions. Moving presentation to the browser does not move the authority to approve operations there: the backend must still validate every request.

Treat mocks as purposeful test doubles with documented limits. Include invalid input, missing resources, permission failures, slow replies, and version mismatches where those cases affect the client. Verify the contract against the real provider before release, and retain integration tests for behavior that a static mock cannot represent. Multiple clients also make compatibility important: a mobile application may remain installed long after a backend deployment. Avoid assuming all callers update together. Add fields and evolve operations with a migration plan that reflects real client lifetimes. This connects team independence to architecture: a shared API enables parallel work only when its semantics are stable enough for each participant to rely on.

chapters.explanation: No. Each client can behave differently or be bypassed; the backend enforces its own contract and authorization.

quiz.answer: One service may succeed while another fails or times out. A cross-service workflow needs explicit consistency and recovery choices, such as idempotent retries and compensating actions.

review.issue: Monolith requires one language and necessarily becomes messy.
review.correction: A monolith is a deployment/architecture choice; modular monoliths can have strong boundaries and mixed-language components. Code quality and coordination costs depend on implementation and organization.

review.issue: Microservices are only a rebranding of SOA.
review.correction: Describe them as a related service-oriented approach emphasizing independently deployable services and bounded responsibilities, not an exact synonym.

review.issue: REST, Thrift, ProtoBuf, GraphQL are interchangeable API formats.
review.correction: These occupy different layers: REST is an architectural style; Protocol Buffers is a serialization/schema system; gRPC is an RPC framework that commonly uses it.

review.issue: Smaller services make testing easy and independent work guaranteed.
review.correction: Unit tests may simplify; contract, integration, failure, and end-to-end tests remain essential. Shared schemas or synchronized releases can recreate tight coupling.

review.issue: Named product architectures read as current facts.
review.correction: Use generic server-rendered and SPA examples; preserve the explicit caveat that many applications combine both.

exercise.prompt: A small team plans a new course-registration application. Compare a modular monolith with separate registration, payment, and notification services. Choose a starting design and define evidence that would justify changing it.
exercise.answer: A modular monolith can keep local transactions and deployment simple while enforcing internal boundaries. Independent services may be justified by distinct ownership, scaling, or release needs, but require network contracts, observability, and partial-failure handling. Payment and registration coordination must be explicit. State team constraints and measure actual bottlenecks before treating distribution as an automatic improvement.

units.title: Load balancing
units.description: Trace requests through local balancers, safe deployments, DNS, CDNs, and anycast.

chapters.title: One service, many workers
chapters.narration: To a client, a load-balanced service can look like one powerful server: it has one familiar interface and accepts requests at a stable entry point. Behind that interface, a balancer selects one of several application workers and relays the exchange. The workers perform the expensive application work; the balancer mainly distributes and forwards it. The diagram makes the apparent single service expand into three workers without changing the client's request format. This is useful only if the selected worker can handle that request. If a session or unfinished operation lives exclusively in another worker's memory, routing to a healthy replica may still produce an incorrect or incomplete result. Distributing equal numbers of requests does not necessarily distribute equal work. Suppose round robin sends one short metadata lookup to worker A, one large export to worker B, and another lookup to worker C. Each has received one request, but B may remain occupied long after the others finish. The diagram assigns different costs to equal request counts. Alternatives such as least-connections or weighted routing use other signals, but those signals are still approximations of useful available capacity. A persistent connection can carry very different amounts of work. Choose a policy based on the service's workload and observe completion latency, queueing, and utilization rather than congratulating the system merely for even counts.

State externalization, database scaling, routing, and redundancy solve related but distinct problems. Trace a request all the way through storage and back before claiming that doubling workers doubles throughput. Finally, define what happens to work already in flight when a worker disappears: routing new requests elsewhere does not automatically finish or safely repeat an interrupted write.

chapters.title: Local routing: L4 and L7
chapters.narration: A layer-four balancer makes routing decisions from transport information such as addresses, ports, and connection state. In a NAT-based implementation, it rewrites addressing information and preserves a mapping so packets belonging to a connection continue to the chosen worker. The return path uses that mapping to make the response appear to come from the public service. The diagram follows one connection through the address translation instead of pretending that every packet is independently assigned to an arbitrary worker. This approach can support protocols beyond HTTP because it does not need to understand application resource names. NAT is one implementation technique, however, not the definition of every layer-four load balancer. An HTTP-aware reverse proxy operates at a different boundary. It can inspect a request path and route image requests to one pool while sending account requests to another. For encrypted HTTP traffic, the proxy must terminate the incoming TLS connection before it can inspect the HTTP message; it may then establish a separate encrypted connection to the selected upstream. The diagram shows the path-based decision after TLS termination, with two possible destinations. That extra understanding enables features such as application routing, compression, and eligible response caching, but also creates configuration and processing work. The proxy must preserve the intended authentication, forwarding, and cache behavior across the boundary.
chapters.focus: Transport routing preserves connection mappings without interpreting HTTP paths.

A reverse proxy can stream data; it need not always hold an entire request or response before forwarding. Likewise, TLS termination does not require unencrypted internal traffic. Choose the layer based on the information the routing decision actually needs, then benchmark realistic requests and failure scenarios. If all connections are equivalent from the routing perspective, transport-level distribution may suffice. chapters.title: Failures and safe deployments
chapters.narration: A rolling deployment replaces workers in stages so the service can remain available. First stop assigning new requests to one worker, then allow its existing work to drain within a defined deadline. Deploy the new version, verify that it is ready to serve, and only then restore it to the active pool before moving to another worker. The illustration separates draining from readiness because removing a worker from new assignments does not instantly end its in-flight work. This procedure needs spare capacity: if the remaining pool cannot handle the workload, a technically orderly rollout can still create excessive queueing and errors for users throughout the deployment. Health checks provide observations that help the balancer decide where to send new work. A failed probe might indicate a crashed process, but it might also reflect overload, a network problem, or a failed dependency. The diagram shows a healthy response maintaining membership and repeated failed observations leading to removal. Thresholds avoid reacting to a single transient failure, at the cost of slower detection. During that interval, some real requests may still reach the affected worker. Explain how the client handles those failures and whether a retry is safe. Removing a worker changes future routing; it does not prove that previous writes did not take effect.
chapters.focus: A safe rollout needs sequencing, spare capacity, and compatibility.

Old and new versions coexist during a rolling update. A client may send consecutive requests to different versions, and both versions may read or write the same database. Compatible API and schema changes are therefore part of deployment design. For example, adding a field before requiring every reader to use it is easier to roll out than abruptly renaming a required field. A deployment that creates a complete new pool before switching traffic uses more temporary resources but can simplify some cutover decisions. Neither strategy eliminates data migration risks. Define rollback behavior, maximum drain time, readiness criteria, and remaining capacity under one additional failure, then rehearse the process under representative load.

chapters.title: DNS and global discovery
chapters.narration: Before a client can contact a service, it often resolves a hostname to an address. DNS distributes this discovery work across a hierarchy and caches answers near clients, avoiding a single central lookup for every request. An authoritative service can provide different addresses to different resolvers or return several candidate addresses. The diagram separates a client's local resolver from the authority that supplies an answer when needed. Many clients may share one cached answer, so varying DNS responses does not imply perfectly even per-request load. After discovery, the client connects to the selected address; DNS is not necessarily consulted again for every application request on that connection. Caching makes a DNS change gradual rather than instantaneous. Suppose a resolver stores Region East at time zero with a ninety-second TTL. At time twenty, the authority begins returning Region West to new lookups. A client asking the same resolver at time fifty can still receive East under the ordinary cache model, because that cached answer has not expired. At time ninety, the resolver can refresh and obtain West. The diagram puts the authoritative change above the still-valid cached copy to explain the overlap. Existing connections and client behavior add further complications, so a TTL is not a promise that every user switches regions at precisely one moment.

Combine global discovery with regional load balancing: discovery selects a region, and a local balancer selects a healthy worker there. Failover also needs the destination's data and dependencies to be ready. A name change cannot recreate missing writes or resolve competing writers in different regions. During an outage exercise, trace a fresh lookup, a cached lookup, and an already established connection separately. That exposes both the time needed to redirect traffic and the correctness assumptions required after it arrives.

chapters.title: CDNs and anycast
chapters.narration: A content delivery network places caching proxies at multiple network locations. A nearby edge can answer an eligible repeated read without contacting the origin that owns the original content. Consider an immutable image identified by a versioned URL. The first edge request misses, fetches the image from origin, and stores a reusable response; later requests use that copy until its policy requires something different. The diagram separates edge storage from origin ownership. This can reduce both origin work and the distance travelled for popular content. A private account page is different: proximity does not make its contents safe to share, and its cache policy must reflect that difference. Anycast solves a traffic-steering problem rather than a content-reuse problem. Multiple network locations advertise reachability for the same address, and routing chooses a path according to topology and policy. The illustration shows one destination address reachable through two sites, with the selected network path deciding which site receives traffic. This does not guarantee the geographically closest server or automatically make either site a cache. A CDN may combine anycast, DNS steering, and caching because those mechanisms answer different questions: where traffic goes, how a client discovers an endpoint, and whether a saved response may replace origin work. Keeping these roles separate prevents misleading claims about what any one layer guarantees.
chapters.focus: A CDN saves origin work only for responses that may be reused.

For a simple load estimate, two thousand eligible requests per second with a ninety-two percent fresh-hit ratio leave about one hundred sixty origin fetches per second, before validation and unrelated traffic. Cache-Control remains authoritative: private excludes shared-cache storage of the whole response, even when a long max-age is present. Global routing also has convergence behavior, and route changes can affect established connections. chapters.title: Design review and self-check
chapters.narration: Design a digital archive for the day a popular collection is released. Public scans use immutable versioned URLs, so an edge cache can answer repeated reads. Reservations for the final research-room seat follow a different route: they must reach application logic and authoritative storage that enforces the booking rule. The diagram deliberately branches after the entry point rather than sending every operation through the same cache. Explain the cache key and eligibility of the read branch, then explain authorization and atomic state change on the write branch. A convincing architecture assigns each layer a responsibility instead of assuming that adding more routing boxes automatically improves correctness or capacity. Now fail one worker while a reservation response is on its way back. The client times out and repeats the request, but the original write may already exist. At the same time, another user tries to reserve the final seat. The diagram shows the retry converging on the original operation record while the competing reservation meets the same capacity constraint. These are two different correctness concerns: deduplicating one user's repeated operation and preventing two users from winning the same seat. A load balancer can select another healthy worker, but the data and operation contracts must make that replacement safe. Describe the uncertain outcome explicitly before claiming the system has recovered.

units.title: A scalable publishing system: the NGVM case
units.shortTitle: A scalable publishing system: the NGVM case
units.description: Evaluate a historical publishing-system design through caching, storage, cost and scaling tradeoffs.

chapters.title: Read the case architecture and its interfaces
paragraphs: Read the publishing architecture by following one request rather than counting boxes. A visitor asks for a memorial page. The web application queries structured records in a relational database and returns HTML containing links to photographs. The browser then requests those media objects separately, potentially through a content-delivery network. A background scraper gathers candidate information for later use, while administrative users edit content through authenticated endpoints. These are different paths with different timing and trust requirements. The application can remain a stateless monolith even though it uses several external services: architectural scalability does not require splitting every function into an independently deployed microservice at the beginning.

Now follow an administrative change. The request must identify the user and check authorization before modifying records. The database owns structured facts such as page details, photo relationships, comments and edit history. The media store owns image bytes. A background task and a public read can therefore touch different components without all work passing through the same synchronous chain. Draw public reads and administrative writes as distinct arrows into the application, then identify which data each operation accesses. This makes the interfaces meaningful. A label such as database says little until we know whether an arrow performs a lookup, commits a change or transfers a large object.

The case is useful because it connects an understandable product to deployable components. A relational schema can express page-to-photo relationships and editor activity, while object storage serves media without treating each image as a relational query result. External email or payment services should appear as dependencies only where their role affects a workflow. Component boundaries also define failure behavior: a media-delivery problem need not prevent reading the text of an already published page, whereas an unavailable authoritative database can block edits. For each arrow, ask what the caller sends, what the callee promises, whether the call must finish before the user receives a response, and what happens if it fails. Those answers turn the diagram into an architecture explanation rather than a catalog of technology names.
chapters.prediction: Does changing an administrative URL to DELETE /victim/{id} make the operation authorized?
chapters.explanation: No. HTTP semantics and naming do not replace authentication or authorization checks.

chapters.title: Place media, caching and operating cost in context
paragraphs: Photographs are stored as objects, with derived sizes for different uses. A page showing a small thumbnail should not force every visitor to download the original full-size image. Generating reusable variants trades some processing and storage for lower repeated transfer cost and faster display. The application can return a media URL while the browser fetches the bytes directly from the delivery path. This separates the cost of constructing a page from the cost of transferring its images. The diagram should show one source image producing several named variants, then a page choosing the size it actually displays. This is a concrete example of moving repeated work out of the request path.

A content-delivery network places reusable media nearer users and reduces repeated requests to the origin. It is not free, and a high hit rate does not mean there is no delivery bill: bytes still travel from the cache to visitors. The case's historical cost breakdown shows why architecture discussions need measurements of both demand and spending. Compute instances, database capacity, object storage, requests and data transfer are separate cost drivers. A fast media path can dominate cost even when application servers are small. Treat the historical dollar amounts as evidence about that particular workload and time, not as current prices or a universal budget for another publishing system.

Cacheability comes from content semantics. Immutable image versions can be reused for a long period, while replacing bytes at the same URL needs an explicit freshness policy. A new versioned URL can make updates predictable, although references and abandoned versions still require lifecycle management. Public content and administrative responses also need different caching rules; a shared cache must not accidentally reuse private editor information. To evaluate a change, estimate requests, bytes per response, cache hit ratio and origin work avoided. Then inspect whether the extra storage, transformation and delivery costs justify the latency improvement. The lesson is that media delivery is an architectural subsystem with its own workload, rather than a decorative attachment to the page-generating application.
chapters.prediction: If an image URL contains a random UUID, is the image necessarily private?
chapters.explanation: No. Anyone with a publicly accessible URL may retrieve it; access permissions determine authorization.

chapters.title: Scale the read path deliberately
paragraphs: Scale the publishing system by asking which resource is doing repeated work. If most requests read public pages, the database may first benefit from more memory, better queries and additional read replicas. A read replica serves another copy of the records, while edits still go through the primary. If page construction becomes the bottleneck, add stateless application instances behind a load balancer. Those instances can share the same authoritative storage because they do not require local per-user state to answer the next request. The progression keeps each change connected to a measured limit. Adding machines to a tier that is not limiting throughput will not solve a bottleneck elsewhere.

The next step can avoid application work altogether for eligible requests. Put a response cache in front of public HTML pages and keep media delivery cached as well. Anonymous visitors requesting the same page can reuse the same response, provided the freshness policy permits it. The architecture now has two filters on origin demand: media hits bypass object-origin retrieval, and HTML hits bypass page construction and its database queries. Follow a cache hit and a miss as separate paths. A hit is short; a miss still uses the complete origin path. The origin must therefore tolerate miss bursts, cache eviction and recovery instead of assuming that the average hit rate will always protect it.

This design works particularly well because the workload permits shared responses. Public readers do not require a personalized recommendation model, and many visible changes can tolerate a short propagation delay. If every response became unique or had to reflect a just-completed write immediately, the same cache arrangement would provide less benefit. Keep edit confirmation and other freshness-sensitive operations on appropriate paths rather than weakening their behavior to improve a headline hit rate. Evaluate tail latency, cache-key correctness and invalidation as part of the scaling change. A stateless monolith, shared cache and relational primary with replicas can support a substantial read-heavy workload; the architecture should become more complicated only when the requirements or measurements justify the additional coordination.
chapters.prediction: Will doubling application instances necessarily double completed requests when the database is saturated?
chapters.explanation: No. The limiting shared resource remains; measure demand and address that constraint.

chapters.title: Evaluate scaling claims with workload evidence
paragraphs: A large monthly total can sound more demanding than its rate actually is. The case projects roughly four hundred thousand monthly write-generating events at two hundred times the traffic: eighty million events per month. Dividing by approximately 2.6 million seconds gives about thirty-one events per second on average. This calculation does not prove that the system can handle the workload, but it challenges the assumption that a large audience automatically requires sharded writes. The diagram should show the conversion from events per month to events per second. Always attach the unit to a number; comparing a monthly event count directly with a per-second device capacity is meaningless.

Next compare the projection with measurements. If a current workload uses about ten storage operations per second, a simple two-hundred-fold projection suggests about two thousand, subject to the assumption that operations grow proportionally. CPU observations provide another estimate, but multiplying core count by current spare capacity is only a rough bound. Lock contention, serial work, memory pressure and changed cache behavior can break linear extrapolation. Likewise, one application event is not necessarily one database write or one storage operation. The purpose of the estimate is to identify plausible capacity and the next experiment, not to replace a load test with arithmetic that ignores the execution path.

Explain why this case is unusually favorable. Much of the traffic is reading public, reusable content; the number of published pages does not increase merely because more visitors arrive; and visitor interactions do not require immediate person-to-person delivery. More repeated visits can even improve cache reuse, so origin load need not grow exactly with audience size. Peak bursts, skew toward popular pages and failure recovery still matter. A defensible claim combines a workload model, current measurements, explicit scaling assumptions and a test at the expected peak with headroom. If requirements change to personalized feeds or strongly coordinated interactions, repeat the analysis instead of transferring the old conclusion. Architecture evidence belongs to the workload that produced it.

exercise.prompt: Design the read and write paths for a 200-fold increase. State what can be cached and how a volunteer sees a just-completed edit.

units.title: Push notifications and connected clients
units.description: Connect devices, choose a delivery channel, and route notifications across changing connections.

chapters.title: Why the server cannot simply call the phone
paragraphs: Imagine a passenger waiting for a car with the ride application in the background. The driver reaches the pickup point and sends an arrival update. The passenger has not clicked anything, so there is no fresh request waiting for a response. Draw the event starting at the driver, entering the ride service, and then needing to reach the passenger. An auction ending is even clearer: a timer can create the event while every participant is idle. Ordinary request and response handles a user asking for information; this requirement adds a path for information to arrive because something elsewhere changed. The notification should point to the saved ride state, so losing the alert does not lose the arrival itself.

A ride arrival or an auction bid happens because another participant acts. The recipient needs an update without repeatedly asking whether anything changed. Yet a phone is not an ordinary public server: its address changes, NAT and firewalls restrict inbound connections, and the application may be suspended. Email and SMS provide useful notification channels, but do not replace every in-app interaction.

Suppose the passenger moves from home Wi-Fi to a mobile network. An address remembered a minute ago may no longer locate the phone. Even a current address may belong to a shared router that does not accept unsolicited inbound traffic. A firewall may block the connection, and the operating system may have suspended the application to save resources. These are separate obstacles; solving only address discovery does not wake a stopped application. Reverse the connection setup instead: the device establishes an outbound path to infrastructure that stays reachable. When connectivity disappears, the path disappears too. Therefore delivery also needs a retention and expiry policy, and the application must refresh authoritative state when it returns.

The architectural requirement is therefore a reachable delivery path, not merely an HTTP endpoint on the device. An outbound connection can establish that path while the device is online. Offline periods still require a policy for retaining, expiring or replacing messages. Distinguish notifying a person from synchronizing the authoritative state: a missed alert should not erase the underlying ride or bid.
chapters.prediction: Would assigning a phone a REST endpoint guarantee that a backend can reach it?
chapters.explanation: No. Address changes, NAT, firewalls and offline periods remain obstacles.
