chapters.title: Registration and mobile delivery
paragraphs: Follow the registration triangle before attempting a notification. First the installed application asks the platform service for a routing identifier, subject to the relevant notification permissions. Next it sends that identifier to its own backend over an authenticated connection. The backend associates the installation with the account. Later a domain event identifies the account, the backend retrieves its registered destinations, and the provider delivers through its connection to the device. The provider identifier is a route to an installation, not a substitute for the account identity. A person may have a tablet and phone, while reinstalling an application may change the route. This is why the registration table must support updates and multiple destinations.

Mobile push services let an application backend address a registered app instance through platform infrastructure. The app obtains a provider-issued identifier and sends it to its authenticated backend. Later, the backend associates an event with the relevant installations and submits a notification. The operating system manages the delivery connection, avoiding a separate continuously active connection for every installed application.

Now compare one hundred applications each maintaining their own connection with one operating-system connection serving them all. Keeping a network path alive requires periodic activity, and reconnecting costs work when the device changes networks. Sharing that responsibility avoids repeating the same machinery for every app. The application backend submits a notification to the platform, which handles the device-facing connection. But a successful submission only establishes that the provider accepted the request. It does not prove that the phone was online, that a banner appeared, or that the person read it. For a ride arrival, keep the current ride status on the backend and let opening the app retrieve it. Treat the notification as a timely prompt to inspect that state.

Treat registration identifiers as changeable routing information rather than permanent user identities. A user can own multiple devices, and a device installation can receive a new identifier. Update registration records and remove invalid destinations. Provider acceptance is not proof of display or user attention; retention limits, connectivity and device policy affect delivery. Use notifications to prompt a state refresh when correctness matters.
chapters.prediction: A push provider accepts a request. Has the user necessarily seen it?
chapters.explanation: No. Acceptance, device receipt, application processing and human attention are separate milestones.

chapters.title: WebSockets, long polling and alternatives
paragraphs: Consider an inbox checked once every sixty seconds. A message arriving immediately after a check can remain invisible for almost a minute. Checking every second improves freshness, but one thousand idle browsers then generate about one thousand requests per second even when no mail arrives. The interval trades resource use against update delay. Long polling changes the exchange: the browser asks for an update and the server leaves that request pending until a message exists or a timeout occurs. The browser immediately starts another request after the response. Draw the long quiet interval as a pending request, not as repeated empty responses. This explains both the low update latency and the need to manage many outstanding connections.

An active browser can open a WebSocket and exchange messages in both directions while the connection remains alive. Long polling instead leaves an HTTP request pending until data or a timeout arrives, then starts another request. Both permit an update to arrive without a fresh user action. Their latency and operational behavior differ from repeatedly making short periodic polling requests.

A WebSocket establishes a persistent channel that supports messages in both directions. For an active collaboration page, cursor updates can travel to the server while document changes travel back without opening a new application-level request for every update. Long polling instead completes an HTTP response and opens the next request. Neither transport removes failure: a laptop sleeps, a proxy closes an idle path, or a server restarts. When reconnecting, the client should identify what it last received and recover missing state according to the application protocol. Otherwise a successful new connection can hide an incomplete view. Choose server-sent events when a one-way server stream fits; choose a bidirectional channel when the interaction actually requires it.

Choose transport from communication needs. Server-sent events provide a server-to-browser stream over HTTP; WebSockets support bidirectional messages. Browser background Web Push is a separate mechanism from an open page connection. Every active connection can break, so design reconnection, authentication renewal and recovery of missed state. A timeout such as sixty seconds is an implementation choice, not part of the definition of long polling.

chapters.explanation: No. Replay or state resynchronization belongs to the application protocol.

chapters.title: Routing to the correct connection
paragraphs: Suppose a browser's live connection terminates at notification worker B. A ride update happens on application worker A. Sending the update to an arbitrary notification worker is insufficient because only B owns the existing socket. A routing registry therefore maps the user's active session to B and its connection identifier. Worker A sends a logical notification to the notification service; the service looks up the destination and forwards to B. The registry is the bridge between a stable business identity and a temporary physical route. Adding a load balancer helps distribute new connections, but does not make all established connections available on every worker. Trace ownership explicitly when drawing a distributed push design.

A distributed notification service must find the worker holding each live client connection. Other backend services should send a logical user notification rather than guess the physical socket owner. A registry connects user and installation identities to provider destinations or live connection identifiers. This allows the notification service to serve multiple devices and browser tabs without duplicating routing logic across domain services.

Now let the user open two browser tabs and also register a phone. One logical event can map to three destinations, possibly using two different delivery mechanisms. Closing a tab makes one route obsolete; restarting its worker can make many routes obsolete at once. A lookup can race with a disconnect, so a routing result is not a guarantee of delivery. Remove invalid destinations and use connection lifetimes or leases to prevent abandoned records accumulating. Decide whether every destination needs the event or whether one current device is sufficient. Persist the business event separately from this transient registry. After a failure, the user can reconnect and retrieve the current ride even if none of the old routes still exists.

Connection records become stale when clients disconnect or workers fail. Remove obsolete entries, renew registrations and tolerate races between lookup and delivery. A managed gateway may expose a connection identifier rather than a raw socket address; the same lifecycle problem remains. Store durable business state separately so reconnecting clients can recover even when transient delivery fails, and authorize both subscription and outbound routing.

chapters.explanation: No. It needs the intended set of current destinations, with per-connection or per-installation lifecycle handling.

chapters.title: Choose what the architecture model must explain
paragraphs: An architectural model records selected design decisions, not every fact about the program. Components, connectors, interfaces, configurations and rationale answer different stakeholder questions. The web-system examples show how a cache, application, database, object store and external services can be placed in a shared picture. The important question is what each element and edge means and which decision the picture helps evaluate.

Choose detail and formality according to the benefit of creating and maintaining the model. Include constraints on interaction, concurrency or behavior when those constraints matter. Static structure and runtime state are different perspectives, although a running system can also change topology through scaling or redeployment. Functional and quality concerns can both be modeled; “prints medical records” leaves speed and confidentiality unresolved until the description specifies relevant conditions and evidence.
chapters.prediction: Is a more detailed model always more useful?
chapters.explanation: No. Detail incurs maintenance and cognitive costs; select what answers consequential stakeholder questions.

chapters.title: Estimate before committing to implementation
paragraphs: Performance modeling can reveal a costly design before a full system exists. Execution graphs estimate scenario work; queueing networks estimate contention; other approaches can use simulation or learned relationships. Models allow early comparison of alternatives and resource needs, but their answers remain conditional on assumptions about operations, infrastructure and workload. A plausible model is an engineering aid rather than a performance guarantee.

Execution models in this unit omit resource contention. Their service costs therefore provide a baseline, not the response a busy production system must achieve. Finding an unacceptable baseline is valuable because queueing will not rescue it. Passing that check does not prove adequate loaded performance. Combine early models with prototypes and subsequent measurements, revising parameters as evidence becomes available instead of treating modeling and testing as mutually exclusive stages.

chapters.title: Reduce execution graphs
paragraphs: Execution graphs make a scenario’s control flow explicit. Basic nodes represent processing steps; expanded nodes refer to another graph. Repetition nodes specify loops, case nodes select alternatives, parallel-and-join nodes wait for all branches and division nodes start work that need not finish before continuation. These distinctions determine whether work contributes directly to the response being measured.

Reduce simple structures while preserving the chosen metric. Sequential times add, a fixed loop multiplies its body cost by the repetition count and a case uses the minimum, maximum or probability-weighted average according to the question. Parallel elapsed time can depend on the longest branch only under assumptions about available resources and synchronization. Keep best path separate from best resource conditions: an average path without contention is still not an average loaded response.

chapters.explanation: 0.9×10+0.1×90=18 ms, plus any case-node overhead.

chapters.title: Translate software actions into resource demand
paragraphs: A basic operation may request abstract software services such as server work, database access and messaging. An overhead matrix maps each service unit onto CPU instructions, disk operations and network messages. Multiplying requested service units by that matrix yields resource quantities, which are then converted into time using device-specific service costs. Carry units through every multiplication to avoid confusing instructions with thousands of instructions.

The authorization illustration combines 3,110 CPU units at .00001 seconds, fourteen disk operations at .02 seconds and one network operation at .01 seconds. The total no-contention service time is .3211 seconds, approximately .32 seconds. These costs can also become device demands for a later queueing model. Keep the per-device vector as well as the scalar sum, because equal total work can create very different bottlenecks on different resources.

chapters.explanation: A contention model needs each resource’s demand to identify utilization and bottlenecks; the scalar total loses that information.

chapters.title: From execution cost to resource contention
paragraphs: A software execution model estimates the resources a scenario demands without competition from other requests. A queueing model adds that competition. A service station contains waiting work and one or more servers, where a server might represent a processor, disk or network link rather than a physical computer. Residence time includes both waiting and service; service time measures the resource work alone.

Kendall notation records assumptions about arrivals, service times, server count, capacity, population and scheduling. In the slide example, total capacity twenty includes three jobs in service and seventeen waiting. State this convention explicitly because “buffer” is ambiguous. Model choices matter: bursty arrivals, finite populations and priority scheduling can produce different behavior even when average service demand is unchanged. A useful model is precise about its boundary and assumptions.
chapters.prediction: Does a two-millisecond service demand imply a two-millisecond response at high load?
chapters.explanation: No. Waiting behind other work adds residence time even if the service demand is unchanged.

chapters.title: Measure throughput and apply operational laws
paragraphs: An execution profile records arrivals, completions and busy intervals over a measurement period. For the supplied twenty-second observation, eight completions yield throughput 0.4 jobs per second and sixteen busy seconds yield utilization 0.8. Average service demand is two seconds per completed job under the accounting assumptions. These measurements describe different quantities; utilization is a fraction, throughput is a rate and residence time is a duration.

The utilization law connects throughput and service demand, U=X×S for a single service resource. Little’s law relates average jobs inside a boundary to throughput and average residence time, N=X×R. Use consistent boundaries and a stable observation regime; do not mix system throughput with a device queue length. The NFS exercise completes 10,800 requests in 1,800 seconds, giving six per second; three active requests imply average residence of half a second.
chapters.prediction: A single encoding device is busy 40% of the time at 800 frames/s. A firmware change reduces mean service per frame to 0.3 ms. What mean service time did the measurements imply before the change, and what utilization is predicted afterward?
chapters.explanation: Before: S=U/X=.40/800=.0005 seconds, or 0.5 ms per frame. After: U=800×.0003=.24, or 24%, assuming the throughput and device boundary stay the same. Lower utilization alone does not establish an end-to-end latency target.

chapters.title: Understand single and multiple server queues
paragraphs: The M/M/1 model assumes Poisson arrivals, independent exponentially distributed service times and one server with an unbounded waiting room. In steady state it requires arrival rate λ below service rate μ. Its utilization is ρ=λ/μ, mean residence time is 1/(μ−λ), and mean jobs is ρ/(1−ρ). These expressions describe long-run averages under the model, not deterministic limits on individual requests.

Birth–death balance explains the geometric state distribution. At an empty system, departure rate is zero; at nonempty states it is μ. Multiple servers change departure capacity to min(n,m)μ and require a different waiting calculation such as Erlang C. Finite buffers change the model again: an infinite-queue tail probability is not automatically the exact blocking probability of a bounded system. Always define whether capacity includes the job being served.
chapters.prediction: What happens to M/M/1 residence time as λ approaches μ from below?
chapters.explanation: It grows without bound in the model; the stable formula cannot be used at or above capacity.

chapters.title: Build an open queueing network
paragraphs: An open network receives external requests, routes them among resources and eventually releases them. A request may visit a device repeatedly. If external arrival rate is λ and average visits are V, device throughput is λV. Multiplying by service time per visit gives utilization. Total demand D=VS separates how often a resource is used from the cost of each use.

Under the simplified single-server station assumptions, each device contributes D/(1−λD) to request response time. Sum these contributions using consistent per-request accounting, and calculate average system population as λR. The ATM example exposes nonlinear scaling: doubling arrival rate increases CPU utilization from 0.468 to 0.936 when CPU visits are twenty-six. Corrected response rises from about 0.447 seconds to 2.699 seconds, rather than simply doubling. The source arithmetic needs repair before reuse.
chapters.prediction: At two transactions/s, 4.5 disk visits per transaction and 20 ms per visit, what are disk throughput and utilization?
chapters.explanation: Disk throughput is 9 I/O/s; utilization is 9×0.02=0.18, or 18%.

chapters.title: Closed populations and model construction
paragraphs: A closed model keeps a fixed population circulating through the modeled workload. Interactive users alternate between thinking and requesting service; their next request depends on completing the previous cycle. An open model instead specifies arrivals from outside. Mixed models can contain both classes. Choosing the workload model is a behavioral decision, not a cosmetic change in how the same diagram is drawn.

To derive a queueing model from execution results, identify resource stations, connect their routes, choose the workload population or arrival rate and estimate service demand. Preserve whether quantities are per visit or per request. Check sensitivity to uncertain inputs and report average-model limitations. In the authorization example, CPU demand 0.0311 seconds and utilization 0.0933 give a CPU response contribution near 0.0343 seconds, exposing the source’s factor-of-ten error before computing the system total.
chapters.prediction: Does a fixed group of users who wait for each response generate a constant external arrival rate independently of delay?
chapters.explanation: No. Their request rate changes with response and think times; a closed interactive model captures that coupling.

quiz.question: A team applies the steady-state M/M/1 response formula at 60 jobs/s with mean service 20 ms. What must you flag before accepting its answer?
quiz.answer: Utilization is 60×.020=1.2. The infinite-buffer M/M/1 station has no finite steady-state mean at this load; a negative value from S/(1−λS) is not a valid response time. Reduce admitted load or increase effective service capacity.

quiz.question: Why cannot device throughputs simply be added to obtain external throughput?
quiz.answer: Each request may visit multiple devices or repeat visits; adding device completions double-counts request work.

quiz.question: A stable processing stage completes 120 jobs/s with mean in-system time 80 ms. Its dashboard labels 9.6 as the mean number waiting. What is wrong with that label?
quiz.answer: Little’s law gives 120×.080=9.6 jobs inside the whole measured stage, including jobs receiving service. It is not the waiting-only population. Use waiting-only time for a waiting-queue population or subtract the measured mean number in service.

quiz.question: For a stable M/M/1 stage with 40 jobs/s and mean service 15 ms, a teammate claims mean residence is also 15 ms. Calculate the missing waiting contribution.
quiz.answer: Utilization is .6 and residence is .015/(1−.6)=.0375 s=37.5 ms. Mean waiting is 37.5−15=22.5 ms. Service time alone excludes queueing delay.

quiz.question: Twelve interactive users each wait two seconds for a response, then think for four seconds before submitting again. With one outstanding request per user and a stable cycle, what throughput is implied?
quiz.answer: X=N/(R+Z)=12/(2+4)=2 requests/s. Only XR=4 users on average are inside the request-processing system; the other eight are thinking. Do not use all twelve as the in-system population with response time alone.

quiz.question: A storage device is busy 60% of the time while completing 150 operations/s. A proposed index makes each request use three such operations instead of two. At the same request rate, what utilization do you predict if per-operation service cost is unchanged?
quiz.answer: The current request rate is 150/2=75 requests/s, and mean device service per operation is .60/150=.004 s. Three visits give 225 operations/s and utilization 225×.004=.90. The extra index may speed reads elsewhere while pushing this device close to saturation.

units.title: Jeromy: Quality-Oriented Decision Analysis (QODA)
units.description: Build a quality tree, prioritize with rank-order-centroid weights, assess alternatives, and defend a decision with evidence and sensitivity analysis.

chapters.title: 1. Define the decision and its business context
paragraphs: Quality-Oriented Decision Analysis (QODA) is Jeromy’s lightweight method for making architectural decisions informed, shared and durable, while allowing deliberate revision. A technology choice becomes an architectural decision when it commits a system to consequential tradeoffs. Jeromy’s approach begins by making the context explicit: whose problem is being solved, what outcomes matter, which constraints apply, and what future changes are plausible. A favorite product is not a substitute for this definition.

The lecture uses a data-querying example at Datadog, where diverse kinds of data and different storage systems make a unified query experience difficult. Keep that as the motivation for the method, rather than assuming any historical product comparison remains a current recommendation.

New worked example used throughout this unit: a campus information service must search course data, export records, survive worker failures, and integrate new data sources. Alternative A is a tailored service; B is a shared platform. Before comparing them, record stakeholders, workload, operating limits, and non-negotiable constraints. The example’s targets and scores are teaching assumptions.
chapters.prediction: Two teams both want a “good platform.” Have they agreed on a decision criterion?
chapters.explanation: No. They may value latency, incident recovery, development effort or cost differently. Name those priorities and the circumstances in which each matters before comparing products.

chapters.title: 2. Turn quality goals into observable scenarios
paragraphs: A scenario gives a quality claim a concrete meaning. The lecture uses context, stimulus and response: the conditions in force, the event that occurs, and the result the system must produce. Make the response measurable where possible. A scenario can concern normal execution, failure, or a development change.

Facilitate the process with stakeholders. The case describes agreeing on context, inviting participants to brainstorm scenarios, refining vague statements, and then clustering the resulting scenarios into a quality tree. This bottom-up collection helps expose concerns that a preselected taxonomy or a product-led debate might miss.

For the campus example, Search means: at 200 requests/second on a specified representative dataset, a user issues a search and p95 latency is at most 250 ms during a defined test window. Export means: an authorized user requests 10,000 records and receives a complete export within eight seconds. Specify hardware, data size and concurrency in an actual evaluation.

Worker loss means: during a request, one serving worker terminates and the request completes correctly within two seconds. New source means: with the platform in production, the team integrates a new catalog source and produces a tested adapter within three engineer-days. These are new scenarios, not copied lecture questions. Check data correctness and authorization as well as timing.

Agree on how evidence will be collected for every scenario: a load test, a fault-injection experiment, a prototype integration, or a justified analysis. A threshold without a test context is not yet a reproducible requirement.

chapters.title: 3. Organize a quality tree
paragraphs: A quality tree organizes the meaning of success. Its upper nodes are qualities such as performance, availability and maintainability. Lower nodes refine those qualities, and concrete scenarios sit at the leaves. The example’s larger tree also illustrates operational and reliability concerns; choose a tree suited to the system rather than treating one taxonomy as universal.

Our compact worked tree has Performance → Search and Export; Availability → Worker loss; Maintainability → New source. The two performance leaves make a tradeoff inside that branch visible. Availability and Maintainability each have one leaf in this teaching example.

Rank only children of the same parent. Ranking Availability against Performance is one conversation; ranking Search against Export is another. Do not mix a top-level quality with a scenario several levels below it. Record the rationale for each ordering and involve the people who bear the consequences.

Check coverage before calculating. Missing a security requirement or representing latency with many near-duplicate scenarios can distort the decision. Mandatory requirements should be recorded explicitly. A high weighted total cannot justify violating a requirement that stakeholders have declared non-negotiable.

Delay advocacy for particular solutions until the criteria and priorities are established. QODA borrows scenario thinking from ATAM, but the lecture presents it as a lightweight decision exercise, not as a complete execution of ATAM.
chapters.prediction: If Performance has ten leaves and Availability has one, must Performance receive ten times the weight?
chapters.explanation: No. The top-level allocation is determined by sibling priorities. Leaf weights subdivide their parent’s allocation. Carefully avoid redundant leaves that double-count the same concern.

chapters.title: 4. Convert rankings to ROC weights
paragraphs: Jeromy uses rank-order-centroid, abbreviated ROC, to turn an ordered set of siblings into weights. For N children and rank k, where 1 is highest priority, w(k) = (1/N) × Σ from i=k to N of (1/i). Each sibling set receives positive weights that sum to one. This is a rule for translating an ordering, not a measurement of how many times one stakeholder value exceeds another.

With three ranked qualities, w(1) = (1 + 1/2 + 1/3)/3 = 11/18 ≈ 0.6111; w(2) = (1/2 + 1/3)/3 = 5/18 ≈ 0.2778; and w(3) = (1/3)/3 = 1/9 ≈ 0.1111. If Performance ranks first, Availability second and Maintainability third, assign those values respectively.

For two siblings the weights are 0.75 and 0.25. Thus Search above Export receives 0.75 and 0.25 within Performance. A node with one child gives it weight 1. Compute weights independently at every branching node; do not reuse the three-child numbers for a two-child branch.

The lecture uses stack rankings. If stakeholders cannot agree on an ordering, capture the disagreement and compare alternative rankings. Do not silently invent a tie-breaking convention or claim that the resulting decimal values remove subjective judgment.

chapters.title: 5. Multiply weights down each path
paragraphs: The combined weight of a scenario is the product of all local weights on its root-to-leaf path. Do not add the weights. The parent allocates a share of the total, and each descendant allocates a share of that share.

Using the worked tree: Search = (11/18) × (3/4) = 11/24 ≈ 0.4583. Export = (11/18) × (1/4) = 11/72 ≈ 0.1528. Worker loss = (5/18) × 1 ≈ 0.2778. New source = (1/9) × 1 ≈ 0.1111. The four leaf weights sum to one, and the two performance leaves sum to 11/18.

A deeper tree works the same way. If a Performance → Latency branch has local weight 0.6111 and a particular latency scenario has local weight 0.75, multiply those by the top-level Performance weight as well. Omitting an intermediate level changes the meaning of the allocation.

Useful checks are local sibling sums, complete path products and the total over all leaves. If the model includes branches with no assessed scenarios, disclose the uncovered weight. Do not silently renormalize the covered leaves and pretend the original decision criteria were fully evaluated.

chapters.title: 7. Test sensitivity and revisit the decision
paragraphs: Change an assumption deliberately and recalculate. If Availability becomes first and Performance second, with Maintainability still third, the top-level weights become 0.6111 for Availability, 0.2778 for Performance and 0.1111 for Maintainability. Search and Export keep their local ordering but receive smaller combined shares.

Under that new ordering, the same score matrix gives A ≈ 1.3750 and B ≈ 2.5139. The preferred alternative changes because stakeholder priorities changed, not because the arithmetic was inconsistent. Explain that causal chain in a recommendation.

Also vary uncertain ratings. In the original ordering, reducing A’s Search rating from 3 to 2 lowers its total by about 0.4583, easily reversing the narrow lead. This identifies where a prototype or benchmark may be valuable. Sensitivity analysis asks whether the conclusion survives plausible changes, not how to tune the inputs until a favorite wins.

The case emphasizes revisiting the framework during planning cycles as business priorities and technologies change. Retain the scenarios, rankings, evidence and rationale so the team can update the decision without reconstructing every discussion. Add new alternatives or scenarios when justified.
chapters.prediction: The ranking changes after stakeholders prioritize recovery. Does that prove the method is broken?
chapters.explanation: No. A preference-sensitive method should respond to a real priority change. Report which assumption changed and whether uncertainty makes the recommendation fragile.

chapters.title: 8. Understand technical debt as a quality gap
paragraphs: Jeromy extends the same framework to technical debt. A deliberate shortcut can buy delivery time by accepting lower quality in specific scenarios. The time saved is the benefit obtained; the obligation is the gap between the desired and actual quality of the system. Repayment effort need not equal the effort initially saved.

New example: a team ships a fixed-format importer in two weeks instead of spending six weeks on a general adapter framework. It gains four weeks now, but the actual system performs poorly on a future “add a source” scenario. Later integrations, changed code and new requirements may make closing that gap more or less expensive than four weeks.

Compare the actual design and a desired design against the same current scenario tree. Inspect weighted per-scenario gaps to locate the important deficiencies, then estimate the work and risk of addressing them. Do not confuse a quality-score difference with engineer-days; the score helps prioritize investigation, while the effort estimate comes from engineering analysis.

The target can change over time. If new-source integration becomes central to the business, its quality gap matters more. If the system is retired, that particular investment may no longer have value. Document the shortcut, affected scenarios, intended benefit, current consequences, and a review trigger. The lecture does not establish a fixed interest-rate formula for technical debt.

chapters.explanation: No. What remains is a quality gap, and the system and its requirements may change. Estimate the current effort to close the relevant gap rather than equating it with the original time saving.

chapters.title: 9. Produce a decision record another team can audit
paragraphs: Your deliverable is a defensible decision record: decision and context; stakeholders and hard constraints; quality tree; concrete scenarios; sibling rankings and rationales; ROC calculations and path products; alternative-by-scenario ratings with evidence; weighted comparison; sensitivity checks; recommendation and review triggers.

Use the interactive lab to reproduce the worked example. First predict the winner, then calculate. Change the top-level order, test an unknown rating, and activate the hard recovery constraint. For each change, write one sentence explaining why the recommendation changes or why the comparison becomes incomplete.

Independent exercise: evaluate two notification architectures for a campus safety service. Create your own contexts, stimuli and responses for urgent delivery, failure behavior, and adding a new channel. Use at least one two-level branch, compute ROC path weights, and compare two alternatives using stated hypothetical evidence. Do not reuse the Search/Export scores as if they were measurements.

Mastery means explaining the reasoning behind every cell. A correct spreadsheet with vague scenarios, hidden missing evidence or post-hoc priorities is not a sound architectural evaluation. A strong answer makes disagreement visible and proposes the next experiment that could change the decision.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of a quality scenario?
quiz.answer: Context, stimulus and response. Make the response observable and specify enough workload and environment detail to support a meaningful assessment.

quiz.question: How do local ROC weights become scenario weights?
quiz.answer: Compute ROC weights among siblings at each node, then multiply the local weights along each root-to-leaf path. Check sibling sums and complete leaf coverage.

quiz.question: Why is a weighted winner not automatically the final choice?
quiz.answer: The ranking depends on priorities, rating anchors, evidence and additive-model assumptions. Missing evidence, mandatory constraints and sensitivity may require further work or exclude a candidate.

exercise.prompt: Create a quality tree and evaluate two architectures for campus safety notifications. Include one hard constraint, four scenarios, a complete ROC calculation, evidence-backed or explicitly hypothetical ratings, and one priority-change analysis.

units.title: Security: Trust, Identity and Access
units.description: Define trust boundaries, protect credentials, and separate authentication from authorization.

chapters.title: Policies, threats and the guard
paragraphs: Imagine a document service where a student successfully logs in and requests another student's private submission. Authentication can correctly identify the requester while the requested read must still be denied. Put a guard before the document operation: it receives the authenticated identity, the action, and the specific document. The policy might permit the owner and assigned marker to read, but nobody else. Draw those inputs separately so identity is not mistaken for authority. Confidentiality is violated if the read succeeds incorrectly; integrity is violated if an unauthorized edit succeeds. Availability asks whether legitimate readers can still obtain access. A useful threat model specifies which requests an attacker can send and which boundaries the system promises to enforce.

Security begins with an explicit policy: who may perform which actions on which resources. A threat model states what an adversary can observe, control or compromise. Confidentiality protects information from unauthorized disclosure, integrity protects permitted changes, and availability protects legitimate access. Attacks are adaptive rather than independent random failures, so one unguarded path may defeat otherwise reliable components.

A permission check can be undermined if later code lets untrusted input rewrite the operation being checked. Suppose a profile query is intended to select only public records. If the application builds SQL by joining strings, hostile input may alter the query's condition instead of remaining a value. The guard may have approved a public-profile lookup while the database executes a broader query. Parameter binding keeps the query structure fixed and supplies input as data. The architectural lesson extends beyond this example: validate the operation that actually reaches the protected resource, and avoid alternate paths that skip mediation. Test a denied request, a malformed request, and an allowed request so the evidence covers the boundary rather than only successful use.

The guard model places a decision before protected operations. Identify the requester, protect the request against modification, and check permission for this resource and action. The SQL example shows why a check is insufficient if untrusted input changes the query structure: a public-profile condition can be bypassed by altered logic. Parameterized queries preserve the distinction between data and commands. Security confidence comes from bounded evidence, not a claim that no defect can exist.

chapters.explanation: No. Authentication identifies the requester; authorization must check permission to view the selected profile and fields.

chapters.title: Security principles as architecture decisions
paragraphs: A backup worker needs to read production data and create a protected copy. Giving it the administrator account also lets it delete production records, disable auditing, or erase every backup. Those powers are unrelated to its purpose. Draw separate credentials for reading production and writing a backup destination, then remove deletion rights where the workflow does not need them. If an attacker compromises the worker, the remaining damage is bounded by those permissions. Least privilege is therefore a design decision about component responsibilities and interfaces, not merely a checkbox on an account. Follow the recovery path too: a backup is useful only if the recovery process can access a trustworthy copy after the production system is compromised.

Least privilege limits the power of each component. Fail-safe defaults deny access unless it is granted. Economy of mechanism favors security logic that can be understood and reviewed. Complete mediation asks where each access decision is enforced and what happens when permissions change. Open design assumes an adversary can understand the mechanism; cryptographic keys and other credentials still need secrecy.

Consider an authorization service that is temporarily unavailable. If an application interprets a timeout as permission, an outage becomes an access bypass. A fail-safe design rejects the protected operation or uses an explicitly bounded, previously authorized decision whose freshness rules are understood. Complete mediation requires examining every route, including batch jobs and internal APIs, rather than protecting only the public page. Defense in depth then adds independent boundaries: a narrow service identity, network restrictions, and storage permissions can still constrain damage when one check fails. These controls must remain understandable to operators. A complicated emergency procedure that routinely requires disabling all checks creates an operational weakness even if the normal architecture diagram looks secure.

Separation of privilege makes sensitive actions depend on multiple conditions, while least common mechanism reduces unnecessary sharing across protection domains. Psychological acceptability makes secure behavior practical for users and operators. Defense in depth combines independent barriers, such as authentication, restricted service permissions and isolation. Apply these principles to the backup example: reading backup data should not automatically imply permission to erase production files. Describe failure behavior and recovery instead of merely listing controls.

chapters.explanation: No. Grant the narrow read and destination-write privileges it needs, and separate restore or delete authority where practical.

chapters.title: Passwords, hashes and protected transport
paragraphs: Suppose a database leak exposes account records. If the records contain plain passwords, the attacker can immediately try them on other services where people reused those passwords. Password verification should instead compare against a dedicated password-hashing result with a unique salt per account. During login, the server repeats the configured calculation using the submitted password and stored salt. The salt is not a secret replacement password: its role is to prevent one reusable precomputed result from serving many accounts. An expensive password-hashing function increases the work required for offline guesses. Rate limiting helps with guesses sent through the login endpoint, but it cannot control an attacker computing guesses independently from a stolen verifier database.

Authentication establishes control of an authenticator associated with an account; it does not automatically prove a legal identity or grant permission. Enrollment binds the authenticator to the account, and later verification checks it. Knowledge, possession and inherence describe different factor categories. HTTPS protects traffic in transit when peer identity and the connection are verified, but application logs and compromised endpoints remain outside that protection.

Trace a password from the browser to the login service over HTTPS. Transport protection prevents an observer along that connection from simply reading or changing the request, provided the peer and connection are correctly verified. Once the request reaches the application, however, the plaintext password may be available to its code. Logging the entire request can copy that secret into another system with different access controls and retention. Requiring the password on every API operation multiplies these opportunities and forces the client to keep a powerful long-lived secret available. Authenticate through the login workflow, then use an appropriately protected session credential for later operations. Transport security, secret handling, and account verification solve different parts of the same journey.

Never store account passwords as plain text or treat a fast general-purpose hash as sufficient password storage. A dedicated password-hashing function with a unique salt makes stolen verifier data more expensive to guess. Salts defeat reusable precomputed tables, not guessing itself. The course examples contrast online guessing, which can be rate-limited, with offline guessing after a database leak. Repeating a password in every API request unnecessarily spreads a valuable long-lived secret.

chapters.explanation: No. The attacker can still test guesses against each verifier; a suitable password-hashing cost raises the work per guess.

chapters.title: Sessions, cookies and phishing resistance
paragraphs: After a successful login, the backend generates an unpredictable session identifier and stores its association with the user and expiry. The client sends that identifier on subsequent requests. In a feed request, the API first translates the token into a user identity, then reads the feed for that identity; it should not trust a separately supplied username as proof of ownership. A cookie can carry the identifier automatically for a browser, while another client may use an authorization header. These are transport choices around the same underlying session idea. Revoking the session invalidates that credential without changing the user's memorized password. The token is still a secret: possession can be enough to impersonate the session while it remains valid.

After authentication, an application can issue an opaque random session identifier and keep its meaning on the server. A browser cookie is one transport and storage mechanism for that identifier. Alternatively, a server can authenticate structured claims using a standard message-authentication or signature scheme. A plain hash of public fields proves nothing about their issuer; inventing a keyed-hash construction is not a substitute for a reviewed protocol.

Now place a cache in front of session verification so every API request does not make another network round trip. Performance improves, but a session revoked at the authentication service may still be accepted by a cache holding an older decision. Choose a bounded lifetime or invalidation mechanism that matches the harm of stale authorization. A temporary browsing session and an administrator action may require different policies. Keep tokens out of ordinary URLs because request paths often reach histories, logs, and monitoring systems. A second factor adds another check, but recovery must protect the same account: a weak reset process can bypass a strong login. Evaluate both normal access and credential loss as complete workflows, including revocation and renewed authentication.

Treat bearer sessions as credentials: whoever steals one may use it until expiry or revocation. Protect transmission, avoid secret-bearing URLs, and design logout, rotation and recovery. A central authentication service changes dependency and caching tradeoffs; cached decisions need a freshness policy. The slides also motivate phishing resistance, but hashing a password with a challenge alone does not provide it. Account recovery and additional factors must be evaluated against the same threat model as login.
chapters.prediction: Would adding H(username | expiration) to a cookie stop a client from changing the username?
chapters.explanation: No. Both the fields and hash algorithm are public, so the client can recompute the hash. Use a standard authenticated token or an opaque server-side session.

chapters.title: Authorization: lists, capabilities and labels
paragraphs: A shared document can authorize access by consulting a list: the guard identifies the requester and checks whether that identity may read the document. A capability-style design instead gives a principal an unforgeable reference carrying narrowly defined authority, such as permission to download one object until a deadline. Presenting the valid capability proves that authority under the scheme's rules. Draw where the policy lives in each case. With a list, changing one central entry can affect future checks. With a copied ticket, revocation may require short expiry, an online revocation check, or another explicit mechanism. Neither design is automatically safer; the choice depends on delegation, sharing, and how quickly permission changes must take effect.

Authorization decides whether an identified principal may perform a particular action on a particular object. In a list-based model, the guard consults permissions associated with identities. In a capability-style ticket model, possession of a valid unforgeable authority-bearing reference grants defined access. The distinction changes delegation, revocation and what a verifier must store. A ticket must not be confused with a printable string anyone can forge.

Suppose an export service must let a browser download one generated report. Giving the browser the service's storage administrator credential would expose unrelated files and future operations. Instead issue authority limited to that report, the download action, and a short validity period. If the user shares that ticket, the recipient may gain the same limited authority, so this sharing behavior must be intentional. Contrast this with mandatory labels: a centrally defined policy can prevent a document owner from granting access outside an approved classification boundary. A hybrid can authenticate the user against organizational policy and then issue a narrow capability for delivery. Trace who can create, copy, inspect, and revoke authority at every stage of that workflow.

Discretionary control allows designated owners to manage access, whereas mandatory control enforces centrally defined policy, often using security labels. Every access-control scheme is policy-based in a broad sense, so that phrase alone does not distinguish mandatory control. Hybrid designs are common: an identity check can issue a short-lived capability for a narrowly scoped action. Trace how permissions are added, delegated and withdrawn, including copies and cached decisions.
chapters.prediction: Why can revoking a transferable ticket be harder than removing a principal from an access list?
chapters.explanation: The ticket may have been copied or delegated. Revocation needs expiry, a revocation check, indirection or replacement of the authority accepted by guards.

chapters.title: Impersonation, replay and trust
paragraphs: Imagine a valid approval message for transferring ten dollars. An attacker captures it and submits it twice. The signature or authentication code may still verify because the contents are genuine; that check alone does not establish that this is a new authorized action. Include an operation identifier, bind the approval to its intended recipient and purpose, and define whether repeated delivery returns the same result or creates another transfer. An expiry limits the usable time window but does not by itself prevent two uses within that window. Freshness, origin, integrity, and authority are separate claims. The protocol must state which evidence supports each claim rather than using the word authenticated as shorthand for all of them.

An authenticated-looking message can still be dangerous if its credential was stolen or its valid contents are replayed at the wrong time. Distinguish origin, integrity, freshness and authority. A legitimate old approval may not authorize a new purchase. Protocols therefore need explicit rules about challenges, expiration, audience and whether an operation can be repeated safely. Compromised keys change the trust assumptions rather than merely producing another bad input.

A login challenge can be sent through an already registered channel to test control of that channel. The challenge must be unpredictable, bound to the relevant attempt, and accepted under explicit expiry and reuse rules. If an attacker controls the recovery mailbox, that control may undermine the protection expected from the login flow. Likewise, a service's good reputation is evidence about past behavior, not a credential authorizing a particular action today. In a collaborative marketplace, reputation might determine how urgently a transaction is reviewed, while access to private records still follows an enforceable policy. Separate confidence in a participant from validation of this message, this account, and this requested effect. Otherwise a favorable history can become an accidental bypass around concrete controls.

The slides broaden the discussion to misrepresentation, collusion, fraudulent actions and unknown participants. Trust is a contextual expectation; reputation is evidence from past behavior. Neither replaces enforceable permissions or proof that a specific message is valid. Credential-and-policy systems and reputation-based systems answer different questions. In a collaborative service, a strong reputation might influence review priority while a resource access decision still follows explicit authorization rules.
chapters.prediction: Can a valid signature alone prove that a request has not already been used?
chapters.explanation: No. Signature validity does not establish freshness or uniqueness; the protocol needs replay controls appropriate to the action.

chapters.title: Browser isolation and the patching lifecycle
paragraphs: A browser renders pages supplied by parties the user does not control. Suppose a malicious page exploits a renderer bug. If the renderer runs with broad access to local files, the exploit can immediately become a data theft problem. A restricted renderer process changes that consequence: privileged operations must cross a boundary to a component that can enforce policy. Draw the boundary between rendering content and accessing sensitive operating-system resources, then label the allowed messages. The design assumes defects may exist and tries to limit what a successful exploit can reach. It does not make malicious content harmless, nor does it prove the boundary implementation is correct. Evaluate both the compromise and the attempted next step beyond the compromised component.

A browser processes content from many parties, so architecture should limit the damage if a parser or renderer is compromised. The historical Chrome case separates a more privileged browser component from restricted rendering processes. Sandboxing and site isolation establish boundaries, while mediated communication allows only selected operations across them. A boundary limits consequences; it does not prove the code inside is free of vulnerabilities.

Once a vulnerability is known, a patch can remove the specific defect while isolation continues to limit damage from other defects. The patch must reach users, so distribution and adoption time matter as much as producing a corrected binary. Regression checks help establish that the fix works without breaking expected behavior. Dangerous-site warnings address a different point in the chain by reducing exposure to known hostile destinations. Draw prevention, containment, and repair as separate stages rather than treating them as interchangeable controls. The detailed browser process topology changes across versions, so use the historical architecture as an example of reasoning about privilege boundaries. The enduring question is what the attacker can do after one layer has failed.

Other measures address different parts of risk. Updates shorten the period in which a known vulnerability remains exposed, and tests help check both the fix and regressions. Dangerous-site warnings reduce encounters with known threats. These mechanisms evolve: the slide-era process and Safe Browsing lookup description should be labeled historical. Connect each control to confidentiality, integrity or availability, and ask what remains possible if one layer fails.
chapters.prediction: Why keep sandboxing if the team rapidly patches every reported renderer bug?
chapters.explanation: Bugs can be exploited before discovery or update installation. Isolation limits consequences during that exposure window.

quiz.question: A student is authenticated but requests another student’s unpublished grades. Which decision is still required?
quiz.answer: Object-level authorization must deny access unless the policy explicitly grants it; authentication alone is insufficient.

quiz.question: What does a unique salt accomplish, and what does it not accomplish?
quiz.answer: It prevents reusable precomputed password tables and identical verifiers for identical passwords. It does not prevent per-account offline guesses; a suitable password-hashing scheme and strong credentials remain necessary.

quiz.question: A file permission is revoked while a process holds an already opened descriptor. What architectural question does this expose?
quiz.answer: Whether revocation affects existing authority or only future opens. State the revocation semantics and avoid assuming a cached authorization decision always reflects current policy.

review.issue: Slides 2-7 extract only page numbers.
review.correction: No visual content was inferred; inspect original visuals before claiming full visual review.

review.issue: Historical UNIX/root/wheel/SSH examples are stated as universal rules.
review.correction: Treat platform behavior as illustrative. Clarify existing-handle revocation semantics; SSH private keys, not public keys, need confidentiality and may need passphrase protection.

review.issue: TLS is said to make interception impossible and never authenticate clients.
review.correction: TLS protects an authenticated channel, not endpoints or logs. Client certificate authentication is supported; ordinary HTTPS commonly authenticates only the server.

review.issue: Generic hash length and slow_hash pseudocode can be mistaken for an implementation recipe.
review.correction: Use a maintained password-hashing implementation with unique salts and an appropriate work factor; do not select an algorithm solely by digest length.

review.issue: H(secret | message) is proposed as cookie protection.
review.correction: Replace the homegrown construction with standard HMAC or a vetted signature/session library; unkeyed hashes do not authenticate origin.

review.issue: HTTP cookies use plaintext URLs and credential query parameters are called reasonable.
review.correction: Use HTTPS and appropriate cookie protections; keep bearer credentials out of URLs and logs. Distinguish cookie transport from the authentication mechanism.

review.issue: AWS access key identifiers are treated like bearer API tokens.
review.correction: Separate public identifiers, secret signing credentials and bearer tokens; do not teach them as interchangeable. Prefer scoped, expiring credentials and explicit rotation.

review.issue: Hashing password plus challenge is claimed to prevent phishing and password recovery.
review.correction: This simple construction permits offline guessing of weak passwords and may permit real-time relay. It is not a phishing-resistant authentication protocol.

review.issue: Email/SMS are described as trusted interchangeable second factors.
review.correction: Account recovery can weaken login assurance. NIST does not allow email as an out-of-band authenticator; PSTN use is restricted, and phishing resistance requires a suitable protocol.

review.issue: All auth tokens are described as random server-stored strings.
review.correction: Opaque sessions fit that model; signed self-contained tokens are another model and require claim validation and revocation planning.

review.issue: The Chrome and Safe Browsing details are presented without dates.
review.correction: Label this as a historical case. Modern site isolation and privacy-preserving real-time lookups go beyond the old two-process/local-list explanation.

exercise.prompt: Design access to a course grade service. Students read their own grades, instructors update grades for their courses, and a backup job reads records. Mark guards, identities, permissions and durable state. Then explain password-verifier theft, session theft and instructor-access revocation without running any attacks.
exercise.answer: Place authorization before each grade read/write and bind it to course and student identifiers. Give students self-read, instructors course-scoped update, and backup read-only authority. Store password verifiers with a dedicated salted hashing scheme, use protected expiring sessions, and define logout/revocation behavior. Separate authentication from permission checks, minimize credential logging, and document how cached decisions and existing sessions react to role changes.

units.title: Design exercise: feeds, fan-out and locality
units.shortTitle: Design exercise: feeds, fan-out and locality
units.description: Compare read-time and write-time feed assembly, partitioning and celebrity fan-out.

chapters.title: Start with normalized data and a read workload
paragraphs: Start with a simple social-feed model: users, follow relationships and posts. Publishing a post inserts one record associated with its author. To read a viewer's feed, find the authors that viewer follows, retrieve their recent posts, join any required author information and order the result. The write path is compact because each post has one authoritative representation. The read path reconstructs a personalized view from several sets of records. This is a sensible starting point, especially at modest scale. The problem is not that relational databases cannot store social data; it is that a heavily used personalized query can require increasingly expensive access to scattered data as the workload grows.

Follow one reader who subscribes to three authors. Their posts are mixed with many other authors' posts in storage and may live on different shards. Indexes help locate relevant rows, but they do not make every reader's selected posts physically adjacent. A feed query can require multiple lookups, remote requests and a merge before returning a small page. Storage systems generally benefit from useful locality, while many small scattered accesses add work and latency. The diagram should branch from the reader's follow list to several author histories and then converge at a sorted feed. This makes the read amplification visible instead of attributing the delay vaguely to a join.

Evaluate the baseline before replacing it. Measure feed reads per second, followed-author counts, posts examined per request, cache reuse and shard participation. Pagination should use stable ordering and bounded work rather than retrieving an unlimited history each time. An index or a better query plan may be enough for the current scale. If reads dominate and the same assembly work repeats frequently, precomputing a reader's view becomes attractive. That change trades work at read time for work when posts arrive, and it introduces derived state that must remain usable after retries and failures. The design exercise is to compare those costs under a stated workload, not to declare one storage category universally fast and another universally slow.
chapters.prediction: Is the presence of a SQL JOIN enough to prove the feed architecture cannot scale?
chapters.explanation: No. Query shape, indexes, locality, caching and workload determine cost.

chapters.title: Materialized feeds and asynchronous publication
paragraphs: Prebuilding feeds moves the join's work earlier. When an author publishes, the system finds the followers and inserts a reference or suitable representation into each follower's materialized feed. A later feed read can use the viewer's identifier to retrieve a compact prepared result. Partitioning feeds by viewer makes the common read involve a bounded storage destination rather than a growing collection of author shards. The benefit is concrete: the reader does less assembly while waiting. The cost is equally concrete: one publication creates many feed updates, and the system stores derived copies. A post with a thousand followers can create roughly a thousand insertions rather than one.

Do not make the publishing request wait for every follower update. First durably record the post and the work that must be performed, then let background workers update feeds. The client can receive an accepted response while propagation continues. This reduces the publisher's waiting time but does not reduce total fan-out work or guarantee that every follower sees the post immediately. In the diagram, separate durable acceptance from background completion. A queue absorbs temporary imbalance between incoming publications and worker capacity, but sustained overload makes backlog and delivery delay grow. Monitor the age of pending work as well as queue length, because a small number of huge fan-out jobs can still produce a long delay.

Retries and partial completion are normal cases. A worker can update some feeds and fail before acknowledging the job. Reprocessing should not create duplicate feed entries, so use a stable post identifier and an idempotent insertion rule. Storing the post and scheduling its distribution also needs a reliable handoff, such as a transactional outbox or an equivalent mechanism, to avoid accepting a post whose fan-out job disappears. Follow changes, deletion and visibility rules require explicit policies for derived feeds. Precomputation is therefore not simply a faster query: it is a maintained read model with a freshness contract and a repair path. Assess its storage and write amplification against the read work it eliminates.
chapters.prediction: If one post targets ten million feeds, does returning immediately make those writes disappear?
chapters.explanation: No. It moves the work into a background pipeline and creates a freshness and recovery obligation.

chapters.title: Partitioning a social graph
paragraphs: Partitioning social data is difficult because different readers want the same post near different places. A viewer's user row and follow-list entries can share a shard, but the authors they follow may be distributed across the entire service. Placing one author's posts beside one follower helps that follower without necessarily helping the others. A popular author can have followers on every shard. This is a conflict in the access pattern, not a failure to invent a clever enough hash function. The diagram should place followers on two shards and connect both to one author, showing why a single physical home cannot be local to every reader at once.

Represent the follow structure as a graph. Users are nodes and follow relationships are edges. A balanced partitioning tries to distribute load while keeping frequently used edges within partitions. Communities can improve locality, but cross-community relationships and high-degree users still create crossings. A perfectly balanced count of users can also conceal large differences in query rate and audience size. Weight the graph by the operations that actually traverse it, not just by the existence of a relationship. Moving an account between partitions can change locality for several neighbors and requires routing and migration work. The useful question is how much communication a placement avoids for the measured workload, rather than whether it makes an appealing picture.

Materialized feeds respond by changing data placement through duplication. Instead of forcing every read to follow all those cross-shard edges, publication pushes post information toward the readers who need it. That makes feed reads local at the expense of a distributed update. There is no disappearance of the graph's work: its traversal moves to a different time and can be handled asynchronously. Keep a durable source of posts so derived feeds can be rebuilt or repaired, and define how deletions and access changes affect existing entries. Compare the alternatives using read frequency, publication frequency, follower distribution and freshness requirements. Good partitioning and denormalization are tools for controlling communication, not guarantees that an arbitrary social workload scales without limits.
chapters.prediction: Can placing an author’s post on one shard make it local to all followers on different shards?
chapters.explanation: No. Readers need remote access, replication or a derived copy; the placement conflict remains.

chapters.title: Hybrid feeds and the celebrity exception
paragraphs: A single publication policy becomes inefficient when follower counts vary by orders of magnitude. An ordinary author with a few hundred followers may be inexpensive to fan out. A highly followed author can create millions of feed updates for one post, delaying propagation and consuming resources even for followers who never open the application. A queue keeps the publisher from waiting for all those updates, but it does not make them disappear. The hybrid idea is to keep materialized feeds for ordinary publications while storing very high-fan-out authors' posts in a separate path that can be consulted when a reader requests a feed.

A feed request now has two inputs. Fetch the reader's prepared ordinary-author entries, then fetch recent posts from the exceptional authors that reader follows, and merge them using the feed's ordering rules. This adds bounded read-time work in exchange for avoiding enormous publication-time expansion. The exceptional-post store can have read replicas or caches because relatively few authors generate its writes while many readers retrieve them. The important asymmetry is write amplification per publication, not a claim that famous users intrinsically perform more API writes than reads. Draw both sources converging at the merge step so students can see precisely which work was retained and which work was deferred.

The cutoff should be a workload decision rather than a fixed celebrity label. Follower count, posting rate, active-follower fraction, freshness target and available worker capacity all affect the tradeoff. If an author changes category, a transition protocol must avoid missing or duplicating posts across the two paths. The merge also needs stable identifiers, consistent ordering, pagination and access checks. A robust implementation can maintain a bounded prepared feed and retrieve additional history when required, instead of assuming unlimited materialization is free. Compare the hybrid against the simpler designs with a skewed audience distribution. Its value comes from recognizing that the expensive tail of the workload behaves differently, then giving that tail a path whose costs are easier to control.
chapters.prediction: What makes a celebrity post expensive in fan-out-on-write?
chapters.explanation: Its very large follower set, not necessarily a high posting rate or writes exceeding reads.
chapters.narration: A single publication policy becomes inefficient when follower counts vary by orders of magnitude. An ordinary author with a few hundred followers may be inexpensive to fan out. A highly followed author can create millions of feed updates for one post, delaying propagation and consuming resources even for followers who never open the application. A queue keeps the publisher from waiting for all those updates, but it does not make them disappear. The hybrid idea is to keep materialized feeds for ordinary publications while storing very high-fan-out authors' posts in a separate path that can be consulted when a reader requests a feed. A feed request now has two inputs. Fetch the reader's prepared ordinary-author entries, then fetch recent posts from the exceptional authors that reader follows, and merge them using the feed's ordering rules. This adds bounded read-time work in exchange for avoiding enormous publication-time expansion. The exceptional-post store can have read replicas or caches because relatively few authors generate its writes while many readers retrieve them. The important asymmetry is write amplification per publication, not a claim that famous users intrinsically perform more API writes than reads. Draw both sources converging at the merge step so students can see precisely which work was retained and which work was deferred.

quiz.question: What work shifts when feeds are materialized?
quiz.answer: Repeated read-time joins/assembly are partly replaced by publication-time fan-out and ongoing view maintenance.

quiz.question: Why can asynchronous fan-out still violate a five-second freshness target?
quiz.answer: The queued workload may exceed processing capacity, especially for high-fan-out authors; acceptance is not completed propagation.

quiz.question: What must a hybrid feed do when the same post appears in both inputs?
quiz.answer: Merge with stable ordering and deduplicate by a canonical post identifier, while enforcing visibility and deletion rules.

review.issue: NoSQL equated to DHTs with perfect scaling and no coordination.
review.correction: This is an idealized partitioned key-value model, not a universal NoSQL guarantee; practical systems have skew, replication and membership overhead.

review.issue: SQL cannot handle large feeds; celebrity writes exceed reads.
review.correction: Performance comes from workload and materialization strategy. Celebrities cause high fan-out; SQL/NoSQL labels do not determine the trade-off.

review.issue: Exercise could be mistaken for real current Twitter architecture.
review.correction: Label all three versions hypothetical teaching designs; the slides themselves call the model theoretical.

exercise.prompt: For a campus feed with 30,000 students and an account followed by all of them, propose a hybrid and define failure recovery.
exercise.answer: Precompute ordinary-author entries; merge campus-wide announcements on read or cache their recent list. Use canonical IDs, stable ordering and bounded pagination; resume fan-out from durable progress and make insertions idempotent; propagate visibility changes and measure freshness.

units.title: Lizhi Liao: from local measurements to system performance
units.description: Combine local performance evidence with architectural models, trace shared-resource contention, and evaluate capacity and asynchronous-design alternatives.

chapters.title: Why local performance is not end-to-end performance
paragraphs: A performance regression is a deterioration in a relevant performance measure after a change. Functional tests can still pass. Lizhi contrasts expensive whole-system tests with small-scale tests that provide earlier, more localized feedback, and asks how to combine their strengths.

Local execution time alone does not determine user-visible response time. In a new fork-and-join example, two independent branches take 40 ms and 12 ms and then join. If the short branch rises to 18 ms, the ideal parallel portion still takes 40 ms. This simplified example assumes no shared-resource contention or other path changes.

Workload mix can also change the importance of a component. A path used by a small fraction of requests may become important when that fraction grows. An architectural model represents call paths, synchronization, resource sharing and workload so the local measurements can be interpreted in context.

The model alone is not sufficient either: a coarse subsystem model can miss a changed function’s service demand. The lecture therefore connects fine-grained performance observations to the broader architectural model.
chapters.prediction: Does a 50% increase in one function’s time imply 50% worse end-to-end response?
chapters.explanation: No. Frequency, critical-path position, parallel execution, shared resources and workload determine how the change propagates. Measure and model those relationships.

chapters.title: Measure deviations with repeated, comparable experiments
paragraphs: The first step runs small-scale tests on original and changed code and collects local performance observations. Keep the inputs, environment and measurement boundaries comparable. Repetition matters because timing varies with operating-system activity, competing processes, warmup and other effects.

The displayed method compares distributions using a Mann–Whitney U test and Cliff’s delta, then uses the mean difference as a performance-deviation quantity. Statistical evidence and effect size answer different questions; neither should be replaced by a single noisy timing run. The slide illustrates repeated runs, not a universal sample size requirement.

When teaching or applying the method, report the measurement protocol, distributions, effect direction and magnitude, thresholds and uncertainty. A small p-value is not the size of a slowdown, and a local distribution difference does not by itself establish a user-visible regression.

New scenario: an updated serializer is consistently slower in isolated tests, but its inputs are larger than the baseline’s. Correct the comparison before attributing the difference to code. Comparable workload is part of the evidence, not an optional detail.
chapters.prediction: A statistically detectable timing difference is automatically a serious production problem. True or false?
chapters.explanation: False. Consider effect size, measurement conditions, the modeled execution path and workload, and the relevant user requirement.

chapters.title: Map code-level changes into an architectural model
paragraphs: The next step maps local deviations to the higher-level modeled activities. The lecture illustrates structural matching using maximum common subgraph analysis, followed by propagation up the relevant call structure so the affected architectural service-demand parameters can be updated.

A mapping must preserve the meaning and units of the measurement. A function’s elapsed time may include waiting or downstream calls; it is not automatically an independent CPU service demand. Record call frequency and nesting so the same cost is not counted once in a parent measurement and again in its child.

Keep original and updated model versions. Change parameters supported by the local evidence and preserve other assumptions unless the code or architecture changed them. Then evaluate both models under relevant workloads and compare the resulting performance distributions.

The approach is useful for prioritizing costly system tests, but a model is only as credible as its structure, mapping, parameters and workload. Validate the baseline and use independent measurements to check predictions. The experimental results shown for TeaStore and TrainTicket are evidence for those studied cases, not a universal no-false-alarm guarantee.
chapters.prediction: Can you add a function’s entire elapsed time to its parent’s demand without further analysis?
chapters.explanation: Not safely. The parent may already include the child’s time or waiting. Establish measurement boundaries, call counts, resource meaning and a mapping that avoids double counting.

chapters.title: Read the QPN model: activities share resources
paragraphs: The demonstration uses QPME, the Queueing Petri Net Modeling Environment. Request paths move through modeled activities and transitions. Queues provide resource contention, while the model can represent different request classes and routing through the system.

An important clarification in the recording is that each visible green place is not necessarily an independent hardware resource. Several places can reference the same underlying queue. In the demonstrated naming scheme, the prefix identifies the resource queue. Different request paths can therefore compete for the same web or authentication resource.

For each shared queue, inspect scheduling discipline, number of servers and service-time assumptions. For each request class, inspect routing, visits and synchronization. Counting diagram nodes as independent servers would understate contention and produce misleading predictions.

Follow one request from entry to completion. For an add-to-cart operation, identify which modeled activities use the same resource and which downstream work the caller waits for. Write a small activity-to-resource table before changing the model. The point is to understand the semantics behind the diagram, not memorize its colors.
chapters.prediction: Two places on different request paths both use the WebUI queue. Do they run on independent capacity?
chapters.explanation: No. They share the modeled queue’s capacity unless the model explicitly assigns separate resources. Distinct places can compete at one resource.
