chapters.title: Use simulation for capacity and architecture experiments
paragraphs: The demo first adds capacity to a highly utilized web resource, then explores moving work into a separate cart service with asynchronous interaction. These are different changes: adding a server changes resource capacity; changing the interaction can change the user’s waiting path and where work contends.

Inspect throughput, utilization, population and residence time as well as end-to-end response. A substantial response-time improvement can occur near saturation even when utilization changes more modestly. Conversely, a quick acknowledgment may leave substantial background work running.

Preserve completion semantics when comparing synchronous and asynchronous designs. Does the response mean the cart update is durable, accepted for later processing, or fully completed? A shorter response is not equivalent behavior if the user-visible contract changed. Also model retries, ordering, failures and backpressure where they matter.

Distinguish uncertainty in a simulation estimate from a latency percentile. A 95% confidence interval for a mean is not p95 request latency. The recording shows simulation output; interpret the reported statistic according to its definition, and avoid transferring its example numbers to a real deployment.
chapters.prediction: Moving work off the response path lowers acknowledgment time. Has the total work necessarily decreased?
chapters.explanation: No. The work may continue elsewhere, with similar utilization or new contention. Compare the same completion semantics and inspect downstream capacity and failure behavior.

chapters.title: Make a prediction and test its limits
paragraphs: The interactive lab is a deliberately smaller model than the lecture’s QPN demonstration. It assumes one M/M/1 queue: Poisson arrivals, independent exponential service times, one server, an unbounded queue and steady state. With service demand S seconds and arrival rate λ per second, utilization is ρ = λS and mean response is R = S/(1−ρ), only when ρ < 1.

New worked example: λ = 75 requests/second and S = 8 ms gives ρ = 0.60 and R = 20 ms. Increasing S to 10 ms gives ρ = 0.75 and R = 40 ms. A 25% increase in local demand doubles the model’s mean response. At λS ≥ 1 the model has no finite steady-state mean; reporting a negative response from the formula would be an error.

Use this calculation to explain amplification, not to claim every request follows an exponential distribution. A real model may need multiple resources, several visits, parallel branches, finite queues and distinct workload classes. Revalidate after an architectural change.

A reviewable analysis records the baseline measurements, local change, mapping, model assumptions, workload, prediction and validation error. Keep calibration evidence separate from validation evidence. Recommend a measurement or experiment that would most reduce uncertainty in the decision.
chapters.prediction: Why is R = S/(1−λS) invalid as a finite steady-state estimate when λS reaches one?
chapters.explanation: Arrivals consume all or more of the service capacity. The assumed queue has no stable finite mean response; the algebra is not a valid continuation beyond the stability condition.

quiz.question: Why combine small-scale tests with an architectural model?
quiz.answer: Local tests expose fine-grained changes early; a system model represents paths, workloads and shared resources that determine end-to-end impact.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a QPN place and a resource queue?
quiz.answer: A place represents part of the modeled execution; multiple places can use a shared underlying queue and compete for its capacity. Inspect mappings rather than counting visible nodes as servers.

quiz.question: Why can asynchronous acknowledgment mislead a performance comparison?
quiz.answer: It may measure acceptance rather than completion. Work, contention and failure handling remain, so compare equivalent semantics and inspect background throughput and delay.

exercise.prompt: Plan a regression investigation for a campus search-and-export service. Identify local tests, a request-to-resource mapping, two workload mixes, an original and changed model, and an independent validation experiment. Explain what your model can and cannot predict.

Compare equivalent completion semantics under stated workloads, record uncertainty, and check predictions against independent system observations. Avoid double counting and treating model output as measured production truth.

units.title: Secure Microservices: Boundaries, Tokens and Response
units.shortTitle: Secure Microservices: Boundaries, Tokens and Response
units.description: Protect service boundaries with verified identities, scoped access, isolation and incident response.

chapters.title: Protect the exposed service boundary
paragraphs: A microservice system has more communication paths and administrative surfaces than one isolated process. Begin by identifying which routes clients actually need. An API gateway can expose those routes, apply common checks and direct requests to internal services. Restricting direct access reduces opportunities to bypass those checks, but the gateway is one control rather than a reason to trust everything behind it.

Client application credentials and user identity answer different questions. A secret embedded in a distributed browser or mobile application cannot be assumed confidential. Apply request limits and protect the infrastructure control plane, while planning gateway capacity and failure behavior. Include outbound dependencies in the trust model: an internal service may call an external endpoint that supplies malicious data or receives sensitive information. Draw both directions of traffic before deciding where checks belong.
chapters.prediction: If only the gateway is publicly reachable, can an internal billing service skip authorization?
chapters.explanation: No. A compromised internal caller or a mistaken route can still reach it. Enforce resource permissions at a trustworthy boundary that cannot be bypassed.

chapters.title: Verify peers and protect channels
paragraphs: Encryption is useful only when the connection reaches the intended peer. Certificate verification links a presented key to a trusted identity under the client’s policy. Accepting every certificate removes that assurance. A self-signed certificate can be deliberately trusted through an authenticated provisioning process; simply accepting any self-signed certificate does not establish the correct peer. Verification includes the intended service identity, not merely a recognizable issuer.

TLS protects data while it crosses the established channel. In mutual TLS, both sides authenticate with certificates; this identifies a workload or client credential, not automatically a human user or permission to perform every operation. Protect private keys and plan issuance, renewal and compromise response. Pinning narrows accepted credentials but adds rotation and recovery responsibilities. Keep authentication, confidentiality and application authorization distinct in the architecture diagram.
chapters.prediction: If a client encrypts traffic but accepts any certificate, has it authenticated the intended server?
chapters.explanation: No. It may establish an encrypted channel to an impostor; identity verification is essential.

chapters.title: Contain compromise inside the cluster
paragraphs: An internal network should not imply unrestricted communication. List the connections each workload requires, then restrict both incoming and outgoing paths. Kubernetes namespaces organize resources but do not automatically isolate their network traffic. NetworkPolicy requires enforcement by the selected networking implementation. Separate intended policy from demonstrated behavior, and test whether an unrelated service can reach a protected dependency.

Outbound restrictions help reduce unwanted destinations and some SSRF consequences, but they complement rather than replace application validation. Runtime monitoring can report suspicious behavior; an alert is not necessarily a preventive control. Resource quotas bound aggregate namespace allocations, while workload requests and limits address individual resource behavior. These measures can reduce blast radius and resource contention without promising to eliminate denial of service. Define who investigates alerts and how a service is isolated without losing essential evidence.
chapters.prediction: Does placing billing and search in separate namespaces block search from contacting billing?
chapters.explanation: No. Namespaces alone do not impose that network boundary; enforced policies and the relevant selectors must establish it.

chapters.title: Token trust, validation and revocation
paragraphs: A signed JWT carries claims plus a signature; its readable payload is not encrypted merely because it is signed. A service needs a validation policy: trusted issuer and keys, permitted algorithms, intended audience, token type and applicable time constraints. A valid signature alone does not establish that this token belongs at this API or that its subject may access the requested record.

Access and refresh tokens have different roles. Short access-token lifetimes limit exposure, while refresh-token rotation or sender constraints address renewal risk. Revoking a refresh token does not magically invalidate every already issued self-contained access token. Central issuance with local verification can reduce repeated authentication calls, but introduces key-distribution and revocation tradeoffs. OAuth concerns delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication conventions. Neither is synonymous with the JWT data format.
chapters.prediction: If a user’s refresh token is revoked, must a locally validated access token stop working immediately?
chapters.explanation: No. Immediate rejection requires an additional mechanism such as introspection or a revocation/version check; otherwise the access token may remain valid until expiry.

chapters.title: Harden each service and its data paths
paragraphs: A service should expose only necessary interfaces and run with limited privileges. Non-root execution, reduced capabilities, a read-only filesystem where feasible and narrowly scoped workload credentials reduce consequences of compromise. Secrets should be managed with explicit access, rotation and revocation rather than hardcoded in source. Environment variables and mounted files each have exposure tradeoffs; a secret store still needs authentication and authorization.

Input handling must match the destination. Parameterized database operations separate data from SQL, contextual output encoding protects HTML contexts, and destination validation plus network controls help constrain outbound URL requests. An ORM can still execute unsafe raw queries. Error handling should avoid disclosing internal details while retaining useful protected diagnostics. Trust forwarded identity or IP information only from configured trusted intermediaries, and order middleware so identity and permission decisions occur before protected work.

quiz.question: A gateway validates a JWT signature. Name two reasons a downstream grade service should still reject a request.
quiz.answer: The token may target a different audience or be expired, and the authenticated subject may lack permission for the specific grade record. Validate the relevant claims and enforce object-level authorization.

quiz.question: Separate namespaces and ResourceQuota objects exist. Does that prove traffic isolation and denial-of-service prevention?
quiz.answer: No. Network policies need supporting enforcement; quotas constrain aggregate allocations and do not stop all runtime exhaustion, request floods or dependency overload.

quiz.question: A service accepts an issuer’s valid signed JWT containing a readable email address. Does the signature make that claim confidential?
quiz.answer: No. Signing protects integrity and issuer authenticity under proper verification; confidentiality requires separate encryption and handling controls.

review.issue: Client secrets and rate limiting are described as universal gateway protections.
review.correction: Public clients cannot safely keep an embedded secret. Rate limiting mitigates some overload and abuse but does not guarantee denial-of-service prevention.

review.issue: TLS and mTLS are framed as one fixed handshake and authentication scheme.
review.correction: Use the conceptual model while noting protocol/cipher-mode differences. Verification must establish intended peer identity; mTLS authentication is distinct from application permission.

review.issue: Self-signed certificates are equated with no trust and pinning with unconditional safety.
review.correction: An explicitly provisioned trust anchor can be self-signed. Accept-all is unsafe; pinning needs deliberate rotation/recovery. Avoid presenting certificate validity as issuer signature alone.

review.issue: Each namespace is described as a network segment.
review.correction: Namespaces alone do not isolate traffic. NetworkPolicy needs a supporting plugin and correctly scoped ingress/egress rules.

review.issue: Egress rules and quotas are claimed to prevent software installation and denial of service.
review.correction: These reduce selected consequences, not all attacks. Quotas govern aggregate namespace resource consumption; combine them with appropriate workload and traffic controls.

review.issue: JWT always has three parts and signature guarantees trust.
review.correction: The three-part example is a compact signed JWS. JWTs may use other protections. Enforce an algorithm allowlist, trusted keys, issuer, audience and relevant claims; signed data is not automatically confidential.

review.issue: Refresh-token use automatically invalidates all compromised user tokens.
review.correction: Token rotation and revocation require explicit server mechanisms. Already issued local-verification access tokens can remain usable until expiry unless additional checks are designed.

review.issue: Not recommended label placement and asymmetric secret-key terminology are ambiguous.
review.correction: Call the issuer key private and verifier keys public. Central issuance with service-side verification is viable; do not condemn it based on ambiguous extracted layout. Clarify OAuth authorization versus OIDC authentication.

review.issue: Forwarded source IP is treated as trustworthy access-control input.
review.correction: Only trust forwarding information from a configured proxy chain that strips or overwrites untrusted values. IP allowlists complement, rather than establish, user/workload identity.

review.issue: One middleware order is presented as universal.
review.correction: Order depends on framework behavior and trust boundaries. Ensure identity exists before authorization, protected work follows checks, and exceptions do not expose secrets.

review.issue: ORMs, sanitization, read-only containers or lack of tools appear sufficient.
review.correction: Use parameter binding and context-specific encoding/validation. Raw ORM queries can remain unsafe. Runtime restrictions and secret-delivery mechanisms need complementary permission, rotation and revocation designs.

review.issue: Uber operations and the slide 50 execution chain may look like current procedures or a lab assignment.
review.correction: Label the case historical and turn it into a discussion-only exercise using synthetic evidence. No RAT execution, credential access, network scanning or exfiltration is part of this generated unit.

exercise.prompt: Draw a course-registration architecture with gateway, identity provider, enrollment service and billing service. State permitted network paths and which identity each hop verifies. Choose triage, containment, evidence and recovery steps; do not interact with live systems.

chapters.title: From polling to separated responsibilities
paragraphs: The historical Uber case begins with rider and driver applications polling for changing trip state. The slides report that polling dominated gateway traffic and that startup requests competed on weak mobile networks. RAMEN separates the decision to send an update from creating its content and delivering it. This division targets both operational efficiency and the difficulty of migrating many existing features.

Fireball reacts to domain events and determines recipients and message types. The API gateway assembles payloads using domain services, reusing logic associated with earlier pull APIs. A delivery system then owns connections and retries. These are case-study responsibilities, not mandatory product names for every architecture. In a course system, enrolment events, timetable composition and device delivery can be separated in the same way.

chapters.title: Priority, expiry and resumable delivery
paragraphs: RAMEN attaches delivery policy to payloads: priority determines which pending updates matter first, expiry limits how long an update remains useful, and replacement can retain the latest state instead of every intermediate version. The historical SSE protocol adds sequence numbers, reconnect cursors and separate acknowledgements. These application mechanisms supply recovery behavior that a persistent transport alone cannot guarantee to the user.

A lost acknowledgement is ambiguous: the client may have processed a message even though the server retries it. Consumers must therefore tolerate duplicates. Expiry also bounds the delivery promise: an offline device cannot receive a timely update indefinitely. Distinguish coalescing state snapshots from deduplicating identical messages; replacing an old location with a new location is reasonable, but dropping an independent payment event is different.
chapters.prediction: If the client processes sequence 3 but its acknowledgement is lost, may sequence 3 arrive again?
chapters.explanation: Yes. Retry can produce duplicates; the client needs safe repeat processing or message-ID tracking.

chapters.title: Scaling connection ownership
paragraphs: The slides describe an early RAMEN implementation using sharded connections and Redis, followed by a redesign separating connection handling, routing and cluster management. Treat the throughput and connection counts as reported historical observations. They illustrate why topology convergence and overloaded event loops can become important even when each individual message is small and the application’s business logic appears straightforward.

In the redesigned case, Streamgate handles protocol and storage work while a frontend routes requests to the appropriate worker. Helix and ZooKeeper manage topology-related responsibilities, and the cache and durable storage layers serve different purposes. The architectural lesson is ownership: changing a worker assignment must be coordinated with routing and recovery. More workers cannot help if clients or producers continue using stale ownership information.
chapters.prediction: Can doubling connection workers help if routing still sends all requests to the old owner?
chapters.explanation: Not reliably. Membership and routing convergence are part of the scaling design.

chapters.title: Protocol evolution and the reliability boundary
paragraphs: The case identifies long-tail delivery problems involving acknowledgement loss, inconsistent client behavior and limitations of the earlier unidirectional stream. Its later protocol work explores bidirectional communication and more standardized client support. Separate the enduring requirement from a particular transport choice: the service needs feedback about progress, recoverable state and a clear policy for clients whose networks disappear for extended periods.

Bidirectional streaming can carry acknowledgements promptly, but it does not turn a network failure into certainty about application effects. Define exactly what each acknowledgement means and which state survives a worker restart. The source’s reported server-side reliability is not an end-to-end guarantee that a person received or acted on an alert. Evaluate transport changes by measured recovery behavior and implementation consistency.
chapters.prediction: Does changing from SSE to a bidirectional RPC stream automatically create exactly-once application processing?
chapters.explanation: No. Durable state, acknowledgement meaning and duplicate handling still determine application effects.

chapters.title: Describe a style through its constraints
paragraphs: An architectural style defines a vocabulary of components and connectors together with constraints on their organization and behavior. A label such as layered or client–server is therefore only the beginning of a description. Identify what components do, what communication means and which arrangements are permitted. The same graph shape can represent different styles if its edges have different semantics.

The opening examples combine several ideas: distributed communication, objects, layers and pipelines. Real systems can combine styles, so classification should clarify a design rather than force an exclusive label. Ask what problem a style addresses, which invariants must hold and what advantages require those invariants. The slide list includes implicit invocation but does not develop a dedicated treatment; event-driven content elsewhere can supply that connection without implying it is fully covered here.
chapters.prediction: Can one system use both repository and pipeline structures?
chapters.explanation: Yes. Different responsibilities or views may combine styles; explain where each applies and how their constraints interact.

chapters.title: Repository and blackboard architectures
paragraphs: A repository architecture centers collaboration on a shared body of information. Independent components read or modify that state according to a common schema. An IDE offers a useful example because multiple tools can inspect and transform program information. A blackboard specialization allows cooperating computations to contribute partial results that other computations use, with coordination organized around the evolving shared information.

Centralized data management can consolidate access policy, backup and concurrency control. It also creates coupling through the data model: a schema change can affect many consumers even when their code does not call one another. Persistence and distribution are implementation choices, not automatic consequences of drawing one repository box. Ask who owns schema evolution, how concurrent updates are coordinated and whether the repository becomes a capacity or availability constraint.
chapters.prediction: If repository clients never call each other, are they independent of each other’s changes?
chapters.explanation: Not completely. They share schema and data semantics, so changes can affect other clients through the repository.

chapters.title: Pipes, filters and compiler hybrids
paragraphs: Filters transform streams and pipes carry output to subsequent input. In the pure style, filters avoid shared state and do not depend on the identity of adjacent filters. Compatible data contracts let stages be replaced or reordered when semantics allow. A pipeline is a linear specialization; batch sequential processing waits for an entire input batch before the next transformation produces its result.

The shell example illustrates composition, while the compiler history shows why pure categories can be insufficient. Compiler phases may follow an ordered pipeline while sharing symbol tables or an intermediate representation, forming a hybrid with repository structure. Streaming can support overlap, but throughput, buffering and synchronization still matter. Data conversion between stages introduces cost, and interactive feedback may require additional coordination beyond a one-way transformational flow.

chapters.explanation: No. It combines pipeline sequencing with shared repository state.

chapters.title: Objects and layers as boundaries
paragraphs: Object-oriented organization groups state with operations that preserve its invariants. Clients should rely on a contract rather than internal representation. Shared mutable objects can still create unexpected interactions when one client changes state another observes. Encapsulation reduces certain dependencies, but does not make every implementation change invisible or require hard-coded identities in every caller; indirection can manage references.

Layering organizes services by abstraction and restricts dependencies between them. Strict layering normally permits adjacent interactions; relaxed designs document deliberate bypasses. A layer is logical organization, while a tier describes deployment separation, so several layers may reside in one process or tier. Stable contracts can localize changes, but effects may propagate when behavior or assumptions change. Evaluate dependency direction and runtime cost instead of assuming a fixed upper bound on affected layers.
chapters.prediction: Does a three-layer codebase require three physical servers?
chapters.explanation: No. Layers express logical responsibility; deployment tiers and server count are separate choices.

chapters.title: Interpreter and virtual-machine architectures
paragraphs: An interpreter architecture represents a program as data and uses an execution engine to advance it. The model distinguishes the interpreted program, its state and the engine’s state. This separation can make an unavailable machine or language executable on an existing platform. It also introduces responsibility for instruction semantics, validation and runtime behavior that ordinary direct execution may not expose in the same way.

Virtual machines need not be implemented solely through interpretation. The JVM specification defines an abstract machine without requiring a particular implementation technique; compilation and hybrid execution are possible. The deck’s Java and compiler-bootstrap examples connect runtime organization to build-time architecture. Portability depends on the specified abstraction and compatible implementations, while performance depends on execution strategy and workload. Treat specific implementation-version statements as historical examples unless they have been rechecked.

chapters.title: Control systems and feedback
paragraphs: A process-control architecture aims to keep a controlled variable near a desired set point. Sensors measure relevant variables, and a controller chooses changes to manipulated variables. Cruise control provides a concrete vocabulary: desired speed is the set point, measured speed is feedback and throttle is manipulated. These roles describe the causal relationship, not merely a chain of function calls.

Feedback adjusts actions using observed results; open-loop control does not use the controlled output to correct its action. An open-loop approach may be adequate under predictable conditions, while disturbances make feedback valuable. A software architecture must also consider measurement delay, failure and actuator limits, even if a simple block diagram omits them. Preserve the distinction between an explanatory teaching model and a design validated for a safety-critical application.
chapters.prediction: If a heater follows a fixed schedule without measuring temperature, is it closed-loop temperature control?
chapters.explanation: No. Without feedback from the controlled variable, it is open loop for temperature.

chapters.title: Client–server responsibilities and remote calls
paragraphs: Client–server organization gives one component a requesting role and another a service-providing role in an interaction. A file server supplies files, while a database server can execute queries near the stored data and return selected results. Remote communication makes message meaning, latency, availability and discovery part of the design. One component may act as server for one interaction and client for another.

Centralizing a service can simplify management and allow heterogeneous clients, but horizontal scaling depends on state, coordination and routing. Query processing at the server may reduce transfer for selective queries; it does not guarantee small responses for every workload. Location transparency can simplify interfaces without removing network failure. Explain timeout, retry and authorization responsibilities alongside the boxes so the design remains meaningful when a service is slow or unavailable.
chapters.prediction: Is a remote database query equivalent to a local procedure call in its failure behavior?
chapters.explanation: No. Communication failures and ambiguous outcomes require explicit timeout, retry and consistency reasoning.
chapters.narration: Client–server organization gives one component a requesting role and another a service-providing role in an interaction. A file server supplies files, while a database server can execute queries near the stored data and return selected results. Remote communication makes message meaning, latency, availability and discovery part of the design. One component may act as server for one interaction and client for another. Centralizing a service can simplify management and allow heterogeneous clients, but horizontal scaling depends on state, coordination and routing. Query processing at the server may reduce transfer for selective queries; it does not guarantee small responses for every workload. Location transparency can simplify interfaces without removing network failure. Explain timeout, retry and authorization responsibilities alongside the boxes so the design remains meaningful when a service is slow or unavailable. Is a remote database query equivalent to a local procedure call in its failure behavior? No. Communication failures and ambiguous outcomes require explicit timeout, retry and consistency reasoning.

chapters.title: Peer-to-peer structure and practical hybrids
paragraphs: Peer-to-peer systems distribute service roles among participants rather than assigning all work to one permanent server. Peers can both request and provide data, and the overlay need not connect everyone directly. BitTorrent distributes pieces among participants, allowing downloaders to contribute verified pieces before completing the entire file. A complete participant can continue serving as a seed, but partial participation is already useful.

Decentralized data transfer does not imply the absence of centralized discovery or bootstrap dependencies. The source’s original Napster characterization should be treated as a hybrid example rather than a proof of fully decentralized control. Availability and privacy depend on the actual protocol, peer behavior and metadata exposure. Networks can partition, peers can disappear and discovery can fail, so assess resilience from concrete replication and routing mechanisms rather than from the peer-to-peer label alone.
chapters.prediction: Must a BitTorrent participant finish the entire file before uploading useful data?
chapters.explanation: No. The protocol allows peers to exchange available pieces while downloads are still in progress.

quiz.answer: A layer organizes logical functionality or abstraction; a tier describes deployment separation.

exercise.prompt: Choose a style or hybrid for an IDE, a log transformation job and a room-temperature controller. State one invariant and one risk for each.
exercise.answer: IDE: repository-centered tools share a program model; schema evolution couples clients. Log job: pipes and filters agree on record format and avoid shared state; buffering and conversion can bottleneck. Temperature controller: feedback adjusts output from measured temperature; delayed or faulty sensing can undermine control.

units.title: Asynchronous processing and message queues
units.description: Separate acceptance from completion and design queue-based work for retries and backpressure.

chapters.title: Accepted is different from completed
paragraphs: Sending an email can involve several relays before the destination accepts it. If the original client waits for that entire chain, a slow or temporarily unavailable destination keeps the compose interface waiting. An asynchronous contract lets the first service accept responsibility and return before final delivery. The response still matters: without it, the client cannot distinguish acceptance from a lost network request. But its meaning has changed from completed to accepted for later work. Draw two separate milestones on the timeline, first acceptance and then delivery. A quick response is honest only if the interface describes the first milestone. The user should not see a delivery guarantee when the system has merely stored work that it intends to attempt.

A synchronous request returns after the promised operation finishes; an asynchronous request can return once the system accepts responsibility for later work. Both can use HTTP. The important distinction is the contract, not whether a response exists. Sending an email, preparing a large download or provisioning a virtual machine can return an operation identifier while the requested work continues elsewhere.

A report export may take several minutes, but the user still needs the finished file or a useful failure explanation. Create an operation record and return its identifier immediately after durable acceptance. The client can revisit that record while its state moves from pending to running to successful or failed. A callback is another option when the receiver has an accessible endpoint, but it needs authentication and retry handling. A browser that closes is not automatically a reliable callback server. For a consequential operation, hiding all failures in an operator log leaves the user unable to act. Choose the feedback path together with the acceptance contract, and retain the result long enough for an interrupted client to recover it.

Clients that need an outcome can poll an operation record, receive an authenticated callback or use another notification channel. Define pending, running, successful and failed states and explain retention. A webhook needs an accessible endpoint and its own retry policy. A user-facing acknowledgement should say accepted when completion is still uncertain; operational logs alone are rarely sufficient feedback for a consequential user action.
chapters.prediction: Does an immediate successful HTTP response prove the email reached its recipient?
chapters.explanation: Only if the API explicitly promises that milestone; an asynchronous acceptance usually does not.

chapters.title: Queues as durable work contracts
paragraphs: A user publishes a short message. The API authenticates the session, records the request, and places a publication job on a queue. The job contains the author, message identifier, content reference, and fields the publication worker needs. That schema plays the role of an interface: a producer and consumer must agree on its meaning even though they do not run simultaneously. The publication worker later finds the followers and updates their feeds. Optional notification jobs go to another queue because sending an alert has different dependencies and retry behavior. Drawing these stages explains why one cheap API call can trigger thousands of later operations without making the user wait for every individual feed write and device delivery.

A queue lets a producer describe work and hand it to consumers that run later. The message schema is an interface contract, including identifiers, required fields and version behavior. In the tweet example, one service accepts publication work, another expands it into feed updates, and another handles optional notifications. This separates stages with different cost, latency and failure requirements.

Now stop a worker immediately after it adds a post to a feed but before it acknowledges the queue message. The broker may deliver that message again because completion was never confirmed. Without duplicate protection, the same post can appear twice. An idempotency key lets the consumer recognize that this logical operation has already produced its effect. A second failure window exists at publication: updating business data and then separately enqueueing a message can leave a committed post with no downstream work if the process crashes between them. A transactional outbox records the business change and pending event together, then publishes the event later. Reliability depends on these boundaries, not merely on calling the queue durable.

Acknowledge consumer work after the intended durable effect, then plan for crashes between effect and acknowledgement. Retried work may repeat, so use idempotency keys or transactional coordination where required. Durable acceptance also depends on how publication reaches the queue; changing a database and publishing separately creates a failure gap. A transactional outbox is one design for recording the event alongside the business change.
chapters.prediction: A worker updates a feed then crashes before acknowledging its job. What may happen?
chapters.explanation: The job can be delivered again; the feed update must tolerate repetition.

chapters.title: Independent scaling and queue boundaries
paragraphs: Suppose requests arrive at three hundred jobs per second for ten seconds, while consumers can process two hundred per second. The queue gains about one thousand jobs during the burst. If arrivals then fall to one hundred per second, the spare processing capacity drains that backlog in roughly ten more seconds, assuming constant job cost. This is demand smoothing: the work is delayed, not eliminated. Producers and consumers can be sized separately because enqueueing a job is different work from executing it. However, the broker must still accept and retain the backlog safely. A useful capacity argument accounts for the burst duration, consumer throughput, and acceptable waiting time instead of saying that a queue makes the system scale.

Queues distribute pending work across consumers and smooth a temporary mismatch between arrival and processing rates. Producers and consumers can scale independently, but the broker has its own capacity and durability limits. An in-process queue is simple but may vanish with the process. A separate broker or replicated service provides different persistence and recovery options, with additional operational cost and coordination.

An in-process queue is convenient for a thread pool, but its pending work can disappear when the process exits. A separate queue service outlives an application restart, provided its own persistence and recovery configuration support that promise. A replicated broker adds another failure boundary and additional coordination. Retained logs add a different property: reading a record does not necessarily delete it, and consumers track their own positions. One analytics consumer can replay older records without forcing a delivery consumer to repeat the same history. These choices determine recovery behavior and storage cost. Draw the producer, storage boundary, and consumer position explicitly rather than representing every queue product as the same anonymous cylinder.

Pull-based and push-based delivery affect connection management rather than determining business correctness. Retained logs differ from destructive work queues: a log keeps records for replay, and consumers track progress. Kafka illustrates partitioned logs, although the slides’ ZooKeeper discussion is historical. Select retention, consumer grouping and acknowledgement semantics deliberately instead of assuming all products listed as queues behave identically under load or failure.

chapters.explanation: No. It delays the symptom while backlog grows; capacity, admission or demand must change.

chapters.title: Backpressure, ordering and recovery
paragraphs: Continue accepting work faster than workers can finish it and a finite queue eventually fills. At that point the system must delay the producer, reject new work, shed a lower-priority class, or increase usable capacity. Pretending that acceptance still succeeds merely moves the failure to an unknown later time. Monitor the oldest waiting job as well as queue depth: one hundred very expensive jobs may be worse than ten thousand trivial ones. Adding consumers helps only if the downstream database or external provider can support them. Draw backpressure as a signal from the saturated stage toward admission, not as a mysterious error at the end. The goal is to preserve a truthful service contract under overload.

A bounded queue must eventually reject, delay or otherwise regulate producers when it cannot safely accept more work. This backpressure is a protective control rather than merely an error to hide. Monitor oldest-message age as well as depth, because a small queue of expensive jobs can still violate latency goals. Retry policies should use limits and backoff instead of continuously recycling failures.

An account receives an address change followed by a shipment request. Even if a queue delivers them in that order, two workers can finish the shipment first while the address update is still running. Retrying an older change can create a second ordering problem after newer work has already completed. When order matters, choose a scope such as account identifier and coordinate processing or use version checks within that scope. Putting every account on one globally serial path avoids some races but sacrifices unnecessary parallelism. Repeatedly failing jobs also need bounded retries and a controlled recovery path; otherwise one poison job can consume capacity forever. Make the business invariant determine the ordering rule, rather than assuming the broker's terminology guarantees it.

Ordering is scoped to the chosen system and partitioning design. Many brokers offer useful per-key or per-partition order, but concurrent consumers and retries complicate observed completion order. Group related work by key or use sequence checks when order matters; merging everything into one giant message is not the only solution. Keep public clients behind an authenticated application boundary unless the messaging service explicitly supports that access model.

chapters.explanation: Yes, for example through account-key partitioning and ordered processing, while allowing different accounts to proceed independently.

quiz.question: What should an asynchronous submission response return when the caller needs a result later?
quiz.answer: An operation ID or status resource and a clear acceptance contract, with eventual outcome retrieval or notification.

quiz.question: Why is idempotency necessary with at-least-once delivery?
quiz.answer: A message can be processed again after an uncertain acknowledgement or retry; repeated processing must not repeat an unintended effect.

quiz.question: Which is more informative than queue depth alone for user-visible delay?
quiz.answer: Oldest-message age and processing latency, alongside arrival/processing rates and failure/retry counts.

review.issue: Queue insertion described as almost free and async always faster.
review.correction: Durable replication, validation and contention have costs; asynchronous work improves decoupling but can increase completion latency.

review.issue: Exactly once and ordering treated as universal impossibilities.
review.correction: Distinguish broker delivery from transactional processing and external effects; define ordering scope and available guarantees.

review.issue: Kafka relies on ZooKeeper today.
review.correction: Mark as historical; Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper mode in favor of KRaft. Consumer offsets are not simply coordinated in ZooKeeper.

exercise.prompt: Design asynchronous lecture-video transcoding with reliable user feedback.
exercise.answer: Accept durably and return a job ID; workers claim jobs and write results idempotently; update status after durable output; retry transient errors with backoff and isolate poison jobs; expose status and optional authenticated notification; apply backpressure when backlog exceeds limits.

units.title: Implicit invocation, pub/sub and event-driven systems
units.shortTitle: Implicit invocation, pub/sub and event-driven systems
units.description: Design event subscriptions, brokered delivery and recovery, then examine the ROS example.

chapters.title: From direct calls to implicit invocation
paragraphs: Imagine a debugger that stops at a breakpoint. A tightly coupled implementation calls the editor to highlight a line, calls the variables pane to refresh, and calls a history component to record the stop. Adding another view requires changing the debugger. With implicit invocation, the debugger announces that execution stopped and registered handlers decide how to react. The event carries enough context, such as the location and execution identifier, for each interested component. The producer now depends on the event contract rather than every view's implementation. Draw one event leaving the debugger and several reactions branching from it. This makes extension easier while preserving an explicit description of what happened and which information accompanies it.

With a direct call, the caller names the operation it wants another component to perform. With implicit invocation, a component announces an event and registered handlers react. A debugger can announce that execution stopped, letting an editor highlight source without the debugger depending on that editor’s implementation. The same idea supports user-interface observers and database triggers inside a single application.

The same event abstraction can run synchronously inside one process. Calling an event dispatcher may invoke every handler before returning, so a slow handler still delays the producer. A distributed broker often introduces asynchronous delivery, but that is a connector choice rather than a definition of events. Ask what happens when a handler fails, whether other handlers still execute, and whether ordering is guaranteed. Without those answers, the simple fan-out diagram hides control-flow obligations. A debugger extension that throws an exception should not accidentally prevent the editor from updating unless that behavior is intentional. Trace a failed handler through the dispatch semantics and document the result; modularity requires a predictable interaction contract as well as separate components.

The connector determines dispatch semantics. An in-process event can invoke handlers synchronously, while a distributed event bus often delivers asynchronously. A publisher should not assume which subscribers exist or that they finish in a particular order unless the contract explicitly provides it. This enables extension and replacement, but makes the full chain of effects harder to see during debugging and error handling.
chapters.prediction: Must every implicit event invocation cross a network or run asynchronously?
chapters.explanation: No. A local connector can invoke handlers synchronously; distributed messaging is one specialization.

chapters.title: Event-driven architecture and brokered fan-out
paragraphs: When a course seat becomes available, a registration system can emit one event. A notification subscriber alerts waiting students, an analytics subscriber updates demand statistics, and an audit subscriber records the change. If all three need the event, they require independent subscriptions or equivalent fan-out semantics. Three competing workers sharing one work queue would instead divide the messages, so some reactions would never happen. Within the notification subscription, multiple workers can share the delivery workload. Draw these two levels separately: copies across responsibilities, competition within one responsibility. This distinction explains why the words producer and consumer do not by themselves tell you whether every service sees every event or whether each event goes to just one worker.

An event describes something that happened, such as a seat becoming available. Consumers can react independently: notify a student, update a dashboard or record an audit trail. A publisher-subscriber intermediary routes events to interested subscriptions, reducing the producer’s need to track every consumer address. Topics and filters let consumers select relevant changes without requiring a new direct integration for each interested service.

Suppose the seat event contains only a course code. A notification consumer may need to query another service for the section and availability version before it can act. Including more facts reduces that dependency but can increase payload size, privacy exposure, and schema evolution work. There is no contract-free event bus: every consumer relies on the meaning of fields and on rules for missing or changed fields. Use identifiers and versions to distinguish the event from the current entity state. If a requester requires a specific reply before proceeding, represent that obligation with correlation and a reply path. Hiding a required response inside an event does not remove the dependency; it only makes that dependency harder to observe and diagnose.

Decoupling does not erase contracts. Event fields, identifiers, versions and authorization rules remain shared responsibilities. Separate subscriptions can maintain their own progress, while competing workers within one subscription may share its load. Request/reply communication needs correlation identifiers and an explicit reply path when a caller requires a specific result. Choose that pattern deliberately rather than hiding a mandatory synchronous dependency behind an event.
chapters.prediction: If analytics and notifications both need each enrolment event, should they compete for a single work item?
chapters.explanation: No. They need independent subscriptions or equivalent fan-out so each receives the event stream.

chapters.title: Delivery, ordering and poison messages
paragraphs: Consider two events for a shipping address: version seven sets one address and version eight replaces it. A handler can deduplicate repeated event identifiers and still get the wrong result if version seven arrives after version eight with a different identifier. Record or compare the entity version when applying a change, or choose an ordered processing scope that preserves the required sequence. Idempotency answers whether the same logical event produces an extra effect; ordering answers whether different valid events produce the correct final state. Draw both the event identifier and entity version in a worked example. This prevents a common reasoning error where a system is called reliable simply because duplicates are ignored while stale updates can still overwrite newer information.

Subscribers must plan for duplicates, failures and delayed delivery. An idempotent handler prevents repeated execution from creating an extra effect, but it does not make out-of-order changes safe. Include entity versions or process related events in an ordered partition when sequence matters. A priority queue changes which message runs first; it is not a substitute for preserving business-event order.

A subscriber receives an event it cannot parse because a required field has an unexpected format. Immediate unlimited retries cannot repair that message and can crowd out valid work. After a bounded retry policy, move it to a dead-letter workflow that preserves the payload, failure reason, and diagnostic context. An operator or repair process can correct the cause and replay deliberately. Some messages should instead expire: an alert that a pickup is arriving may be useless hours after the trip ended. Each subscription needs its own lag monitoring because analytics may tolerate delay that notifications cannot. A successful publisher acknowledgement therefore says little about every downstream result. Observe progress and failure at the consumer responsibility where the useful effect is supposed to occur.

Repeatedly failing messages need bounded retries and a dead-letter workflow with diagnosis and controlled replay. Expiry prevents obsolete work from consuming resources, while scheduled availability postpones otherwise valid work. Monitor each subscription’s lag so one slow consumer is visible without blocking all others. Eventual consistency is an application choice with limits, especially when a stale view can authorize an irreversible action.
chapters.prediction: Does making a handler idempotent guarantee that version 4 cannot overwrite version 5?
chapters.explanation: No. Duplicate safety and ordering are different; compare versions or enforce the required sequence.

A handler can deduplicate repeated event identifiers and still get the wrong result if version seven arrives after version eight with a different identifier. Record or compare the entity version when applying a change, or choose an ordered processing scope that preserves the required sequence. Idempotency answers whether the same logical event produces an extra effect; ordering answers whether different valid events produce the correct final state. Draw both the event identifier and entity version in a worked example. This prevents a common reasoning error where a system is called reliable simply because duplicates are ignored while stale updates can still overwrite newer information. A subscriber receives an event it cannot parse because a required field has an unexpected format. Immediate unlimited retries cannot repair that message and can crowd out valid work. After a bounded retry policy, move it to a dead-letter workflow that preserves the payload, failure reason, and diagnostic context. An operator or repair process can correct the cause and replay deliberately. Some messages should instead expire: an alert that a pickup is arriving may be useless hours after the trip ended. Each subscription needs its own lag monitoring because analytics may tolerate delay that notifications cannot. A successful publisher acknowledgement therefore says little about every downstream result. Observe progress and failure at the consumer responsibility where the useful effect is supposed to occur.

chapters.title: ROS as an architectural example
paragraphs: A robot camera produces frames continuously, so a topic is a natural way to let perception and visualization subscribe independently. Asking for the current map is closer to a request with a result. Asking the robot to navigate to a destination is a longer goal that benefits from progress feedback and cancellation as well as a final outcome. These are different interaction contracts even if all are implemented with messages underneath. Draw the camera stream, map request, and navigation goal as different connectors between nodes. A single generic message arrow would conceal timing and completion expectations. Typed interfaces help components evolve independently, but the architect still has to choose what data and lifecycle each interaction promises.

The robotics example organizes computation into nodes with typed messages. Topics carry streams such as sensor readings, services provide request-and-response interactions, and actions support longer goals with progress and a final result. These interfaces let sensing, planning, control and visualization evolve separately while still communicating through explicit data contracts suited to their interaction patterns and timing needs.

Knowing that a camera node exists does not establish which frames must be retained, how quickly a controller needs them, or what to do when communication stops. A stale image and an emergency-stop command have different consequences, so their delivery and timing policies should not be copied blindly. The centralized registration component in the historical ROS 1 example illustrates naming and discovery; a different version can use a different discovery architecture while preserving the modular node idea. Keep these concerns separate in the diagram. After discovering a peer, a component still needs compatible interfaces, an appropriate communication policy, and defined failure behavior. For safety-related control, a communication abstraction alone is insufficient evidence that the complete system will meet its timing and safety requirements.

The central ROS Master in the slides describes ROS 1 naming and registration. ROS 2 commonly uses middleware discovery rather than that same central master architecture. Do not transfer every topology assumption across versions. A robot also requires deliberate delivery and timing policies: a fresh camera frame and an emergency stop do not have identical needs. Pub/sub modularity helps composition but does not establish safety by itself.

chapters.explanation: An action interface better expresses goal, feedback, cancellation/status and result; topics still carry ongoing observations.

quiz.answer: Independent subscriptions each receive relevant events; competing workers share processing within a delivery group or queue.

chapters.title: Distributed aggregates and data movement
paragraphs: Suppose three workers store sales records and their local maximum orders are eighty, one hundred twenty, and ninety dollars. To find the global maximum, each worker scans its own records and sends just one candidate. The coordinator compares three numbers and returns one hundred twenty. Shipping every original order to the coordinator would do far more network work without improving this result. The key is an algebraic property: the maximum of local maxima equals the maximum of the union. Draw computation beside each partition and only the candidates crossing the network. This reasoning explains why some analyses parallelize easily while others require substantially richer intermediate information or several rounds of communication.

Serving independent requests is different from calculating one answer over a large shared dataset. For a global maximum, each worker can compute a local maximum and send one candidate to a coordinator. The coordinator takes the maximum of those candidates, so little data moves. Other operations need richer summaries or repeated communication, making network cost part of algorithm design rather than an incidental implementation detail.

Means reveal why the summary matters. Suppose one partition contains one order worth ten dollars and another contains nine orders totaling nine hundred dollars. Averaging their local means gives fifty-five dollars, which is wrong because it gives the partitions equal weight. Send each partition's sum and count instead; the global mean is nine hundred ten divided by ten, or ninety-one dollars. An exact median is harder still: local medians alone generally do not determine the global median. A pivot method asks every partition how many values lie below, equal to, and above a candidate, then narrows the target rank. Before selecting a framework, derive what information must cross partitions for the answer to remain correct.

For a mean, combine sums and counts instead of averaging unequal-sized partitions’ means. Exact median selection is more involved: a pivot-based algorithm counts values below, equal to and above the pivot and narrows the target rank. Duplicates and even-sized inputs require explicit treatment. Hardware bandwidth examples provide lower bounds only under stated assumptions; use decimal petabytes consistently or label binary units correctly.

chapters.title: MapReduce and finite batch jobs
paragraphs: Count words in two documents: the first says red blue red, and the second says blue green. Each mapper emits a word and one for each occurrence. The shuffle groups all values with the same word, regardless of which document produced them. Reducers then add the grouped values, producing red two, blue two, and green one. Draw the blue emissions from both documents converging on the same group. This is the important step: the programmer's chosen intermediate key tells the framework which information must meet. The framework handles distribution and grouping, while the mapper and reducer define the calculation. An incorrect key can produce an efficient parallel job that answers the wrong question.

MapReduce asks a programmer to transform input records into intermediate key-value pairs, then combine values sharing a key. For word counting, the mapper emits one pair per word occurrence and the reducer sums counts for each word. The shuffle groups intermediate data by key. Scheduling, distribution and retries belong largely to the framework, so the program can focus on the transformations.

A batch job has a finite input and eventually completes, but its tasks may execute on many machines at once. Scheduling a mapper near its input reduces the need to move the raw data. The shuffle can still be expensive because records with matching keys must meet across partitions. If one word dominates the corpus, the corresponding reducer may become a bottleneck even when the input is evenly divided. Chaining jobs creates more intermediate datasets and communication stages, so sketch those intermediates before assuming that more machines solve the problem. Retries also matter: a failed task may run again, which is safe for framework-managed results under its contract but needs additional care for external side effects such as sending messages.

A batch job works on a bounded input and eventually finishes; it does not imply sequential execution. Multiple tasks can run in parallel, and several jobs can be chained through intermediate results. Data locality can reduce traffic, but shuffle still transfers information among workers. A skewed key can overload a reducer, and retried tasks mean side effects outside the framework need careful design.
chapters.prediction: What happens if the mapper returns immediately on the first word inside its loop?
chapters.explanation: It counts only the first word; it must emit or accumulate a pair for every occurrence.

chapters.title: Continuous streams and state
paragraphs: A dashboard showing orders per minute cannot wait for the entire order stream to finish, because new orders keep arriving. It defines a window and produces an answer for that bounded interval while processing continues. Now let an order happen at 12:00:58 but reach the processor at 12:01:04 after a network delay. Event time places it in the earlier minute; arrival time places it in the later one. Choose which meaning the dashboard requires, then define whether a previously emitted count can be corrected. Calling the system real time does not answer those questions. The architecture needs explicit rules for window boundaries, late data, and the freshness the user can reasonably expect.

Stream processing reacts to an ongoing sequence rather than waiting for a complete dataset. Monitoring and recommendations may benefit from short update latency, while historical reporting can tolerate larger batch intervals. Low latency is a target, not an automatic guarantee. A stream operator may still wait for enough evidence, and overloaded consumers can accumulate lag even when the architecture is called real time.

A stream counter remembers partial results between messages. If it crashes after adding an order but before recording its input position, a restart may read that order again. If it records the position first and loses the counter update, it may skip the order instead. Recovery must coordinate the state with the consumed position under a defined processing contract. Checkpointing and replay are common building blocks, while external effects need their own idempotency or transaction design. A fast operator can also accumulate lag when arrivals exceed its capacity, so low latency is an operating condition rather than a label. Compare a nightly batch report and a continuously updated dashboard on their required freshness and recovery costs, not on whether either can process large data.

Stateful stream computations need rules for windows, late arrivals, duplicates and recovery. Distinguish event time from the time a processor receives the event. The slides introduce Storm through sources and processing components; treat ease-of-operation and feature comparisons as contextual rather than universal. Compare batch and streaming on freshness, boundedness and operational requirements, not on the assumption that one handles large data and the other does not.

chapters.title: The thread-pool Leader/Followers pattern
paragraphs: Imagine three threads sharing an event source. Thread A is the leader waiting for the next event while B and C are followers. When an event arrives, A arranges for a follower to become the new leader, then handles the event itself. B can now wait for another event while A performs application work. Draw leadership as a role that moves between threads, not as a permanently special machine. The handoff avoids having every waiting thread compete unnecessarily for the same event notification. The design also keeps event waiting separate from potentially slower handling. Its value depends on the event system and workload, so the performance argument should identify which coordination or scheduling overhead is actually reduced.

The Leader/Followers concurrency pattern coordinates a pool of threads waiting for events. One thread leads by waiting on an event source; when an event arrives, another follower can become leader while the previous leader handles the work. The purpose is efficient event dispatch with controlled coordination overhead, not replication of durable data across a cluster of machines.

Now compare this thread pool with a replicated database. The thread-pool leader waits on an event source and coordinates dispatch within a process. A database leader may accept writes and coordinate durable state across machines. Replacing a waiting thread does not solve replica agreement after a network partition, and it does not imply that acknowledged data survives a machine failure. Keeping the two meanings separate prevents an architecture explanation from borrowing guarantees from an unrelated pattern. Within the thread pool, still examine what happens if a handler blocks, whether another thread can continue receiving events, and how cancellation works. Correct handoff protects the shared event source; it is not a substitute for timeouts or bounded work in the handlers.

Correct handoff protects shared event sources and avoids having every thread compete for the same notification. Benefits depend on workload and runtime, and a blocked handler still needs appropriate timeout or cancellation behavior. Do not import distributed consensus claims into this thread-pool pattern: a new leading thread is not equivalent to safely electing a database leader after a network partition. Distinguish the two before discussing fault tolerance.
chapters.prediction: Does promoting another waiting thread provide replicated durability after machine failure?
chapters.explanation: No. Thread leadership manages local concurrency; durable distributed recovery is a separate design.

chapters.title: Kafka partition leaders and replicated logs
paragraphs: A partitioned log divides records among several ordered sequences. Each partition can have a leader handling its operations and followers copying its records. Different brokers can lead different partitions, so leadership is distributed across the cluster rather than concentrated in one universal writer. Within a partition, record positions provide an order and consumers track their progress. Across partitions, there is no automatic single global order. For order events, using the order identifier as the partitioning key can keep one order's sequence together while unrelated orders proceed in parallel. Draw partition boundaries before drawing leader and follower arrows. Otherwise a diagram with several brokers can misleadingly suggest that every record is ordered against every other record in the entire system.

Kafka illustrates a different use of leader and follower terminology. A partition has a leader responsible for its log operations and replica followers that copy its data. Leadership can move after failure under a cluster coordination policy. Several partitions can distribute leadership across brokers, so one leader per partition does not mean the entire system has only one active writer.

Suppose a leader accepts a record and fails before a follower receives it. Whether an acknowledged record can be lost depends on the acknowledgement and election rules, not merely on the presence of a follower box in the diagram. A lagging replica should not be treated as an equally current replacement without considering the durability consequence. Downstream, a payment worker can read a safely replicated record and still crash around an external charge. Log durability and effect correctness are separate boundaries. Trace the record from producer acknowledgement through replication, consumption, and external result. The historical coordination service shown in older diagrams is an implementation detail of that version; preserve the reasoning about leadership, progress, and failure rather than assuming the topology never changes.

Durability and availability depend on acknowledgements, in-sync replicas and election policy; replication alone is not an unconditional guarantee. A lagging replica may be unsuitable for safe promotion. The slides’ ZooKeeper control-plane account is historical, while Kafka 4 uses KRaft. For the e-commerce analytics example, distinguish ingestion durability from successful downstream computation and from committing external business effects exactly once.

chapters.explanation: No. Its synchronization state and the configured election and acknowledgement policies matter.

quiz.question: How do you compute a global mean from partitions with unequal record counts?
quiz.answer: Sum all partition sums and divide by the sum of their counts.

quiz.question: Why does batch processing not imply sequential processing?
quiz.answer: Batch refers to bounded input and a finishing job; many map/reduce tasks can execute in parallel.

quiz.question: How do the two leader–follower meanings differ?
quiz.answer: One coordinates event-handling threads locally; the other replicates partition logs across brokers and requires distributed failure policies.

review.issue: Old volume forecasts and incorrect units/arithmetic formatting.
review.correction: Mark forecasts historical. PB is 10^15 bytes; PiB is 2^50. With the assumed 80 GB/s, 10^16/(80×10^9)=125000 seconds, about 34.7 hours; do not assert a universal PCIe maximum.

review.issue: Mean and median oversimplified.
review.correction: Combine sums/counts for mean. Median selection needs target rank, equality handling and a defined even-cardinality policy.

review.issue: return inside word loop stops mapping early.
review.correction: Emit each (word,1) pair or return a completed list after the loop.

review.issue: Batch sequential and product feature judgments universal.
review.correction: Bounded batch work can be parallel; treat Storm feature/operability claims as version- and workload-dependent.

review.issue: Thread pattern conflated with distributed replica leadership.
review.correction: Teach them separately; local thread promotion is not distributed consensus or machine-failure durability.

review.issue: ZooKeeper is the current Kafka coordinator.
review.correction: Label historical; Kafka 4.0 uses KRaft and removed ZooKeeper mode.

review.issue: Replication guarantees consistency and availability without qualification.
review.correction: State acknowledgements, in-sync replica and election assumptions; end-to-end processing needs its own correctness contract.

exercise.prompt: Design enrolment analytics with a nightly historical report and a live dashboard. Explain recovery and the leadership pattern involved.
exercise.answer: Run a bounded batch aggregation for the historical report and a stateful streaming projection for the dashboard. Partition events by an appropriate entity, define event-time/late-data handling, checkpoint progress and make outputs replay-safe. Broker partition leaders replicate logs; a local event-loop thread pool, if used, solves a different concurrency problem.
